Vote No on Prop 45: Rolling Back CEQA Is A Proposition Californians Can’t Afford
October 29, 2026 (https://www.greenbelt.org/2026/10/29/)
CEQA (https://www.greenbelt.org/tag/ceqa/), Voter Guide (https://www.greenbelt.org/tag/voter-guide/)
Updated on October 29 to include links. Originally published on January 16, 2026.
For advocates working at the intersection of environmental protection and climate-smart growth, theCalifornia Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) (https://www.greenbelt.org/land-use-planning-dictionary/california-environmental-quality-act/) has long been a source of both pride and frustration. While it has been a critical tool to protect our natural and working lands, its procedural delays have often been used to stall projects essential to a low-carbon future: dense infill (https://www.greenbelt.org/land-use-planning-dictionary/infill-development/) housing and transit-oriented development (https://www.greenbelt.org/land-use-planning-dictionary/transit-oriented-development/) in our existing communities.
In July 2025, however, at the urging of Governor Newsom, the California legislature passed some of the most impactful changes to CEQA (https://www.greenbelt.org/blog/ceqa-reform-explainer/) since its inception. Taken together, the two bills (AB 130 and SB 131) provide robust statutory CEQA exemptions for infill housing and housing element rezonings, require the state to map infill areas where exemptions would apply, and narrow the scope of the administrative record, helping to curtail anti-housing litigation.
Read my Op-Ed in the East Bay Times on why Prop 45 is a ruse handing shortcuts to polluters disguised as relief. (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/09/12/opinion-vote-no-prop-45-would-take-away-our-best-defense-against-corporate-polluters/amp/)
Check out some highlights of Greenbelt Alliance’s commentary in local and regional press:
Prop. 45: Will California Vote to Trade Environmental Regulation for Quicker Housing Development? – Forum KQED (https://www.kqed.org/forum/2010101915583/prop-45-will-california-vote-to-trade-environmental-regulation-for-quicker-housing-development)
Will Prop. 45 Fix California’s Housing Crisis or Roll Back a Valuable Environmental Law? – Political Breakdown KQED (https://www.kqed.org/news/12101722/will-prop-45-fix-californias-housing-crisis-or-roll-back-a-valuable-environmental-law)
Why are pro-housing groups split on Proposition 45? – CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/10/yimby-prop-45-ceqa/)
Sonoma County stakeholders, cities eye Prop. 45’s potential to broadly reform California’s bedrock environmental law – The Press Democrat (https://www.pressdemocrat.com/2026/10/26/prop-45-california-sonoma-county-housing-environment/)
Despite these monumental changes that address the barriers to critical infill development, California’s business lobby and sprawl developers were left unsatisfied. Now, they are proposing a ballot initiative that would make far more radical changes to the law. After gathering enough signatures to qualify for the November ballot, this is now called Proposition 45.
While the rhetoric of the measure (initially called Building an Affordable California Act, or BACA (https://advocacy.calchamber.com/2025/12/17/calchambers-ceqa-reform-boosting-californias-economy-and-state-budget/) ) seems to be aligned with urbanist goals and those of the broader abundance and affordability movements, the actual policy details and mechanics of the initiative—and the progress we’ve already achieved in the legislature (https://www.greenbelt.org/blog/2025-legislative-priorities/) last year—suggest that the costs it brings far outweigh any potential benefits.
Below, we outline seven reasons why the measure should be rejected (click to read more):
1. Major Reforms Have Already Been Enacted
For years, a primary objective for California’s urbanists was to stop the abuse of environmental law against projects that genuinely help the environment: dense, transit-oriented housing.
In a landmark shift for the state, that goal has largely been realized. Following years of advocacy by urbanists, the legislature passed a clean statutory CEQA exemption for infill housing. AB 130, which Greenbelt Alliance was proud to support (https://www.greenbelt.org/blog/ceqa-reform-ca/), is already being utilized across California, allowing builders to move forward with climate-friendly housing in high-opportunity areas like Palo Alto or Beverly Hills without the threat of being endlessly delayed by the environmental review process. While there is room for technical refinements, the fundamental issue at hand—the misuse of environmental laws to delay environmentally-friendly housing projects—has largely been addressed.
2. Everything is “Essential”
As the saying goes, “the devil is in the details”, and that’s certainly true for the BACA initiative. While modest on the surface, BACA creates a completely new set of rules for what it calls “essential” projects. So what, exactly, is an “essential project”?
The list is incredibly broad. Under Article 2, Section 21013, “essential projects” include housing, water, transportation, clean energy, transmission, broadband, and healthcare infrastructure. In practice, this definition encompasses a wide range of large-scale developments. For example, new freeways and existing freeway expansions would qualify as “essential transportation” projects; large greenfield sprawl developments would be treated as “essential” housing projects; and new dams and reservoirs would qualify as “essential” water projects. The definition even includes all “related and ancillary infrastructure,” meaning that highway interchanges, utility extensions, and water pipelines that enable sprawl developments also receive streamlined approval. All of these are enormous projects in terms of size and scale, with major potential environmental impacts. Yet, just like an apartment building in an urban area, under BACA, they would qualify for a significantly truncated review process.
In effect, this new CEQA process mirrors the fundamental flaw of its predecessor. While the old system failed to exempt low or no-impact projects from excessive review, the new one errs in the opposite direction, fast-tracking high-risk developments with significant potential for harm.
3. All Timelines Are Not Created Equal
The BACA initiative imposes strict timelines for this new class of projects that it deems “essential”: the environmental review process can take no more than one year. On the surface, a one-year limit on an Environmental Impact Report (EIR) seems reasonable. And for certain projects, like an apartment building on a parking lot in downtown San Francisco, or a townhome development in an LA suburb, it would be.
However, the measure’s definition of “essential” includes highways, dams, large-scale subdivisions, and other major projects. The environmental review required for projects at this scale cannot be done in a single year. Surveying hundreds if not thousands (or even tens of thousands) of acres of undisturbed and undeveloped land for species nesting patterns and habitat, water pollution impacts, and other environmental concerns physically cannot be accomplished within the timeframe laid out in the initiative. By forcing these projects into such a condensed timeline, we will be creating a system that overlooks genuine environmental harm in favor of speed.
For projects with unambiguous environmental benefits, such as housing developments within already urbanized areas, such speed makes sense. Many of the project types considered by this measure do not have the same clear, unambiguous benefits.
4. Restrictive Alternatives
One of CEQA’s most critical tools for preventing environmental harm is its alternative analysis provision, which allows for the identification of better project locations and designs. Currently, CEQA requires agencies to analyze a “reasonable range of alternatives” that could reduce environmental impacts, including different sites, reduced intensity options, and designs that avoid sensitive resources. This is how agencies can say, “this housing should be built downtown on a parking lot instead of on farmland,” or “this highway expansion has an alternative transit solution.”
BACA restricts this to just three options: the proposed project, one alternative designed by the applicant themselves (which doesn’t even need to be at a different location), and “no project.” The applicant’s alternative can be a slightly modified version of their original proposal on the same site. This eliminates the core mechanism for steering projects away from environmentally sensitive locations toward more appropriate sites, exactly the tool needed to prevent sprawl, protect open space, and ensure development happens in the right places.
5. The Evidentiary Standard
Maybe the most radical change incorporated in the ballot measure is to CEQA’s standard of review. Right now, CEQA allows a lead agency (generally a city or county) to use its own discretion to explore project alternatives and negotiate environmental mitigations. BACA proposes to eliminate this by requiring that environmental impacts only be found significant if they violate objective, quantifiable standards already in existing law when the project was proposed, which doesn’t sound inherently unreasonable!
However, the measure doesn’t actually require jurisdictions to adopt such standards; instead, it exploits their absence. If numerical thresholds don’t already exist for resources like oak woodlands, groundwater, or wildlife corridors, impacts to them essentially can’t be found significant regardless of severity. A genuine objective standards approach would mandate jurisdictions adopt protective thresholds and update them as science improves. This measure rewards weak standards, freezes them at application date, and prevents improvements based on new knowledge.
6. Ballot Box Permanence
Finally, one of the greatest flaws of the measure is its rigidity. Should it pass, BACA would require a 2/3rds vote of the legislature to amend.
California has a long, storied history with ballot box governance, where initiatives become impossible to adjust as new problems arise. The 2/3rds requirement virtually guarantees the law could never be changed, regardless of what issues may arise. An unchangeable measure, with foreseeable negative impacts for the state, may have lasting consequences for generations.
Some of the project types included in this measure, such as clean energy or transmission infrastructure, may benefit from the types of streamlining being considered if careful, targeted changes were made. Rather than a broad, clunky initiative that will be extremely difficult to change, we should advocate for those reforms through the legislative cleanup process already underway.
7. The Costs Are Just Too High
California faces converging affordability crises: insurers fleeing the state, utility rates climbing, and municipal budgets straining under unsustainable costs. All of these issues stem from the same source: decades of sprawling outward, often into fire-prone areas, leaving us with infrastructure we cannot afford to maintain and risks we cannot afford to insure.
BACA will accelerate these failures by trading short-term speed for permanent costs. By gutting CEQA’s alternatives analysis—the primary tool for steering projects away from costly, high-risk locations—this limits agencies to the developer’s preferred site, one alternative the developer designs themselves, and “no project.” It freezes environmental standards at the date of application, rewarding jurisdictions with weak protections. And it requires agencies to approve permits within strict timelines regardless of fiscal consequences, because most cities lack the quantitative standards BACA requires to find fiscal impacts “significant.”
The result: even if we build some things faster today, we’ll be paying the tab forever. Even more homes in fire zones will continue to destabilize our insurance markets. More infrastructure extensions will push up our utility rates. More sprawling subdivisions that generate less revenue than they cost to maintain will ensure even higher taxes. BACA promises affordability through speed but delivers the opposite: cheaper to build, but financially ruinous to sustain.
At a time when people are struggling to make ends meet, and when the federal government is doing all it can to roll back our environmental protections, the last thing we need is to double down on the failed policies we have tried for decades and know do not work.
Proposition 45 will hurt the environment and your wallet.
Greenbelt Alliance strongly opposes Proposition 45 and urges voters to vote NO on 45 this November.

California voters considering Proposition 45 (https://calmatters.org/newsletter/prop-45-yimby/) will decide the fate of a sweeping infrastructure measure that opponents warn could render the state’s brand-new data center laws virtually toothless. That would make it far easier for developers to force unwanted facilities into local communities, potentially undermining a growing wave of bans, moratoriums, and anti-data-center resolutions (https://calmatters.org/economy/technology/2026/10/california-data-centers-hit-with-local-regulation-flood/) at the city and county level. Data center backers insist the ballot measure will do nothing for them — even as some data center beneficiaries are spending big backing Prop. 45. Supporters have framed Prop. 45 as a tool to accelerate critical infrastructure projects (https://calmatters.org/environment/2026/10/prop-45-california-ceqa-explained/), like housing and schools, and the measure does not directly name data centers among the sorts of projects it considers critical. But some legal scholars and environmental advocates say that the proposition’s technical language creates a loophole. By expediting environmental reviews under the California Environmental Quality Act (https://calmatters.org/environment/2026/10/prop-45-california-ceqa-explained/) for broad categories of projects — including broadband internet facilities and any additional infrastructure required to get them up and running — the measure could quietly allow data centers to bypass recent state safeguards and local scrutiny. Julia Stein, a legal scholar and deputy director at UCLA School of Law’s Emmett Institute on Climate Change and the Environment, warns that the measure acts as a “blunt force instrument when it comes to streamlining” because of how wide its secondary umbrella extends. “What Prop. 45 does is designate an entire class of projects that would be subject to streamlining, and then it also says that projects ancillary to those projects — so something that you might need to do in the course of the development of the project that’s exempted itself — would fall within that same streamlining bubble,” Stein said. Telecommunications projects are explicitly streamlined under the proposition, “and there’s an argument that the development of data centers might be necessary for projects like that,” Stein added. MORE ON DATA CENTERS California cities pull the plug on data centers after state regulations don’t scale up fast enough (https://calmatters.org/economy/technology/2026/10/california-data-centers-hit-with-local-regulation-flood/) October 22, 2026 October 22, 2026 Other projects, like high-speed rail, are explicitly excluded from streamlining under the proposition — but data centers are not on that list, either. Stein and three other environmental law scholars told CalMatters that this opens the door for legal challenges. “The fact that they excluded some projects but have not expressly excluded data centers, a court would probably actually interpret that not as an unintentional oversight, but rather as intent to include data centers in the initiative,” said Matt McKerley, an attorney with Shute, Mihaly and Weinberger. Further, opponents argue that the proposition’s language, which includes a clause that it would supersede other related laws, would override measures like the recently-passed Senate Bill 887 (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb887), which made it harder to fast-track environmental review for data centers. Industry representatives say these objections to Prop. 45 are misplaced. The Data Center Coalition, an industry group supporting Prop. 45, insists their facilities fall outside the initiative’s scope, which focuses largely on housing development (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/10/yimby-prop-45-ceqa/) ad other infrastructure like roads and bridges. Industry representatives also point to a recent legal opinion memo (https://yesonprop45.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/legopinion_DataCenter.pdf) from California’s Office of Legislative Counsel, which provides legal services to members of the Legislature. The memo argues that Prop. 45’s statutory definitions do not apply to data centers. Amelia Matier, from the Yes on 45 campaign, echoed that take, saying, “Data centers are not included in Prop 45.” She added: “The defenders of California’s unaffordable status quo are desperate to distract voters with lies because they cannot defend the costly delays and red tape driving up prices for working families. ” Opponents of the measure include the California Labor Federation, Western Center on Law & Poverty, and various environmental advocacy groups that have spent more than $31 million dollars pushing back against the measure. Despite maintaining that data centers fall outside the proposition’s reach, tech and utility interests benefiting from California’s computing boom are putting massive financial weight (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-45-modifies-environmental-review-certain-projects-initiative-statute) behind its passage. Proponents have poured over $40 million into the Yes on Prop. 45 campaign, including $3.05 million from utility giant PG&E and $500,000 from warehouse and data center developer Prologis — a cash influx that opponents argue reveals who truly expects to profit if the measure passes. The debate over Prop. 45’s data center impact comes at a pivotal moment in California’s AI infrastructure boom. Gov. Gavin Newsom recently signed seven landmark data center laws (https://calmatters.org/economy/technology/2026/09/new-california-laws-data-centers/) aimed at forcing operators to disclose water usage, pay for their own grid upgrades, and undergo environmental review. Yet local communities aren’t waiting for state regulations to take effect. Amid rising fears of rate hikes, grid overload, and water depletion, grassroots opposition has erupted across California. At least 26 cities and counties have proposed or passed moratoriums, bans, or strict limits aimed to stop data center development (https://calmatters.org/economy/technology/2026/10/california-data-centers-hit-with-local-regulation-flood/) in their communities. Why Circulate Planning & Policy Supports Prop 45
California's cost of living is out of control because our outdated system for approving essential projects is too slow, too bureaucratic, and too costly—making it harder to build the housing, transit, and other infrastructure our communities depend on. These unnecessary delays drive up costs for families, businesses, and taxpayers while making California less affordable for everyone.
That's why Circulate supports Prop 45, the Building an Affordable California Act (https://yesonprop45.com/) on the November 2026 ballot.
Prop 45 creates clear, enforceable timelines for environmental review, agency permitting, and judicial review for eligible projects. Rather than allowing projects to become trapped in years of bureaucratic delay and costly litigation, Prop 45 establishes accountability from application through final court decisions. By creating certainty throughout the approval process, the measure is expected to accelerate essential projects by 2 to 10 or more years, reducing costs and delivering benefits to Californians sooner.
Just as importantly, Prop 45 does not eliminate environmental review or weaken environmental protections. Every eligible project must still comply with the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) and all applicable federal, state, and local environmental laws and regulations. The measure simply ensures that environmental review, permitting decisions, and any legal challenges are completed within reasonable, enforceable deadlines instead of dragging on indefinitely.
For too long, unnecessary delays have increased the cost of nearly everything Californians rely on. Permitting delays can add years to building timelines, forcing families to wait even longer to realize the benefits of affordable housing. Further, permitting delays alone add more than $75,000 to the cost of a new home. Prop 45 cuts unnecessary red tape, lowers project costs, and helps deliver the infrastructure Californians need faster. This means California will be able to more quickly deliver affordable housing that strengthens our communities and economy.
Prop 45 also preserves local control. Cities and counties retain their authority to approve or deny projects, and Californians continue to have meaningful opportunities to participate throughout the project approval process. The measure creates a process that is faster, fairer, and more predictable—not one that sacrifices accountability or environmental protections.
More than 145 organizations (https://yesonprop45.com/our-coalition/) representing affordable housing, healthcare, water providers, agricultural producers, clean energy leaders, social justice advocates, and small business leaders support Prop 45 because California cannot afford to keep delaying the essential projects that improve quality of life and make our state more affordable.
California deserves a permitting system that protects the environment and delivers the infrastructure families, workers, businesses, and communities need.
Learn more about Prop 45 at: www.YesOnProp45.com (http://www.yesonprop45.com/)

Why Circulate Planning & Policy Supports Prop 45
California's cost of living is out of control because our outdated system for approving essential projects is too slow, too bureaucratic, and too costly—making it harder to build the housing, transit, and other infrastructure our communities depend on. These unnecessary delays drive up costs for families, businesses, and taxpayers while making California less affordable for everyone.
That's why Circulate supports Prop 45, the Building an Affordable California Act (https://yesonprop45.com/) on the November 2026 ballot.
Prop 45 creates clear, enforceable timelines for environmental review, agency permitting, and judicial review for eligible projects. Rather than allowing projects to become trapped in years of bureaucratic delay and costly litigation, Prop 45 establishes accountability from application through final court decisions. By creating certainty throughout the approval process, the measure is expected to accelerate essential projects by 2 to 10 or more years, reducing costs and delivering benefits to Californians sooner.
Just as importantly, Prop 45 does not eliminate environmental review or weaken environmental protections. Every eligible project must still comply with the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) and all applicable federal, state, and local environmental laws and regulations. The measure simply ensures that environmental review, permitting decisions, and any legal challenges are completed within reasonable, enforceable deadlines instead of dragging on indefinitely.
For too long, unnecessary delays have increased the cost of nearly everything Californians rely on. Permitting delays can add years to building timelines, forcing families to wait even longer to realize the benefits of affordable housing. Further, permitting delays alone add more than $75,000 to the cost of a new home. Prop 45 cuts unnecessary red tape, lowers project costs, and helps deliver the infrastructure Californians need faster. This means California will be able to more quickly deliver affordable housing that strengthens our communities and economy.
Prop 45 also preserves local control. Cities and counties retain their authority to approve or deny projects, and Californians continue to have meaningful opportunities to participate throughout the project approval process. The measure creates a process that is faster, fairer, and more predictable—not one that sacrifices accountability or environmental protections.
More than 145 organizations (https://yesonprop45.com/our-coalition/) representing affordable housing, healthcare, water providers, agricultural producers, clean energy leaders, social justice advocates, and small business leaders support Prop 45 because California cannot afford to keep delaying the essential projects that improve quality of life and make our state more affordable.
California deserves a permitting system that protects the environment and delivers the infrastructure families, workers, businesses, and communities need.
Learn more about Prop 45 at: www.YesOnProp45.com (http://www.yesonprop45.com/)

Vote No on Prop 45: Rolling Back CEQA Is A Proposition Californians Can’t Afford
October 29, 2026 (https://www.greenbelt.org/2026/10/29/)
CEQA (https://www.greenbelt.org/tag/ceqa/), Voter Guide (https://www.greenbelt.org/tag/voter-guide/)
Updated on October 29 to include links. Originally published on January 16, 2026.
For advocates working at the intersection of environmental protection and climate-smart growth, theCalifornia Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) (https://www.greenbelt.org/land-use-planning-dictionary/california-environmental-quality-act/) has long been a source of both pride and frustration. While it has been a critical tool to protect our natural and working lands, its procedural delays have often been used to stall projects essential to a low-carbon future: dense infill (https://www.greenbelt.org/land-use-planning-dictionary/infill-development/) housing and transit-oriented development (https://www.greenbelt.org/land-use-planning-dictionary/transit-oriented-development/) in our existing communities.
In July 2025, however, at the urging of Governor Newsom, the California legislature passed some of the most impactful changes to CEQA (https://www.greenbelt.org/blog/ceqa-reform-explainer/) since its inception. Taken together, the two bills (AB 130 and SB 131) provide robust statutory CEQA exemptions for infill housing and housing element rezonings, require the state to map infill areas where exemptions would apply, and narrow the scope of the administrative record, helping to curtail anti-housing litigation.
Read my Op-Ed in the East Bay Times on why Prop 45 is a ruse handing shortcuts to polluters disguised as relief. (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/09/12/opinion-vote-no-prop-45-would-take-away-our-best-defense-against-corporate-polluters/amp/)
Check out some highlights of Greenbelt Alliance’s commentary in local and regional press:
Prop. 45: Will California Vote to Trade Environmental Regulation for Quicker Housing Development? – Forum KQED (https://www.kqed.org/forum/2010101915583/prop-45-will-california-vote-to-trade-environmental-regulation-for-quicker-housing-development)
Will Prop. 45 Fix California’s Housing Crisis or Roll Back a Valuable Environmental Law? – Political Breakdown KQED (https://www.kqed.org/news/12101722/will-prop-45-fix-californias-housing-crisis-or-roll-back-a-valuable-environmental-law)
Why are pro-housing groups split on Proposition 45? – CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/10/yimby-prop-45-ceqa/)
Sonoma County stakeholders, cities eye Prop. 45’s potential to broadly reform California’s bedrock environmental law – The Press Democrat (https://www.pressdemocrat.com/2026/10/26/prop-45-california-sonoma-county-housing-environment/)
Despite these monumental changes that address the barriers to critical infill development, California’s business lobby and sprawl developers were left unsatisfied. Now, they are proposing a ballot initiative that would make far more radical changes to the law. After gathering enough signatures to qualify for the November ballot, this is now called Proposition 45.
While the rhetoric of the measure (initially called Building an Affordable California Act, or BACA (https://advocacy.calchamber.com/2025/12/17/calchambers-ceqa-reform-boosting-californias-economy-and-state-budget/) ) seems to be aligned with urbanist goals and those of the broader abundance and affordability movements, the actual policy details and mechanics of the initiative—and the progress we’ve already achieved in the legislature (https://www.greenbelt.org/blog/2025-legislative-priorities/) last year—suggest that the costs it brings far outweigh any potential benefits.
Below, we outline seven reasons why the measure should be rejected (click to read more):
1. Major Reforms Have Already Been Enacted
For years, a primary objective for California’s urbanists was to stop the abuse of environmental law against projects that genuinely help the environment: dense, transit-oriented housing.
In a landmark shift for the state, that goal has largely been realized. Following years of advocacy by urbanists, the legislature passed a clean statutory CEQA exemption for infill housing. AB 130, which Greenbelt Alliance was proud to support (https://www.greenbelt.org/blog/ceqa-reform-ca/), is already being utilized across California, allowing builders to move forward with climate-friendly housing in high-opportunity areas like Palo Alto or Beverly Hills without the threat of being endlessly delayed by the environmental review process. While there is room for technical refinements, the fundamental issue at hand—the misuse of environmental laws to delay environmentally-friendly housing projects—has largely been addressed.
2. Everything is “Essential”
As the saying goes, “the devil is in the details”, and that’s certainly true for the BACA initiative. While modest on the surface, BACA creates a completely new set of rules for what it calls “essential” projects. So what, exactly, is an “essential project”?
The list is incredibly broad. Under Article 2, Section 21013, “essential projects” include housing, water, transportation, clean energy, transmission, broadband, and healthcare infrastructure. In practice, this definition encompasses a wide range of large-scale developments. For example, new freeways and existing freeway expansions would qualify as “essential transportation” projects; large greenfield sprawl developments would be treated as “essential” housing projects; and new dams and reservoirs would qualify as “essential” water projects. The definition even includes all “related and ancillary infrastructure,” meaning that highway interchanges, utility extensions, and water pipelines that enable sprawl developments also receive streamlined approval. All of these are enormous projects in terms of size and scale, with major potential environmental impacts. Yet, just like an apartment building in an urban area, under BACA, they would qualify for a significantly truncated review process.
In effect, this new CEQA process mirrors the fundamental flaw of its predecessor. While the old system failed to exempt low or no-impact projects from excessive review, the new one errs in the opposite direction, fast-tracking high-risk developments with significant potential for harm.
3. All Timelines Are Not Created Equal
The BACA initiative imposes strict timelines for this new class of projects that it deems “essential”: the environmental review process can take no more than one year. On the surface, a one-year limit on an Environmental Impact Report (EIR) seems reasonable. And for certain projects, like an apartment building on a parking lot in downtown San Francisco, or a townhome development in an LA suburb, it would be.
However, the measure’s definition of “essential” includes highways, dams, large-scale subdivisions, and other major projects. The environmental review required for projects at this scale cannot be done in a single year. Surveying hundreds if not thousands (or even tens of thousands) of acres of undisturbed and undeveloped land for species nesting patterns and habitat, water pollution impacts, and other environmental concerns physically cannot be accomplished within the timeframe laid out in the initiative. By forcing these projects into such a condensed timeline, we will be creating a system that overlooks genuine environmental harm in favor of speed.
For projects with unambiguous environmental benefits, such as housing developments within already urbanized areas, such speed makes sense. Many of the project types considered by this measure do not have the same clear, unambiguous benefits.
4. Restrictive Alternatives
One of CEQA’s most critical tools for preventing environmental harm is its alternative analysis provision, which allows for the identification of better project locations and designs. Currently, CEQA requires agencies to analyze a “reasonable range of alternatives” that could reduce environmental impacts, including different sites, reduced intensity options, and designs that avoid sensitive resources. This is how agencies can say, “this housing should be built downtown on a parking lot instead of on farmland,” or “this highway expansion has an alternative transit solution.”
BACA restricts this to just three options: the proposed project, one alternative designed by the applicant themselves (which doesn’t even need to be at a different location), and “no project.” The applicant’s alternative can be a slightly modified version of their original proposal on the same site. This eliminates the core mechanism for steering projects away from environmentally sensitive locations toward more appropriate sites, exactly the tool needed to prevent sprawl, protect open space, and ensure development happens in the right places.
5. The Evidentiary Standard
Maybe the most radical change incorporated in the ballot measure is to CEQA’s standard of review. Right now, CEQA allows a lead agency (generally a city or county) to use its own discretion to explore project alternatives and negotiate environmental mitigations. BACA proposes to eliminate this by requiring that environmental impacts only be found significant if they violate objective, quantifiable standards already in existing law when the project was proposed, which doesn’t sound inherently unreasonable!
However, the measure doesn’t actually require jurisdictions to adopt such standards; instead, it exploits their absence. If numerical thresholds don’t already exist for resources like oak woodlands, groundwater, or wildlife corridors, impacts to them essentially can’t be found significant regardless of severity. A genuine objective standards approach would mandate jurisdictions adopt protective thresholds and update them as science improves. This measure rewards weak standards, freezes them at application date, and prevents improvements based on new knowledge.
6. Ballot Box Permanence
Finally, one of the greatest flaws of the measure is its rigidity. Should it pass, BACA would require a 2/3rds vote of the legislature to amend.
California has a long, storied history with ballot box governance, where initiatives become impossible to adjust as new problems arise. The 2/3rds requirement virtually guarantees the law could never be changed, regardless of what issues may arise. An unchangeable measure, with foreseeable negative impacts for the state, may have lasting consequences for generations.
Some of the project types included in this measure, such as clean energy or transmission infrastructure, may benefit from the types of streamlining being considered if careful, targeted changes were made. Rather than a broad, clunky initiative that will be extremely difficult to change, we should advocate for those reforms through the legislative cleanup process already underway.
7. The Costs Are Just Too High
California faces converging affordability crises: insurers fleeing the state, utility rates climbing, and municipal budgets straining under unsustainable costs. All of these issues stem from the same source: decades of sprawling outward, often into fire-prone areas, leaving us with infrastructure we cannot afford to maintain and risks we cannot afford to insure.
BACA will accelerate these failures by trading short-term speed for permanent costs. By gutting CEQA’s alternatives analysis—the primary tool for steering projects away from costly, high-risk locations—this limits agencies to the developer’s preferred site, one alternative the developer designs themselves, and “no project.” It freezes environmental standards at the date of application, rewarding jurisdictions with weak protections. And it requires agencies to approve permits within strict timelines regardless of fiscal consequences, because most cities lack the quantitative standards BACA requires to find fiscal impacts “significant.”
The result: even if we build some things faster today, we’ll be paying the tab forever. Even more homes in fire zones will continue to destabilize our insurance markets. More infrastructure extensions will push up our utility rates. More sprawling subdivisions that generate less revenue than they cost to maintain will ensure even higher taxes. BACA promises affordability through speed but delivers the opposite: cheaper to build, but financially ruinous to sustain.
At a time when people are struggling to make ends meet, and when the federal government is doing all it can to roll back our environmental protections, the last thing we need is to double down on the failed policies we have tried for decades and know do not work.
Proposition 45 will hurt the environment and your wallet.
Greenbelt Alliance strongly opposes Proposition 45 and urges voters to vote NO on 45 this November.

Vote No on Prop 45: Rolling Back CEQA Is A Proposition Californians Can’t Afford
October 29, 2026 (https://www.greenbelt.org/2026/10/29/)
CEQA (https://www.greenbelt.org/tag/ceqa/), Voter Guide (https://www.greenbelt.org/tag/voter-guide/)
Updated on October 29 to include links. Originally published on January 16, 2026.
For advocates working at the intersection of environmental protection and climate-smart growth, theCalifornia Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) (https://www.greenbelt.org/land-use-planning-dictionary/california-environmental-quality-act/) has long been a source of both pride and frustration. While it has been a critical tool to protect our natural and working lands, its procedural delays have often been used to stall projects essential to a low-carbon future: dense infill (https://www.greenbelt.org/land-use-planning-dictionary/infill-development/) housing and transit-oriented development (https://www.greenbelt.org/land-use-planning-dictionary/transit-oriented-development/) in our existing communities.
In July 2025, however, at the urging of Governor Newsom, the California legislature passed some of the most impactful changes to CEQA (https://www.greenbelt.org/blog/ceqa-reform-explainer/) since its inception. Taken together, the two bills (AB 130 and SB 131) provide robust statutory CEQA exemptions for infill housing and housing element rezonings, require the state to map infill areas where exemptions would apply, and narrow the scope of the administrative record, helping to curtail anti-housing litigation.
Read my Op-Ed in the East Bay Times on why Prop 45 is a ruse handing shortcuts to polluters disguised as relief. (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/09/12/opinion-vote-no-prop-45-would-take-away-our-best-defense-against-corporate-polluters/amp/)
Check out some highlights of Greenbelt Alliance’s commentary in local and regional press:
Prop. 45: Will California Vote to Trade Environmental Regulation for Quicker Housing Development? – Forum KQED (https://www.kqed.org/forum/2010101915583/prop-45-will-california-vote-to-trade-environmental-regulation-for-quicker-housing-development)
Will Prop. 45 Fix California’s Housing Crisis or Roll Back a Valuable Environmental Law? – Political Breakdown KQED (https://www.kqed.org/news/12101722/will-prop-45-fix-californias-housing-crisis-or-roll-back-a-valuable-environmental-law)
Why are pro-housing groups split on Proposition 45? – CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/10/yimby-prop-45-ceqa/)
Sonoma County stakeholders, cities eye Prop. 45’s potential to broadly reform California’s bedrock environmental law – The Press Democrat (https://www.pressdemocrat.com/2026/10/26/prop-45-california-sonoma-county-housing-environment/)
Despite these monumental changes that address the barriers to critical infill development, California’s business lobby and sprawl developers were left unsatisfied. Now, they are proposing a ballot initiative that would make far more radical changes to the law. After gathering enough signatures to qualify for the November ballot, this is now called Proposition 45.
While the rhetoric of the measure (initially called Building an Affordable California Act, or BACA (https://advocacy.calchamber.com/2025/12/17/calchambers-ceqa-reform-boosting-californias-economy-and-state-budget/) ) seems to be aligned with urbanist goals and those of the broader abundance and affordability movements, the actual policy details and mechanics of the initiative—and the progress we’ve already achieved in the legislature (https://www.greenbelt.org/blog/2025-legislative-priorities/) last year—suggest that the costs it brings far outweigh any potential benefits.
Below, we outline seven reasons why the measure should be rejected (click to read more):
1. Major Reforms Have Already Been Enacted
For years, a primary objective for California’s urbanists was to stop the abuse of environmental law against projects that genuinely help the environment: dense, transit-oriented housing.
In a landmark shift for the state, that goal has largely been realized. Following years of advocacy by urbanists, the legislature passed a clean statutory CEQA exemption for infill housing. AB 130, which Greenbelt Alliance was proud to support (https://www.greenbelt.org/blog/ceqa-reform-ca/), is already being utilized across California, allowing builders to move forward with climate-friendly housing in high-opportunity areas like Palo Alto or Beverly Hills without the threat of being endlessly delayed by the environmental review process. While there is room for technical refinements, the fundamental issue at hand—the misuse of environmental laws to delay environmentally-friendly housing projects—has largely been addressed.
2. Everything is “Essential”
As the saying goes, “the devil is in the details”, and that’s certainly true for the BACA initiative. While modest on the surface, BACA creates a completely new set of rules for what it calls “essential” projects. So what, exactly, is an “essential project”?
The list is incredibly broad. Under Article 2, Section 21013, “essential projects” include housing, water, transportation, clean energy, transmission, broadband, and healthcare infrastructure. In practice, this definition encompasses a wide range of large-scale developments. For example, new freeways and existing freeway expansions would qualify as “essential transportation” projects; large greenfield sprawl developments would be treated as “essential” housing projects; and new dams and reservoirs would qualify as “essential” water projects. The definition even includes all “related and ancillary infrastructure,” meaning that highway interchanges, utility extensions, and water pipelines that enable sprawl developments also receive streamlined approval. All of these are enormous projects in terms of size and scale, with major potential environmental impacts. Yet, just like an apartment building in an urban area, under BACA, they would qualify for a significantly truncated review process.
In effect, this new CEQA process mirrors the fundamental flaw of its predecessor. While the old system failed to exempt low or no-impact projects from excessive review, the new one errs in the opposite direction, fast-tracking high-risk developments with significant potential for harm.
3. All Timelines Are Not Created Equal
The BACA initiative imposes strict timelines for this new class of projects that it deems “essential”: the environmental review process can take no more than one year. On the surface, a one-year limit on an Environmental Impact Report (EIR) seems reasonable. And for certain projects, like an apartment building on a parking lot in downtown San Francisco, or a townhome development in an LA suburb, it would be.
However, the measure’s definition of “essential” includes highways, dams, large-scale subdivisions, and other major projects. The environmental review required for projects at this scale cannot be done in a single year. Surveying hundreds if not thousands (or even tens of thousands) of acres of undisturbed and undeveloped land for species nesting patterns and habitat, water pollution impacts, and other environmental concerns physically cannot be accomplished within the timeframe laid out in the initiative. By forcing these projects into such a condensed timeline, we will be creating a system that overlooks genuine environmental harm in favor of speed.
For projects with unambiguous environmental benefits, such as housing developments within already urbanized areas, such speed makes sense. Many of the project types considered by this measure do not have the same clear, unambiguous benefits.
4. Restrictive Alternatives
One of CEQA’s most critical tools for preventing environmental harm is its alternative analysis provision, which allows for the identification of better project locations and designs. Currently, CEQA requires agencies to analyze a “reasonable range of alternatives” that could reduce environmental impacts, including different sites, reduced intensity options, and designs that avoid sensitive resources. This is how agencies can say, “this housing should be built downtown on a parking lot instead of on farmland,” or “this highway expansion has an alternative transit solution.”
BACA restricts this to just three options: the proposed project, one alternative designed by the applicant themselves (which doesn’t even need to be at a different location), and “no project.” The applicant’s alternative can be a slightly modified version of their original proposal on the same site. This eliminates the core mechanism for steering projects away from environmentally sensitive locations toward more appropriate sites, exactly the tool needed to prevent sprawl, protect open space, and ensure development happens in the right places.
5. The Evidentiary Standard
Maybe the most radical change incorporated in the ballot measure is to CEQA’s standard of review. Right now, CEQA allows a lead agency (generally a city or county) to use its own discretion to explore project alternatives and negotiate environmental mitigations. BACA proposes to eliminate this by requiring that environmental impacts only be found significant if they violate objective, quantifiable standards already in existing law when the project was proposed, which doesn’t sound inherently unreasonable!
However, the measure doesn’t actually require jurisdictions to adopt such standards; instead, it exploits their absence. If numerical thresholds don’t already exist for resources like oak woodlands, groundwater, or wildlife corridors, impacts to them essentially can’t be found significant regardless of severity. A genuine objective standards approach would mandate jurisdictions adopt protective thresholds and update them as science improves. This measure rewards weak standards, freezes them at application date, and prevents improvements based on new knowledge.
6. Ballot Box Permanence
Finally, one of the greatest flaws of the measure is its rigidity. Should it pass, BACA would require a 2/3rds vote of the legislature to amend.
California has a long, storied history with ballot box governance, where initiatives become impossible to adjust as new problems arise. The 2/3rds requirement virtually guarantees the law could never be changed, regardless of what issues may arise. An unchangeable measure, with foreseeable negative impacts for the state, may have lasting consequences for generations.
Some of the project types included in this measure, such as clean energy or transmission infrastructure, may benefit from the types of streamlining being considered if careful, targeted changes were made. Rather than a broad, clunky initiative that will be extremely difficult to change, we should advocate for those reforms through the legislative cleanup process already underway.
7. The Costs Are Just Too High
California faces converging affordability crises: insurers fleeing the state, utility rates climbing, and municipal budgets straining under unsustainable costs. All of these issues stem from the same source: decades of sprawling outward, often into fire-prone areas, leaving us with infrastructure we cannot afford to maintain and risks we cannot afford to insure.
BACA will accelerate these failures by trading short-term speed for permanent costs. By gutting CEQA’s alternatives analysis—the primary tool for steering projects away from costly, high-risk locations—this limits agencies to the developer’s preferred site, one alternative the developer designs themselves, and “no project.” It freezes environmental standards at the date of application, rewarding jurisdictions with weak protections. And it requires agencies to approve permits within strict timelines regardless of fiscal consequences, because most cities lack the quantitative standards BACA requires to find fiscal impacts “significant.”
The result: even if we build some things faster today, we’ll be paying the tab forever. Even more homes in fire zones will continue to destabilize our insurance markets. More infrastructure extensions will push up our utility rates. More sprawling subdivisions that generate less revenue than they cost to maintain will ensure even higher taxes. BACA promises affordability through speed but delivers the opposite: cheaper to build, but financially ruinous to sustain.
At a time when people are struggling to make ends meet, and when the federal government is doing all it can to roll back our environmental protections, the last thing we need is to double down on the failed policies we have tried for decades and know do not work.
Proposition 45 will hurt the environment and your wallet.
Greenbelt Alliance strongly opposes Proposition 45 and urges voters to vote NO on 45 this November.

California voters considering Proposition 45 (https://calmatters.org/newsletter/prop-45-yimby/) will decide the fate of a sweeping infrastructure measure that opponents warn could render the state’s brand-new data center laws virtually toothless. That would make it far easier for developers to force unwanted facilities into local communities, potentially undermining a growing wave of bans, moratoriums, and anti-data-center resolutions (https://calmatters.org/economy/technology/2026/10/california-data-centers-hit-with-local-regulation-flood/) at the city and county level. Data center backers insist the ballot measure will do nothing for them — even as some data center beneficiaries are spending big backing Prop. 45. Supporters have framed Prop. 45 as a tool to accelerate critical infrastructure projects (https://calmatters.org/environment/2026/10/prop-45-california-ceqa-explained/), like housing and schools, and the measure does not directly name data centers among the sorts of projects it considers critical. But some legal scholars and environmental advocates say that the proposition’s technical language creates a loophole. By expediting environmental reviews under the California Environmental Quality Act (https://calmatters.org/environment/2026/10/prop-45-california-ceqa-explained/) for broad categories of projects — including broadband internet facilities and any additional infrastructure required to get them up and running — the measure could quietly allow data centers to bypass recent state safeguards and local scrutiny. Julia Stein, a legal scholar and deputy director at UCLA School of Law’s Emmett Institute on Climate Change and the Environment, warns that the measure acts as a “blunt force instrument when it comes to streamlining” because of how wide its secondary umbrella extends. “What Prop. 45 does is designate an entire class of projects that would be subject to streamlining, and then it also says that projects ancillary to those projects — so something that you might need to do in the course of the development of the project that’s exempted itself — would fall within that same streamlining bubble,” Stein said. Telecommunications projects are explicitly streamlined under the proposition, “and there’s an argument that the development of data centers might be necessary for projects like that,” Stein added. MORE ON DATA CENTERS California cities pull the plug on data centers after state regulations don’t scale up fast enough (https://calmatters.org/economy/technology/2026/10/california-data-centers-hit-with-local-regulation-flood/) October 22, 2026 October 22, 2026 Other projects, like high-speed rail, are explicitly excluded from streamlining under the proposition — but data centers are not on that list, either. Stein and three other environmental law scholars told CalMatters that this opens the door for legal challenges. “The fact that they excluded some projects but have not expressly excluded data centers, a court would probably actually interpret that not as an unintentional oversight, but rather as intent to include data centers in the initiative,” said Matt McKerley, an attorney with Shute, Mihaly and Weinberger. Further, opponents argue that the proposition’s language, which includes a clause that it would supersede other related laws, would override measures like the recently-passed Senate Bill 887 (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb887), which made it harder to fast-track environmental review for data centers. Industry representatives say these objections to Prop. 45 are misplaced. The Data Center Coalition, an industry group supporting Prop. 45, insists their facilities fall outside the initiative’s scope, which focuses largely on housing development (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/10/yimby-prop-45-ceqa/) ad other infrastructure like roads and bridges. Industry representatives also point to a recent legal opinion memo (https://yesonprop45.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/legopinion_DataCenter.pdf) from California’s Office of Legislative Counsel, which provides legal services to members of the Legislature. The memo argues that Prop. 45’s statutory definitions do not apply to data centers. Amelia Matier, from the Yes on 45 campaign, echoed that take, saying, “Data centers are not included in Prop 45.” She added: “The defenders of California’s unaffordable status quo are desperate to distract voters with lies because they cannot defend the costly delays and red tape driving up prices for working families. ” Opponents of the measure include the California Labor Federation, Western Center on Law & Poverty, and various environmental advocacy groups that have spent more than $31 million dollars pushing back against the measure. Despite maintaining that data centers fall outside the proposition’s reach, tech and utility interests benefiting from California’s computing boom are putting massive financial weight (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-45-modifies-environmental-review-certain-projects-initiative-statute) behind its passage. Proponents have poured over $40 million into the Yes on Prop. 45 campaign, including $3.05 million from utility giant PG&E and $500,000 from warehouse and data center developer Prologis — a cash influx that opponents argue reveals who truly expects to profit if the measure passes. The debate over Prop. 45’s data center impact comes at a pivotal moment in California’s AI infrastructure boom. Gov. Gavin Newsom recently signed seven landmark data center laws (https://calmatters.org/economy/technology/2026/09/new-california-laws-data-centers/) aimed at forcing operators to disclose water usage, pay for their own grid upgrades, and undergo environmental review. Yet local communities aren’t waiting for state regulations to take effect. Amid rising fears of rate hikes, grid overload, and water depletion, grassroots opposition has erupted across California. At least 26 cities and counties have proposed or passed moratoriums, bans, or strict limits aimed to stop data center development (https://calmatters.org/economy/technology/2026/10/california-data-centers-hit-with-local-regulation-flood/) in their communities. Photo by Anna Hoch-Kenney, CalMatters In summary Prop. 45, billed as a pro-housing development measure, may have the unintended consequence of making it easier to build data centers, opponents say. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. California voters considering Proposition 45 (https://calmatters.org/newsletter/prop-45-yimby/) will decide the fate of a sweeping infrastructure measure that opponents warn could render the state’s brand-new data center laws virtually toothless. That would make it far easier for developers to force unwanted facilities into local communities, potentially undermining a growing wave of bans, moratoriums, and anti-data-center resolutions (https://calmatters.org/economy/technology/2026/10/california-data-centers-hit-with-local-regulation-flood/) at the city and county level. Data center backers insist the ballot measure will do nothing for them — even as some data center beneficiaries are spending big backing Prop. 45. Supporters have framed Prop. 45 as a tool to accelerate critical infrastructure projects (https://calmatters.org/environment/2026/10/prop-45-california-ceqa-explained/), like housing and schools, and the measure does not directly name data centers among the sorts of projects it considers critical. But some legal scholars and environmental advocates say that the proposition’s technical language creates a loophole. By expediting environmental reviews under the California Environmental Quality Act (https://calmatters.org/environment/2026/10/prop-45-california-ceqa-explained/) for broad categories of projects — including broadband internet facilities and any additional infrastructure required to get them up and running — the measure could quietly allow data centers to bypass recent state safeguards and local scrutiny. Julia Stein, a legal scholar and deputy director at UCLA School of Law’s Emmett Institute on Climate Change and the Environment, warns that the measure acts as a “blunt force instrument when it comes to streamlining” because of how wide its secondary umbrella extends. “What Prop. 45 does is designate an entire class of projects that would be subject to streamlining, and then it also says that projects ancillary to those projects — so something that you might need to do in the course of the development of the project that’s exempted itself — would fall within that same streamlining bubble,” Stein said. Telecommunications projects are explicitly streamlined under the proposition, “and there’s an argument that the development of data centers might be necessary for projects like that,” Stein added. MORE ON DATA CENTERS California cities pull the plug on data centers after state regulations don’t scale up fast enough (https://calmatters.org/economy/technology/2026/10/california-data-centers-hit-with-local-regulation-flood/) October 22, 2026 October 22, 2026 Other projects, like high-speed rail, are explicitly excluded from streamlining under the proposition — but data centers are not on that list, either. Stein and three other environmental law scholars told CalMatters that this opens the door for legal challenges. “The fact that they excluded some projects but have not expressly excluded data centers, a court would probably actually interpret that not as an unintentional oversight, but rather as intent to include data centers in the initiative,” said Matt McKerley, an attorney with Shute, Mihaly and Weinberger. Further, opponents argue that the proposition’s language, which includes a clause that it would supersede other related laws, would override measures like the recently-passed Senate Bill 887 (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb887), which made it harder to fast-track environmental review for data centers. Industry representatives say these objections to Prop. 45 are misplaced. The Data Center Coalition, an industry group supporting Prop. 45, insists their facilities fall outside the initiative’s scope, which focuses largely on housing development (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/10/yimby-prop-45-ceqa/) ad other infrastructure like roads and bridges. Sign up for free Δ “The Data Center Coalition has reviewed Proposition 45 and concluded that data centers are not eligible for Prop. 45’s streamlining, nor are they a covered entity under any part of the measure,” said Khara Boender, the coalition’s Director of Government Affairs—West. Industry representatives also point to a recent legal opinion memo (https://yesonprop45.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/legopinion_DataCenter.pdf) from California’s Office of Legislative Counsel, which provides legal services to members of the Legislature. The memo argues that Prop. 45’s statutory definitions do not apply to data centers. Amelia Matier, from the Yes on 45 campaign, echoed that take, saying, “Data centers are not included in Prop 45.” She added: “The defenders of California’s unaffordable status quo are desperate to distract voters with lies because they cannot defend the costly delays and red tape driving up prices for working families. ” Opponents of the measure include the California Labor Federation, Western Center on Law & Poverty, and various environmental advocacy groups that have spent more than $31 million dollars pushing back against the measure. Despite maintaining that data centers fall outside the proposition’s reach, tech and utility interests benefiting from California’s computing boom are putting massive financial weight (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-45-modifies-environmental-review-certain-projects-initiative-statute) behind its passage. Proponents have poured over $40 million into the Yes on Prop. 45 campaign, including $3.05 million from utility giant PG&E and $500,000 from warehouse and data center developer Prologis — a cash influx that opponents argue reveals who truly expects to profit if the measure passes. The debate over Prop. 45’s data center impact comes at a pivotal moment in California’s AI infrastructure boom. Gov. Gavin Newsom recently signed seven landmark data center laws (https://calmatters.org/economy/technology/2026/09/new-california-laws-data-centers/) aimed at forcing operators to disclose water usage, pay for their own grid upgrades, and undergo environmental review. Yet local communities aren’t waiting for state regulations to take effect. Amid rising fears of rate hikes, grid overload, and water depletion, grassroots opposition has erupted across California. At least 26 cities and counties have proposed or passed moratoriums, bans, or strict limits aimed to stop data center development (https://calmatters.org/economy/technology/2026/10/california-data-centers-hit-with-local-regulation-flood/) in their communities. Proposition 45 is backed by the California Chamber of Commerce and supported by a long list of homebuilders whose vision for California's future comes from the past.
'This is the Chamber of Commerce saying, 'We need to bring back the kinds of growth that California had in the 1960s,'' said Christopher Elmendorf, a law professor at the University of California, Davis, who studies land-use regulations.

Modifies Environmental Review for Certain Projects.
Initiative Statute.
## Analysis of Measure
### Proposal
Proposition 45 creates new procedures for reviewing certain types of projects that it defines as “essential.”
Figure 1 lists the types of projects eligible for the new procedures.
The proposition (1) tightens time limits for CEQA review, permits, and court challenges; (2) changes parts of the CEQA review process; and (3) changes the court’s review process for CEQA lawsuits.
The proposition gives eligible project applicants the option of using the new procedures or existing procedures.
***Tightens Time Limits for Review and Court Challenges of Eligible Projects.*** Proposition 45 creates more binding time limits for state and local governments to do both CEQA and permitting reviews.
This includes time limits for determining if a project application is complete, finishing the EIR, and granting other types of approvals and permits.

# Endorsement: CEQA is a mess. Prop 45 is even messier
Proposition 45 would significantly expedite the CEQA review process for eight categories of projects and potentially make it easier to build  environmentally ruinous projects.
...
Proposition 45, placed on the November ballot via signatures gathered by the California Chamber of Commerce, would significantly expedite the CEQA review process for eight categories of projects its authors deem “essential”: housing, water (other than the Delta tunnel), clean energy (excepting nuclear power), healthcare, public safety, wildfire mitigation, broadband internet access, education and transportation (other than high-speed rail).
...
First, it establishes a litany of strict deadlines — some of which are technically already in CEQA but rarely enforced.
Government agencies, for example, would have 30 days to determine whether a project application is complete, 365 days to conduct an environmental review and decide whether to certify it and 90 days to decide on permits.
If agencies fail to meet these deadlines, applicants could trigger a public hearing within 60 days, at which time a final decision must be made.
Applicants can sue if agencies don’t follow these procedures.

Why Circulate Planning & Policy Supports Prop 45
California's cost of living is out of control because our outdated system for approving essential projects is too slow, too bureaucratic, and too costly—making it harder to build the housing, transit, and other infrastructure our communities depend on. These unnecessary delays drive up costs for families, businesses, and taxpayers while making California less affordable for everyone.
That's why Circulate supports Prop 45, the Building an Affordable California Act (https://yesonprop45.com/) on the November 2026 ballot.
Prop 45 creates clear, enforceable timelines for environmental review, agency permitting, and judicial review for eligible projects. Rather than allowing projects to become trapped in years of bureaucratic delay and costly litigation, Prop 45 establishes accountability from application through final court decisions. By creating certainty throughout the approval process, the measure is expected to accelerate essential projects by 2 to 10 or more years, reducing costs and delivering benefits to Californians sooner.
Just as importantly, Prop 45 does not eliminate environmental review or weaken environmental protections. Every eligible project must still comply with the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) and all applicable federal, state, and local environmental laws and regulations. The measure simply ensures that environmental review, permitting decisions, and any legal challenges are completed within reasonable, enforceable deadlines instead of dragging on indefinitely.
For too long, unnecessary delays have increased the cost of nearly everything Californians rely on. Permitting delays can add years to building timelines, forcing families to wait even longer to realize the benefits of affordable housing. Further, permitting delays alone add more than $75,000 to the cost of a new home. Prop 45 cuts unnecessary red tape, lowers project costs, and helps deliver the infrastructure Californians need faster. This means California will be able to more quickly deliver affordable housing that strengthens our communities and economy.
Prop 45 also preserves local control. Cities and counties retain their authority to approve or deny projects, and Californians continue to have meaningful opportunities to participate throughout the project approval process. The measure creates a process that is faster, fairer, and more predictable—not one that sacrifices accountability or environmental protections.
More than 145 organizations (https://yesonprop45.com/our-coalition/) representing affordable housing, healthcare, water providers, agricultural producers, clean energy leaders, social justice advocates, and small business leaders support Prop 45 because California cannot afford to keep delaying the essential projects that improve quality of life and make our state more affordable.
California deserves a permitting system that protects the environment and delivers the infrastructure families, workers, businesses, and communities need.
Learn more about Prop 45 at: www.YesOnProp45.com (http://www.yesonprop45.com/)
