Key Questions
Risks & Benefits
California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Quick Facts
Official ballot title: “Modifies Environmental Review for Certain Projects. Initiative Statute.” (Attorney General title and summary, December 26, 2025)
Measure’s own name: The Building an Affordable California Act (AG No. 25-0023A1)
Type: Initiated state statute
A vote YES means: A new “essential projects” category (most housing, water, clean energy, medical, public safety, broadband, and transportation projects) gets hard deadlines for CEQA review, a slimmed-down alternatives analysis, and tighter limits on lawsuits, all written into the Public Resources Code [1, Sec. 21013].
A vote NO means: CEQA’s existing review timelines, alternatives requirements, and judicial-review rules stay in place for these projects.
Sponsor/proponent: California Chamber of Commerce. Proponent of record: Kurt R. Oneto of Nielsen Merksamer LLP.
On the ballot because: Qualified by random-sample signature check on June 16, 2026, and certified eligible June 25, 2026. The measure needed 546,651 valid signatures.
Full legal text: Initiative 25-0023A1, “Building an Affordable California Act,” Office of the Attorney General (PDF) (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0023A1%20%28%26quot%3BEssential%20Projects%26quot%3B%29.pdf)
LAO analysis: Ballot analysis of Initiative 25-0023 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-023)
1. What would it do?
Proposition 45 would carve a new fast-track lane through the California Environmental Quality Act for what it calls “essential projects.” It adds a new chapter, Chapter 1.5, to Division 13 of the Public Resources Code, the part of state law that is CEQA. It does not repeal CEQA, and it does not touch the other environmental statutes it names, such as the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act, and the California Coastal Act. What it changes is CEQA’s procedure for a defined set of projects [1, Sec. 1 (21011(h)), 21012-21033].
The measure does three main things for essential projects. First, it puts public agencies on a clock. An agency has thirty days to decide whether an application is complete or the application is deemed complete automatically. Once complete, a lead agency has 365 days to decide whether to certify an environmental impact report (EIR), 180 days to act on a negative declaration, and 90 days to document an exemption. For the 365-day and 90-day review clocks the measure counts only business days, not weekends or state holidays, so the real-world calendar is longer than the raw numbers suggest [1, Secs. 21017-21019, 21028(c)].
Second, it shrinks the alternatives analysis. Today a CEQA environmental impact report must study a reasonable range of alternatives to a project. Under Proposition 45, an EIR for an essential project needs to analyze only the project itself, one alternative developed by the applicant, and the “no project” alternative. The measure declares that any additional alternatives are “unnecessary” and that no agency may require them [1, Sec. 21025].
Third, it narrows the courtroom. A challenger must sue within thirty days of the agency’s notice of determination, the case must finish within 270 days including any appeal, and the court must use the deferential substantial-evidence standard rather than independent judgment. A court that finds a defect may order the agency to redo only the specific study at issue. It “may not order or direct” the agency to rescind its approval of the project, and once a project clears review its later construction and implementation approvals cannot be challenged again [1, Secs. 21026-21027].
2. The legal language
Full text: Initiative 25-0023A1, “Building an Affordable California Act,” California Office of the Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0023A1%20%28%26quot%3BEssential%20Projects%26quot%3B%29.pdf) (amended language submitted November 24, 2025)
Key language:
“‘Essential project’ means a project that meets all of the following requirements … The project does not include a jail or other detention facility, or involve the development of a new oil or natural gas production facility.” [1, Sec. 21028(h)]
“A court may not order or direct via writ or any other form of order, injunction, or decision that an agency rescind its approval of the essential project.” [1, Sec. 21027(d)]
What it amends: Adds Chapter 1.5 (commencing with Section 21010) to Division 13 of the Public Resources Code. Because it is an initiative statute rather than a constitutional amendment, the legislature could later amend it, but only in ways that further the measure’s purposes unless it says otherwise. The measure also adds a self-defense clause. If the governor and attorney general both decline to defend it in court, the attorney general must appoint independent counsel, funded by a continuous general fund appropriation [1, Secs. 21010, Section 4].
3. What, Where, When, Why?
Who? Sponsored by the California Chamber of Commerce, with the initiative filed by attorney Kurt R. Oneto of Nielsen Merksamer. Supporters include the California Building Industry Association, the California Hospital Association, NAACP California, and Pacific Gas and Electric. Opposition is led by environmental organizations, including Sierra Club California, the Planning and Conservation League, and CalBike.
What? A new “essential projects” category covering most housing, water, clean energy, medical, public-safety, broadband, and transportation projects, given fixed review deadlines, a one-alternative EIR, and tighter judicial review. Jails and detention facilities and new oil and gas production facilities are excluded, and by definition Delta conveyance and high-speed rail are left out of the water and transportation categories. [1, Secs. 21013, 21028].
Where? Statewide, applied to all public agencies and written into the Public Resources Code [1, Sec. 21014(d)].
When? On the November 3, 2026, ballot. It takes effect the day after the election if it passes and applies to applications deemed complete after that date, including projects that withdraw and resubmit to opt in [1, Secs. 21014(f)-(g), 21033].
Why? The proponents frame CEQA delay and litigation as a driver of California’s high housing, energy, and infrastructure costs. Their stated purpose is to “make California more affordable by streamlining and speeding up approval of essential projects” while keeping the state’s other environmental laws intact [1, Secs. 21011-21012].
4. Trade-offs
CEQA review and the lawsuits that follow can add years and cost to housing and infrastructure, and the delay is not evenly aimed at the most polluting projects. The legislature itself has spent recent sessions passing narrower CEQA exemptions for infill housing and other priorities, which shows that the cost-of-building concern is bipartisan and real, not manufactured. Proposition 45 is the broadest response yet because it does by initiative, and across seven whole project categories, what the legislature has done piecemeal.
Every lever the measure pulls to go faster also removes a check that CEQA built in on purpose. Hard deadlines with a “deemed complete” default speed things up, and they also let a clock, rather than a finished analysis, decide when review ends. A one-alternative EIR is cheaper and quicker, and it also means the public document may never study the option that would have reduced harm the most. The substantial-evidence standard and the bar on rescinding approvals cut litigation risk for builders, and they also make it harder for a neighbor or a tribe to stop a project that was genuinely under-analyzed. None of these is a free lunch. Each is a real gain in speed bought with a real reduction in review.
Two things keep this from being a simple pro-building versus pro-environment fight. First, the measure leaves the substantive environmental statutes standing. A project that violates the Clean Water Act or the Endangered Species Act is still illegal under those laws. What changes is CEQA’s procedural review, which is disclosure and analysis, not the pollution limits themselves. Second, the fight will be about the word “essential.” The definitions are broad. “Essential clean energy” reaches carbon-capture and hydrogen infrastructure, and the categories sweep in “related and ancillary” infrastructure as part of the “whole of the project.” How wide that lane runs, and how much of California’s building actually qualifies, is the question the ballot label cannot answer [1, Secs. 21028(f), (h)].
Many CEQA issues are not about acceptable levels of environmental damage. Instead, project opponents use procedural complaints under CEQA to slow down projects that they dislike for reasons having nothing to do with the environment. The proposition’s backers wish to reduce the use of CEQA for such purposes.
5. Potential risks and benefits
Potential benefits
It replaces open-ended CEQA timelines with firm deadlines, which can cut the years of delay that raise the cost of housing, water, clean energy, and hospitals [1, Secs. 21018-21019].
The streamlined one-alternative EIR reduces the cost and length of environmental review while still requiring a “no project” comparison [1, Sec. 21025].
Tighter judicial rules, a 270-day case clock, and a bar on rescinding approvals reduce the litigation risk that can stall financing on approved projects [1, Secs. 21026-21027].
The LAO expects state and local governments to see long-run net savings from reduced administrative and legal workload once the system is running.
It leaves the underlying pollution-control statutes—the Clean Water Act, Clean Air Act, Endangered Species Act, and Coastal Act—in force, so it narrows CEQA procedure rather than repealing environmental protection [1, Sec. 21011(h)].
Potential risks
A one-alternative EIR and a “deemed complete” default can end review before the analysis is finished, so real environmental or community harms may go unstudied [1, Secs. 21017, 21025].
The bar on rescinding an approval and on challenging later construction approvals sharply limits the public’s ability to stop an under-reviewed project [1, Sec. 21027(d)-(e)].
The “essential project” definitions are broad and include ancillary infrastructure, so fights over what qualifies will be frequent and consequential [1, Sec. 21028(h)].
The LAO estimates implementation costs in the tens of millions of dollars annually for the first several years, with uncertain long-run court effects that could run from savings to added costs.
The self-defense clause commits an open-ended general fund appropriation to hired outside counsel if state officials decline to defend the measure [1, Section 4].
6. Open questions
How much of California’s actual building pipeline meets the “essential project” definition once ancillary infrastructure and the seven categories are counted?
Will the 365 business-day and 90 business-day clocks, which run longer than calendar deadlines, deliver the speed proponents promise?
Does limiting an EIR to one applicant-designed alternative meaningfully weaken the document’s ability to surface lower-impact options?
How will courts read “objective, quantifiable, and written standards” as the new test for a valid CEQA challenge, and how many suits does that screen out?
If the measure passes, how much litigation will target the boundaries of the definitions themselves, and who pays for the state’s defense under the independent-counsel clause?
7. The questions to ask before you vote
CEQA delay is a real driver of what it costs to build housing, water projects, and energy capacity in California. Proposition 45 speeds up those projects by shortening deadlines, shrinking the alternatives study, and limiting lawsuits. The questions are whether faster building is worth a lighter environmental and public review and whether to trust the broad definition of “essential” to stay in its lane.
Every provision that makes a project go faster also removes a check that CEQA put there on purpose. Which risk weighs more: a needed project stalled for years by process and litigation or a harmful project approved before the harm was fully studied?

Endorsement: CEQA is a mess. Prop 45 is even messier
Proposition 45 would significantly expedite the CEQA review process for eight categories of projects and potentially make it easier to build environmentally ruinous projects.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 17, 2026
What’s the most polarizing four-letter word in California politics?
CEQA.
That wasn’t always the case. When then-Gov. Ronald Reagan signed the California Environmental Quality Act into law in 1970, the need could not have been more obvious. Californians were fed up with planners bulldozing low-income neighborhoods and communities of color for miles of polluting freeways. They were horrified by the ecological damage and habitat destruction caused by suburban sprawl. They were tired of top-down infrastructure projects that left communities feeling disempowered and voiceless.
CEQA laid out a basic protective framework: Before approving a project, government officials needed to evaluate potential negative environmental impacts and identify ways to mitigate or avoid them while providing ample opportunity for public review and input.

But it didn’t take long for the law to be easily manipulated for ends that had little or nothing to do with the environment.
NIMBYs used the process to delay new infill housing — driving up costs and reducing the likelihood projects get built. Unions leveraged CEQA to extort favorable labor terms on projects (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/article/california-housing-union-labor-17802611.php). Courts showed a predisposition for allowing just about anything to become grounds for a CEQA challenge — which is how we ended up with a 2022 lawsuit against a UC Berkeley housing project (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/Editorial-UC-Berkeley-students-are-now-16931016.php) that effectively branded students as a form of pollution.
This editorial board has repeatedly decried CEQA abuses and has urged politicians to take decisive action (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/uc-berkeley-peoples-park-housing-ceqa-newsom-17816129.php).
In recent years, they have, to a degree.

Article continues below this ad
State lawmakers passed, and Gov. Gavin Newsom signed, bills to, among other things, permit more units on many single-family-home lots (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/California-cities-rush-to-limit-new-law-16647764.php), streamline the development of dense housing near transit (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/openforum/article/sb79-now-law-fight-affordable-housing-goes-21094908.php), exempt almost all infill housing from CEQA (https://sfchronicle.com/california/article/ceqa-housing-roadblocks-newsom-20402835.php) and speed up permitting timelines for large clean-energy projects (https://modelclimatelaws.org/resources/californias-sb-205-2022/).
But it’s still far too easy to bury certain essential projects in delay, litigation and costly uncertainty.
Proposition 45 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop45-text-proposed-laws.pdf), placed on the November ballot via signatures gathered by the California Chamber of Commerce, would significantly expedite the CEQA review process for eight categories of projects (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop45-110326.pdf) its authors deem “essential”: housing, water (other than the Delta tunnel (https://www.sfchronicle.com/news/article/will-california-ever-build-the-delta-tunnel-22237021.php)), clean energy (excepting nuclear power), healthcare, public safety, wildfire mitigation, broadband internet access, education and transportation (other than high-speed rail).
How would the measure aid these kinds of projects?
First, it establishes a litany of strict deadlines — some of which are technically already in CEQA but rarely enforced. Government agencies, for example, would have 30 days to determine whether a project application is complete, 365 days to conduct an environmental review and decide whether to certify it and 90 days to decide on permits. If agencies fail to meet these deadlines, applicants could trigger a public hearing within 60 days, at which time a final decision must be made. Applicants can sue if agencies don’t follow these procedures.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 45 also significantly reduces paperwork. Government agencies could no longer repeatedly ask developers for more information to determine whether an application is complete — they would have one chance to produce an “exhaustive written corrections list.” Agencies would also be prohibited from changing the criteria or scope of their assessments mid-review. Agencies would no longer have to come up with multiple alternatives to environmentally impactful projects; instead, the applicant would propose just one alternative. The measure also restricts the public comments that can be included in the administrative record.
Finally, Prop 45 permits courts to halt only portions of a project determined to have “a specific, adverse impact upon public safety.” If courts sign off on an environmental review, no further lawsuits would be allowed. Lawsuits, including appeals, would need to be resolved within 270 days, with a possible 90-day extension.
In aggregate, these changes are far bigger in scope than any previous CEQA reform.
Some of the stipulations are eminently reasonable.
Enforcing deadlines is a no-brainer, as is eliminating excess paperwork and reducing frivolous litigation. Project applicants are not entitled to approvals, but they are entitled to decisions being made in a timely manner.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Furthermore, some of the projects Prop 45 seeks to streamline — like public transit, bike lanes and infill housing — are objectively good for the environment. They shouldn’t be subject to extreme CEQA scrutiny.
Others, however, are beyond questionable.
Prop 45 applies its streamlining process to freeway expansions and greenfield housing development in wildfire zones. And why does it specifically exempt the one transportation project that arguably needs the most help: California’s voter-approved high-speed rail, which is years behind schedule and billions over budget thanks in part to costly CEQA challenges? (https://grist.org/transportation/billions-spent-miles-to-go-the-story-of-californias-failure-to-build-high-speed-rail/)
Poll testing, said Emma Manoukian Chung, a strategist for the Yes on Prop 45 campaign. There was “voter appetite” for freeways and sprawl, but not high-speed rail.
But throwing a grab bag of poll-tested projects together and suggesting they should be evaluated on substantially similar terms is neither reasonable nor good policy.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Huge infrastructure projects — such as freeways and dams — have fundamentally different environmental impacts than infill housing. And infill housing has different environmental consequences than single-family homes in car-centric, high-wildfire-risk zones.
It makes no sense to apply the same scrutiny and deadlines to each.
It’s also unclear whether Prop 45 applies to data centers (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/article/data-centers-artificial-intelligence-dakotas-22362642.php). Opponents insist the “broadband internet access” category leaves open the possibility, while proponents insist that it doesn’t.
Ultimately, that question will likely have to be answered through litigation — ironically, the very thing Prop 45 is trying to curb.
It’s also ironic that Prop 45, despite aiming to reduce uncertainty, actually creates much more of it.
“This is deep, deep, deep in the weeds of environmental law,” Chris Elmendorf, a UC Davis law professor and one of California’s preeminent CEQA experts, told us. “It’s a super complicated body of law that they’re trying to change, trying to make it easier to build stuff.
“Some of the changes are good and some may be bad, and who knows what kind of second-order effects they will have?”
That’s why the state Legislature is best suited to handle complicated, nuanced policy, tweaking laws as needed — unlike the all-or-nothing blunt instrument of the ballot box.
“An initiative should be considered a last resort … when the Legislature is doing nothing,” Prop 45 opponent Darrell Steinberg, a former Sacramento mayor and state Senate leader, told us. But, he said, “just the opposite” is occurring.
We agree.
Lawmakers need to craft more fundamental CEQA reforms, particularly when it comes to housing, transportation and green energy projects. Some of those solutions are contained within Prop 45.

But the measure as written would lock California into a regulatory regime that makes it easier to build the same environmentally ruinous projects that gave us CEQA in the first place.
Prop 45 is poll-tested political Swiss cheese, not a thoughtful effort to produce better outcomes. Vote no.

The basic concept of the initiative (as noted in this Twitter thread by Chris Elmendorf) is that it would create a new CEQA process for “essential” projects.
That CEQA process would have strict timeframes for completion of any environmental review, timeframes that can be enforced by a court, requiring an agency doing CEQA review to make a final decision within a set period.
The process would allow the proponent of the project to define the project’s scope (in other words, what the project involves) and to identify a single alternative (as opposed to multiple alternatives) to be considered in the analysis.
For this new process, a project proponent can require that the only “significant” impacts under CEQA that might trigger a duty to analyze and mitigate would be impacts that are the result of a violation of a written standard in a preexisting law, regulation or policy.
Legal challenges to CEQA compliance can only invoke violations of “objective,” written standards of law, and courts cannot generally speaking stop projects based on violations of CEQA.
But perhaps most importantly, the initiative would require all agencies approving projects by private applicants to only apply the law in place at the time the applicant submitted their application for the project – the initiative thus “vests” rights to develop or proceed with projects by immunizing proposals from any changes in law after the proposal is submitted.

Proposition 45
Modifies Environmental Review for Certain Projects. Initiative Statute.
Analysis of Measure
Background
State Law Requires Government Agencies to Review the Environmental Impacts of Proposed Projects. State and local government agencies are responsible for reviewing and approving certain projects before they can be built. As part of this process, the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) requires an agency to consider how a project might negatively affect the environment before approving it. CEQA applies to many types of public and private projects, such as housing developments, school facilities, and highway expansions. Some exceptions apply. For example, state law exempts certain housing developments located near public transit from needing a CEQA review.
How the CEQA Process Works. The government agency first determines if CEQA applies to a project. If so, it then determines if the project could significantly affect the environment and if those impacts could be avoided or reduced with minor changes to the project. If making minor changes cannot avoid or reduce significant impacts, the agency must do a more detailed review called an environmental impact report (EIR). (The majority of projects do not require an EIR; however, EIRs are somewhat more common for large and complex projects.) The EIR analyzes possible environmental impacts the project could cause and considers alternatives that could reduce those impacts. After finishing the environmental review, the agency decides whether to approve the project. At certain times during this process, the government agency must seek and consider comments about the project's environmental review from the public and other government agencies.
People Can Sue the Government Agency About Its CEQA Review. After a government agency has completed the CEQA review and decided whether to approve a project, people who think the agency did not follow the CEQA process correctly can sue the agency. For example, a project opponent might argue that the environmental analysis was inadequate. If the court finds that the agency did not follow CEQA correctly, it can stop the whole project and require the agency to fix the part of the process that was problematic.
Many Projects Also Need to Get Other Approvals. Besides CEQA review, many projects need approval or permits from other local and/or state government agencies before they can proceed. For example, a business that wants to build a health clinic might need the local government to change land use rules before it can proceed. It also may need state agencies to review and approve how the project might affect certain wildlife species and water quality.
Proposal
Proposition 45 creates new procedures for reviewing certain types of projects that it defines as "essential." Figure 1 lists the types of projects eligible for the new procedures. The proposition (1) tightens time limits for CEQA review, permits, and court challenges; (2) changes parts of the CEQA review process; and (3) changes the court's review process for CEQA lawsuits. The proposition gives eligible project applicants the option of using the new procedures or existing procedures.
Tightens Time Limits for Review and Court Challenges of Eligible Projects. Proposition 45 creates more binding time limits for state and local governments to do both CEQA and permitting reviews. This includes time limits for determining if a project application is complete, finishing the EIR, and granting other types of approvals and permits. For example, Proposition 45 allows an applicant to request an agency hearing-and potentially file a lawsuit with the courts-if an agency does not meet the 365-business-day time limit for finishing the EIR. The proposition also creates a time limit for courts to resolve legal challenges.
Changes CEQA Review for Eligible Projects. For eligible projects, Proposition 45 makes several changes to the CEQA review process, including:
Application Process. Requires the government agency to specify all information that must be included in an application before it is submitted. (Current law allows agencies to repeatedly request additional information or project changes.)
How Environmental Impacts Are Assessed. Requires the agency to assess potential environmental impacts based on the laws and standards in place at the time the project application is submitted. (Current law lets the agency consider new information and revise its review standards when doing the EIR.)
Project Alternatives. Allows the applicant to develop only one project alternative for the agency to consider. (Current law requires the agency-not the applicant-to develop and consider multiple project alternatives that could reduce environmental impacts.)
Consultation With Native Tribes. Requires the agency and applicant to consult about the project only with California native tribes that have been formally recognized by the federal government. (Current law requires consultation with a wider range of tribes.)
Public Comment Periods. Limits how long the agency can accept comments from the public and other government agencies about the project. (Current law sets a minimum number of days-not a maximum-for public review.)
Changes How Courts Review Challenges to Eligible Projects. Proposition 45 makes several changes to the court's review process when someone challenges a government agency's approval of an eligible project. For example, it reduces the scope of what the court can consider in CEQA lawsuits. The proposition also prevents the court from stopping the whole project if it finds that the agency did not follow CEQA correctly. Instead, the court can only stop the part of the project where the environmental review did not comply with CEQA while the agency fixes the problem.
Fiscal Effects
Initial Costs for State and Local Governments. During the first several years, Proposition 45 likely would increase costs for the state and local governments, including state courts. These costs likely would be in the high tens of millions of dollars annually, potentially exceeding $100 million annually . For example, state and local governments would have costs to develop new guidelines and standards for reviewing eligible projects' environmental impacts, meet tighter time limits, and address court challenges. Fees paid by project applicants and people filing lawsuits would cover some of these costs. After this initial period, while some costs could continue, others likely would decline over time. For example, the changes to how courts can review CEQA lawsuits could mean fewer people will sue in the future, which could reduce costs for agencies and state courts in the long term.
In the Longer Term, Uncertain but Potentially More Significant Fiscal Effects. Proposition 45's changes to project review and court challenge procedures for eligible projects could have various fiscal effects for state and local governments. The overall fiscal effect of these changes-positive or negative-is uncertain but could be more substantial than the near-term effects. For example, two effects that could have significant but uncertain impacts are:
More Projects and Faster Timing. To the degree that Proposition 45's changes to project review and court challenge procedures lead to eligible public projects being constructed more quickly, state and local governments likely would have lower project costs. Additionally, if the proposition's changes result in more projects being completed overall, it could lead to an increase in tax revenues, such as from property taxes.
Negative Environmental Impacts. To the degree that Proposition 45's changes to project review and court challenge procedures lead to approval of projects with negative environmental impacts that would not have otherwise occurred, government agencies could face higher costs to respond to those impacts.
Yes/No Statement
A YES vote on this measure means: Certain public and private projects would be eligible for new project review and court challenge procedures. For example, new procedures would tighten time limits for environmental review and reduce the scope of what courts can consider when reviewing legal challenges.
A NO vote on this measure means: Public and private projects would continue to use existing project review and court challenge procedures.
Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact
Initial costs for state and local governments, likely in the high tens of millions of dollars annually-potentially exceeding $100 million annually-to implement new project review and court challenge procedures for eligible projects. Fees paid by project applicants and people filing lawsuits would partly cover these costs.
In the longer term, uncertain, but potentially more significant positive or negative fiscal effects for state and local governments. The overall effect depends, in part, on how the new procedures change the number of eligible projects that get built and whether those projects have different environmental impacts.
Ballot Label
Fiscal Impact : Initial costs for state and local governments, likely in the high tens of millions of dollars-potentially exceeding $100 million-annually, partly covered by fees. Uncertain, potentially more significant positive or negative longer-term fiscal effects.

What does the Building an Affordable California Act do?
Proposed ballot initiative from Cal Chamber of Commerce to change CEQA could have broad implications.
The California Chamber of Commerce is currently collecting signatures for an initiative (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0023A1%20%28%26quot%3BEssential%20Projects%26quot%3B%29.pdf) that would substantially change the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). Given the Chamber’s resources, I think it’s likely they will get enough signatures to qualify the initiative, which means either the legislature cuts a deal with the Chamber to enact legislation and take the initiative off the ballot, or it goes before the voters this fall. So a thorough evaluation of what this initiative might do is important.
The basic concept of the initiative (as noted in this Twitter thread (https://x.com/CSElmendorf/status/2006838194135065038) by Chris Elmendorf) is that it would create a new CEQA process for “essential” projects. That CEQA process would have strict timeframes for completion of any environmental review, timeframes that can be enforced by a court, requiring an agency doing CEQA review to make a final decision within a set period. The process would allow the proponent of the project to define the project’s scope (in other words, what the project involves) and to identify a single alternative (as opposed to multiple alternatives) to be considered in the analysis. For this new process, a project proponent can require that the only “significant” impacts under CEQA that might trigger a duty to analyze and mitigate would be impacts that are the result of a violation of a written standard in a preexisting law, regulation or policy. Legal challenges to CEQA compliance can only invoke violations of “objective,” written standards of law, and courts cannot generally speaking stop projects based on violations of CEQA.
But perhaps most importantly, the initiative would require all agencies approving projects by private applicants to only apply the law in place at the time the applicant submitted their application for the project – the initiative thus “vests” rights to develop or proceed with projects by immunizing proposals from any changes in law after the proposal is submitted. That is a fundamental change from California law in general (which mostly “vests” rights at later stages of project review and approval, with some exceptions).
These are major changes compared to current CEQA – because of their scope, I will break my analysis up over a series of blog posts. The key points I will elaborate on, each in a subsequent blog post, are:
Primacy: The initiative is a broad one, which is to be aggressively interpreted, and which overrides all other conflicting law.
Vested rights: Vesting rights as of the date of submission of application creates the possibility of strategic behavior – project proponents might submit projects very early, maintain projects in process for extended periods of time, or file repeated applications, to try and “freeze” law with respect to their projects. This could fundamentally undermine the ability of the state and local governments to update legal protections for the environment.
Changed procedures: The statute imposes new, rigorous timeframes and procedures for all agency permitting, not just permitting through CEQA, overriding any inconsistent provisions in any other law.
Significance standard: CEQA review would ultimately only consider whether a project meets pre-existing, written legal standards. And enforcement of CEQA review would only apply to “objective” written standards, with a definition of “objective” that may well exclude all non-quantitative legal standards. For instance, prohibitions on “substantial” negative impacts on the habitat of endangered species may not fall within the scope of CEQA anymore. The result may be that CEQA is transformed into a checklist of whether the project complies with existing laws, leaving no independent significance for CEQA.
Self-identification of project scope and alternatives: Project proponents can self-identify what their project’s purpose is, what the physical scope of the project is, and what the alternative to the project is. That may allow project proponents to narrowly define their project (and thus its possible impacts) to avoid finding impacts that will inevitably result from the construction of the project. And the limited judicial remedies mean that courts may not be able to prevent major changes to a project after the CEQA review is completed. The upshot is that CEQA review may not actually cover what is actually built, allowing major components of projects to avoid any CEQA review at all.
Breadth: The breadth of the kinds of projects that are deemed “essential” is large. Freeways certainly count. As do almost all dam, irrigation, and water projects in the state. Logging in general probably does. It is plausible data centers, light industrial facilities, and other similar projects might well count as well. And it is plausible that any development of any natural area in the state qualifies. This initiative is not just about housing or renewable energy.
Lock in: The initiative requires a two-thirds vote in the legislature to amend the initiative, meaning that drafting flaws, unintended consequences and policy changes may not be able to be implemented.
Undercuts other environmental laws: The implementation of many other California environmental laws depends on CEQA. For instance, most of the habitat protections for species listed under the California Endangered Species Act (CESA) occur through CEQA review. Those might be wiped out with this initiative. Local land-use regulations would still apply, but any changes to local land-use law for a covered project appear to be covered by the accelerated review process for the initiative.
What the measure gets right: I’m sympathetic to a number of the goals of the initative. There are real problems with CEQA: Local governments (and probably more importantly, neighborhood groups) sandbagging applicants with endless requests for more environmental review, dragging out timeframes. Mission creep in which CEQA is invoked for an increasingly broad range of any impact in the world, such as the noise produced by students in new housing. Local governments delaying CEQA decisions endlessly. Providing greater clarity over what CEQA covers, what kinds of impacts are “significant,” and timeframes for decisionmaking would have real benefits. But they are also in tension with other important goals, such as the role that environmental review plays as a “backstop” for emerging or new environmental harms, for gaps in other statutory systems, and for cumulative impacts.
My analysis hits what I think are the most important points of the initiative. There are other issues (such as a fairly drastic restriction on public comments for CEQA review of essential projects) that matter as well, but which I will not focus on here.
One final note: This is based on my initial review of what is quite a complicated ballot initiative. I’m sure I’ve made some errors and omissions in the analysis, and if so, please do let me know in the comments. As appropriate, I’ll update the writeups.

A Practitioner’s View of Prop. 45 – Potential Benefits and Challenges to CEQA Practice
Thinking
/
10.26.2026
by Greta Brownlow, PhD; Curtis E. Alling, AICP; Gary D. Jakobs, AICP; Mike Parker, AICP; and Pat Angell
CEQA in Two Worlds – “Essential” Projects vs. Traditional CEQA Processes
Introduction
Proposition 45 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/45/index.htm) (Prop. 45), “The Building an Affordable California Act,” is a voter initiative appearing on this November’s statewide ballot. Prop. 45 would add a new chapter to the CEQA Statute (Chapter 1.5 of the Public Resources Code) that is intended to expedite CEQA compliance for eight categories of “essential project” types: housing, clean energy, water, public health, public safety, broadband, education facilities, and transportation. ”Essential projects” would still be subject to CEQA but would follow a set of compliance requirements that are distinct from current CEQA processes, including strict application and documentation timelines, an (optional) preliminary scoping process, a new tribal consultation framework, and significant changes to how impact significance determinations are made and legal challenges are evaluated.
Prop. 45 is clear regarding its intent and is a shift from CEQA as originally drafted. Whereas CEQA’s original declared legislative intent (Public Resources Code [PRC] Section 21000) is the maintenance of a quality environment for the people of the state now and in the future, recognizing the need to balance ecological systems and people’s needs, the proposition’s policy (proposed PRC Section 21029[a]) emphasizes approval of essential projects: “It is the policy of the people of the State of California that this chapter be interpreted and implemented to afford the fullest possible weight to the interest of, and the approval and realization of, essential projects.”
In a prior publication, we provided a high-level summary of Prop. 45 with the intent of alerting voters to the primary provisions of this new CEQA compliance framework. Here, we take a deeper dive into the proposition’s directives and explore some of its potential challenges and benefits. Much opinion is being published concerning Prop. 45; our intent is to present a neutral perspective informed by Ascent’s CEQA expertise and experience working on both public and private sector projects, whether for lead agency or applicant proponents or lead agencies processing private applications. If passed by a “yes” vote, Prop. 45’s provisions would become law immediately upon election certification. We acknowledge we are not attorneys, and while we weigh in on what ultimately may become legal matters, we do so from the perspective of professionals who implement CEQA on a daily basis. Our opinions are not, and should not be used as, legal advice.
The sections below focus on several, though not all, of the most important components of Prop. 45, including those that may be most subject to interpretation or a source of difficulty for implementing agencies. Each section summarizes the relevant provisions, then discusses potential benefits and challenges, along with initial practice considerations where applicable.
We hope this AscentShare helps you understand the overall implications of Prop. 45. It is neither an endorsement of the proposition nor an argument to oppose it.
1: DEFINITION OF ESSENTIAL PROJECTS
Proposed PRC Article 7, “Definitions,” Section 21028(m), defines an “essential project” as a project within one of eight defined categories identified below.
Essential broadband projects (Section 21028[i]) consisting of mass-market retail internet service, by wire, wireless, or radio, that can reach all or substantially all internet endpoints. Dial-up is excluded.
Essential education projects (Section 21028[c], [g], and [k]), including acquiring, building, expanding, renovating, or equipping property owned by a California educational institution; includes projects by school districts, county offices of education, charter schools, community college districts, the California State University system, the University of California system (including the Regents of the University of California), University of California Law San Francisco, and nonprofit colleges that belong to the Association of Independent California Colleges and Universities.
Essential clean energy projects that support the state’s climate or energy objectives (Section 21028[j]).
Producing or storing renewable electricity, as well as associated transmission lines. Includes solar, wind, geothermal, fuel cells that meet California Air Resources Board emission standards, hydroelectric of 30 megawatts or less, digester gas, solid waste conversion, landfill gas, and ocean wave, thermal, or tidal energy.
Clean hydrogen that is not made from fossil fuels.
Microgrids as defined in subdivision (d) of Section 8370 of the Public Utilities Code.
Carbon capture, transport, and permanent storage, including from energy, manufacturing, and refining sources.
Transmission or distribution projects identified in the state grid operator’s (CAISO’s) transmission planning process or the state Integrated Energy Policy Report.
Nuclear power generation is expressly excluded.
Essential housing projects (Section 21028[l]).
Residential-only projects.
Qualifying mixed-use projects as defined under PRC Section 21028(y).
Transitional housing, emergency shelters, and supportive housing as defined in Government Code Section 65582.
Farmworker housing as defined in subdivision (h) of Section 50199.7 of the Health and Safety Code.
Group living projects such as convents and monasteries.
Student housing.
Senior housing for people 55 and older. Includes residential care facilities for the elderly and continuing care retirement communities.
Subdivisions or common interest developments of homes or residential lots.
Conversions of existing commercial buildings to housing.
Essential public health projects (Section 21028[n], [w], and [x]) including medical treatment facilities or a medical office building.
Essential public safety projects (Section 21028[o], [t], and [ag]) consist of two types:
First responder facilities: Fire stations run by the state, local agencies, joint powers authorities, special districts, or a consulting tribe, and local police or sheriff’s stations. Jail space is excluded, as are federal facilities, immigration detention facilities, and state prisons.
Wildfire risk reduction projects that reduce wildfire risks to residential and commercial structures. Examples include hardening or undergrounding power lines, roads and infrastructure, vegetation management, fuel reduction, fuel breaks, and access roads.
Essential transportation projects (Section 21028[p]), including projects eligible for state fuel-tax and vehicle-fee funding (streets, highways, and transit) and EV charging and refueling infrastructure. High-speed rail—the train system, corridors, usable segments, and any other part of the 2008 high-speed rail bond act—is excluded.
Essential water projects (Section 21028[q]) consist of building, expanding, repairing, replacing, or improving a public water system, systems that supply public water systems (directly or indirectly), and a system within the scope of the State’s Water Resilience Portfolio. Delta conveyance facilities are excluded.
In addition to these projects, proposed PRC Section 21028(m)(1)(B) states that an essential project also includes the related public, private, and utility infrastructure needed to serve it. That infrastructure covers anything required by a utility or agency or which is included in the application as part of the “whole of the project.” Examples include electric, telecom, gas, water, wastewater, stormwater, transit, police, fire, and transportation improvements.
Benefits and Challenges in Essential Project Definitions
While Article 7 clearly lays out broad classes of projects, there also is room for interpretation, both in the definitions of the classes and the infrastructure needed to serve them. Perhaps the largest focus leading up to the election has been on a currently unpopular type of project: data centers. Some groups have argued that Prop. 45 allows data centers under the broadband or infrastructure support provisions. These groups have used this argument to support a “no” vote on Prop. 45. Others (supporting “yes” on 45) have argued the definition of broadband is clear and does not include data centers. The nonpartisan Office of Legislative Counsel, whose attorneys advise state lawmakers, have opined that data centers are not included in the definition of broadband. Nevertheless, given the controversy surrounding this issue and the financial implications of this use, it is likely an issue that would be settled by the courts if the initiative passes.
Given the language of the proposition, infrastructure needed to serve an essential project may also include wind farms, wastewater treatment facilities, electric distribution lines, and highway capacity improvements, subject to the rules discussed in Article 7 of the initiative.
2: COMPLETENESS REVIEW PROCESS
As a component of the initial screening process in Article 3, Prop. 45 lays out new provisions in PRC Section 21017 related to determining completeness of an application for essential projects. When a lead agency receives an initial application for an essential project, that agency will have 30 days to provide a written determination of completeness after the initial application or after any submittal of supplemental or revised applications (PRC Sections 21017[a][2] and [c][2]). If the lead agency finds the application incomplete, it must provide an “exhaustive written corrections list of items and specific information, or lack thereof,” that resulted in the finding of incompleteness. The applicant has up to 90 days to respond and can request an extension. After the exhaustive list is initially provided to the applicant, if multiple rounds of supplementation by the applicant are needed, the lead agency may not add new items to the initial list. If the lead agency fails to meet any of the 30-day review time frames, the application will be deemed complete for purposes of the essential project CEQA review (PRC Section 21017[c][4]).
Proposed PRC Section 21017 establishes restrictions regarding what a lead agency may ask of an applicant as part of the completeness review (PRC Section 21017[a][3]). The lead agency may only ask for information described in a written “submittal requirement checklist or similar document” publicly available at the time of application or in “statutes, regulations, rules, standards, or ordinances” that are existing laws at the time of the application. An application may not be deemed incomplete because of information beyond these two sources. If lead agencies do not have a written checklist of application requirements, they will only be able to request in applications the requirements of existing laws, as described in statutes, regulations, rules, standards, or ordinances.
An applicant has two recourses if they object to a determination of incompleteness. The applicant may appeal to the planning commission, planning director, or other official with final authority. The final written determination of the appeal must occur within 60 days or the application becomes automatically deemed complete (PRC Section 21017[d]). Within 90 days of the appeal conclusion, the applicant may also bring a civil lawsuit against the lead agency challenging an adverse appeal determination (PRC Section 21017[e]).
Benefits and Challenges of the Completeness Review Process
Comparing the time frames in Prop. 45 to existing law, primarily as defined by the Permit Streamlining Act (Government Code Section 65943), the limitations on application review time are substantially similar, such as a 30-day requirement for a lead agency to determine completeness of a submitted application or a 60-day period to respond to an applicant’s appeal of an incompleteness finding.
Benefits of the proposition’s completeness review process accrue primarily to an applicant in terms of greater certainty about information needed to achieve completeness and the explicit right to file litigation against a lead agency for an adverse finding after appeal. By prohibiting a finding of incompleteness based on any information beyond the “written, publicly available submittal requirement checklist or similar document” or requirements of existing law, a lead agency may not add requirements for other special or additional studies or analysis not included in those two sources. Similarly, if a lead agency is seeking information lacking from the application, after it provides an exhaustive, written list in response to the initial application, it may not add to that list in subsequent review of supplemental application information from the applicant. If an applicant believes an incompleteness appeal determination is not proper, there is an explicit opportunity to file a civil lawsuit against the lead agency.
While the time frames for review of an application or response to an applicant’s appeal of an incompleteness finding are not substantially different from the Permit Streamlining Act, Prop. 45 might prevent a lead agency from adding what it believes is a necessary additional (to what is required in the checklist) study for a peculiar environmental circumstance or in response to new information received during the preliminary scoping process. This provision could be considerably difficult for a complex project requiring review of multiple extensive applicant studies by different lead agency departments with limited staff. In addition, lead agency flexibility to seek important information not anticipated in its application content checklist would be eliminated, which could make it difficult to adequately assess an environmentally complex proposed project.
While not part of Prop. 45, essential projects also could take priority over nonessential projects in an agency’s project review queue. Due to litigation provisions in the proposition, limited staff resources would need to be focused on reviewing application materials for essential projects first and foremost, or risk litigation if deadlines are missed. This could create delays in the processing and approval of nonessential projects (e.g., commercial, industrial, or park projects).
Initial Practice Considerations for Completeness Review under Proposition 45
If Prop. 45 passes, recognizing it would go into effect as soon as the election is certified, lead agencies would need to quickly review their application guidance and checklist for application contents and then update and modify them for thoroughness or create new application materials for essential projects, if needed. If not already posted, the application checklist would need to be uploaded to an accessible place on the agency’s webpage or otherwise made publicly available.
Consideration may be given to updating and adopting a regulation or ordinance (depending on the level of government) to cover the environmental information needed in an essential project application that is tailored to the lead agency’s jurisdiction and geography, including special issues and handling of new information, so an existing law is established upon which to base completeness evaluations. In addition, a lead agency’s appeal process for completeness findings should be made clear in its application checklist guidance, including when to involve the agency’s counsel in the event of an appeal with an adverse outcome for an applicant.
Given the overall time limitations for completion of the CEQA process for essential projects (further discussed below)—365 business days for an EIR, 180 business days for a mitigated negative declaration (Article 4, PRC Section 21018)—lead agencies may need to require complete technical studies, like traffic studies, as part of the application checklist, with careful instructions to applicants discouraging project changes and other factors that could affect completeness of technical studies. Much like what has occurred in practice under NEPA’s tighter preparation timelines, it would not be surprising to see the need for substantially more application materials front-loaded in the application than prepared after project scoping, a dilemma when addressing public and agency concerns in the CEQA process.
3: TIME LIMITS ON CEQA DOCUMENTATION
Article 4 adds strict timelines for completing CEQA documentation for essential projects. Once the application is deemed complete (see above), a local lead agency must meet the following timelines:
Environmental impact report. A lead agency must make a final determination whether to certify an EIR no later than 365 (business) days after the application was deemed complete. (PRC Section 21018[b])
Mitigated negative declaration/negative declaration. A lead agency must make a final determination whether to adopt an MND or ND within 180 (business) days after the application was deemed complete. (PRC Section 21018[c])
Exemption. A lead agency must make a final determination that a project is exempt from or already covered by another document under CEQA within 90 (business) days after the application was deemed complete. (PRC Section 21018[d])
Timeline extensions. The deadlines described herein can be extended upon written request of the applicant (PRC Section 21018[e]) including if the applicant is also the lead agency. (PRC 21020[h])
Similar timelines apply to non-local lead agencies.
Many other timeline-related restrictions are included in the proposition. Some of the key considerations relate to public comments on essential projects (PRC Section 21021). EIRs would be limited to a 45-day public review period and MNDs/NDs to a 20-day public review period. The only comments included in the administrative record would include those received during this period or via oral testimony at a noticed and recorded public hearing, unless there are significant changes to the essential project, subject to certain qualifications. “All other public comments shall be disregarded and excluded from the administrative record,” (PRC Section 21021[d][2]) including those received within 48 hours prior to a public hearing or noticed decision.
Remedies are included for noncompliance with timeline requirements. An applicant may request that the agency hold a hearing on the project. Within 60 days of receiving the request, the lead agency shall complete all environmental review documentation “or assemble available environmental review documentation, including any applicant-prepared environmental review document as is allowed” pursuant to other elements of the Public Resources Code, and hold a hearing to make a final determination on the environmental document and the project (PRC Section 21020[b]). Other remedies are included in PRC Section 21020.
Benefits and Challenges of CEQA Time Limits
Prop. 45 tackles a key frustration surrounding CEQA compliance: time. It does so by imposing strict time frames for document completion and public comments. In particular with regard to public comments, it addresses what is commonly known as “late hits” by restricting the time frame and method by which public comments can be provided. It also alters the balance of power over project schedules by allowing only the applicant to extend the time limits surrounding document preparation.

Proposition 45, its Implementation, and Its Benefits to Public Agencies
Clarification of Impacts of CEQA Reform on Cities and Counties
July 30, 2026
Proposition 45 has raised many questions among stakeholders, including public agencies. To dispel some confusion about how the new law would operate, Hanson Bridgett drafted the letter, below, to help public agencies understand how Proposition 45 would affect their operations, including how it would help these agencies process applications for schools, hospitals, housing, and other essential projects.
To: Interested Parties
Re: Prop. 45 – Local Control and CEQA Litigation Considerations
Hanson Bridgett is representing the California Chamber of Commerce with regard to the proposed Affordable California Act initiative measure, Proposition 45 (Prop. 45). Our firm has many decades of experience in representing local governments on land use matters and a variety of public agencies undertaking significant infrastructure projects, including defending such projects against challenges under the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). I have personally advised public agencies for more than 30 years on infrastructure and development projects.
I have reviewed Prop. 45 with particular attention to its impact on local land use authority and municipal litigation exposure under CEQA. Based on my review, Prop. 45 would not limit an agency’s discretion to approve, deny, or condition a project. While the measure makes changes to the manner in which local governments process what it defines as “essential projects,” it provides valuable public benefits in clarifying the environmental review process and in limiting CEQA litigation.
Some of these benefits will be financial and significant. While agencies recover most costs for private development from the applicants — which won’t change under Prop. 45 — agencies do not have this option with public projects, including programmatic land use plans, public infrastructure projects, and publicly subsidized development such as affordable housing.
Administrative and judicial delays can consume years of staff time, require extensive consultant and outside counsel support, delay critical public infrastructure, and expose taxpayers to escalating costs. With private projects, costs can be recovered from applicants, but time cannot. With streamlined approval and less litigation risk, the time agency staff expends on continuing hearings and preparing administrative records can be better spent on programs that improve the community.
California’s nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (LAO) echoed these points, concluding that Prop. 45 “could reduce the ongoing number of CEQA lawsuits” and that local governments could realize savings through smaller administrative records, reduced litigation demands, and limitations on courts’ ability to rescind a project’s approval. The LAO further noted that faster environmental reviews could help state and local governments avoid inflationary cost increases on public infrastructure projects.
With Prop. 45, cities and counties gain tools to deliver essential public infrastructure more efficiently, improve predictability, and reduce taxpayer costs associated with prolonged project delivery. With private projects, local governments will retain full discretion to approve, disapprove, and condition projects while having better certainty their decisions will not be overturned in court, and without having to overwhelm staff with tasks related to challenges, like the preparation of administrative records.
Local Control Is Preserved
Prop. 45 does not transfer land use authority away from cities or counties. It is a purely procedural streamlining measure that does not require any city to approve a project, create any new right to challenge a project denial, or exempt projects from CEQA review. Local governments retain full discretion to determine the appropriate level of CEQA review, approve, condition, or deny projects, apply zoning and general plan policies, require mitigation measures and technical studies, and impose permit conditions necessary to address local impacts. Local governments also retain authority to adopt new standards and requirements for future projects.
Prop. 45 requires projects to be evaluated using the standards local governments themselves establish. Local governments may rely on any applicable statute, regulation, ordinance, policy, or standard in effect when the application is submitted including standards governing density, height, setbacks, design, noise, traffic, open space, and other local development criteria. Prop. 45 does not limit the substantive standards a city may apply; it simply requires agencies to apply the laws that are in place when an application is submitted. Local governments may also apply subsequently adopted requirements necessary to address a life-safety impact. In short, local governments continue to decide what gets built and under what conditions.
Prop. 45 also preserves local cost recovery. Local governments may continue charging applicants for staff time, consultant expenses, and other project review costs, just as they do today.
Many projects eligible for streamlining — including housing, transportation improvements, fire stations, water infrastructure, schools, healthcare facilities, and broadband projects — are projects local governments frequently sponsor and deliver themselves. When acting as both lead agency and project applicant, local governments retain flexibility to extend review timelines while benefiting from the measure’s litigation protections. A city or county also will have more certainty a responsible agency (e.g., LAFCO, utility provider, resource agency), considering and making determinations about a project that local government wants, will act quickly.
Prop. 45 Strengthens Legal Protections for Local Governments
Under current law, a local government’s decision to approve a project may be challenged by third-parties, many of whom use litigation as a delay tactic to make projects more expensive and less likely to be built. CEQA lawsuits often take years to resolve, imposing significant costs on local governments through prolonged staff commitments, consultant expenses, outside counsel fees, and delayed delivery of public infrastructure. In some cases, the cost and uncertainty of litigation can jeopardize important public projects regardless of the merits of the claims. Prop. 45 reduces the time, cost, and uncertainty associated with CEQA litigation through several targeted reforms:
Common-sense limits on late CEQA comments. Public comment participation is a legal prerequisite to any CEQA lawsuit and local governments must respond to each comment submitted. Some project opponents exploit this requirement by submitting lengthy comments on the eve of a project’s public hearing. Prop. 45 establishes firm public comment periods of 20 days for NDs/MNDs and 45 days for draft EIRs. These periods may not be extended (except by a court), and late comments are excluded from the record except where they could not reasonably have been raised earlier due to project changes or new information. This preserves meaningful public participation while saving agency staff late nights responding to eleventh-hour comments, as well as the time and inconvenience of holding multiple, continued hearings and preparing staff reports and other materials for these purposes. Prop. 45 thereby reduces abuse of the comment process.
30-day statute of limitations. CEQA challenges must be filed within 30 days of the Notice of Determination or Notice of Exemption, allowing local governments to achieve legal certainty sooner.
270-day judicial resolution. CEQA actions, including appeals, generally must be resolved within 270 calendar days. Replacing multi-year litigation with a defined judicial timeline has the potential to save local governments years of delay and substantial legal expense.
Substantial evidence standard. Courts must uphold local decisions supported by substantial evidence, reinforcing deference to local government decisions and making it less likely that locally approved projects will be overturned based on competing interpretations of the record.
Targeted remedies. If a court identifies a deficiency, the remedy is limited to correcting the specific error rather than vacating the entire project approval. This protection will spare local governments from repeating years of environmental review and incurring substantial additional costs to restart project reviews.
Taken together, these provisions provide local governments with meaningful legal protections designed to narrow disputes, expedite their resolution, reduce administrative burdens, and protect taxpayers from the significant costs associated with prolonged CEQA litigation. While it may require some additional effort from cities and counties at the beginning, the benefits will be considerable over time, both to local governments and communities as a whole.
Conclusion
Prop. 45 preserves local control while providing local governments with meaningful legal protections designed to reduce litigation-related delays, improve predictability, and protect taxpayers from the substantial costs associated with prolonged CEQA disputes. While it does impose changes in how local governments process a variety of project approvals, it will make the consideration of many projects more efficient and less costly, adding to the quality of life for the citizens of our state.
Very truly yours,
Michael N. Conneran

Report: Economic and Fiscal Impacts of Proposition 45
About this report: This page is the full text of Economic and Fiscal Impacts of Proposition 45, a report by James Paci and Matthew Newman of the Blue Sky Consulting Group, prepared for the California Chamber of Commerce and published September 25, 2026. Download the original report (PDF) (https://yesonprop45.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/BACA-Full-Economic-and-Fiscal-Impacts-09.25.26_FINAL.pdf).
Key findings

I. Executive Summary
Proposition 45 Overview
Proposition 45 (the “Building an Affordable California Act”) would reform state laws governing the review and approval of certain construction projects in California, including new homes, educational, public health, and public safety facilities, and expansions of transportation, clean energy, and broadband infrastructure (i.e., “essential projects”). This report provides estimates of the economic and fiscal impacts that Prop 45 would generate in California.
Under current law, the approval timeline for essential projects can last several years, resulting in higher construction costs and reduced investment in housing and infrastructure. Prop 45 would reduce review period delays by establishing binding time limits on these review phases and by introducing further procedural reforms related to environmental review litigation, late-filed public comments, and the analysis of project alternatives. Reducing these delays under Prop 45 would result in more housing, lower construction costs, and significant savings for taxpayers and ratepayers.
Prop 45’s Estimated Impacts on Housing, Taxpayers and Ratepayers
Nearly 20,000 additional homes annually. Prop 45’s approval timeline reductions will increase annual housing permitting by 18.1%, or nearly 20,000 additional homes per year, resulting in nearly 200,000 additional homes over ten years.
$774 million in total annual savings on non-residential construction costs. Across both publicly and privately sponsored essential non-residential projects, Prop 45 is estimated to reduce costs by $774 million annually.
Approximately $1.5 billion annually in combined savings and additional revenues for state and local governments and other public agencies. Over the 10-year period following Prop 45’s implementation, the measure’s residential and non-residential impacts are estimated to generate $1.5 billion annually, on average, in additional tax revenues and fiscal savings, including:
$1.1 billion in state and local tax revenues from increased residential construction, and
$386 million in annual savings for public works project sponsors, including $238 million in transportation projects, $73 million in water projects and $52 million in educational facilities.
$250 million in annual savings for California ratepayers. Prop 45’s impact on clean energy project costs is estimated to save California ratepayers $250 million annually.
Prop 45’s Estimated Impact on CEQA Review Timelines
Under current law, EIR reviews take approximately three years. Prop 45’s time limits would reduce delays related to project reviews under the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). For residential projects requiring an Environmental Impact Report (EIR), as shown in Figure 1, the CEQA review period lasts 1,141 days (3.1 years), on average, under current law; non-residential EIR review periods average 1,101 days (3.0 years).
Most EIR reviews exceed Prop 45’s time limit. Under current law, 59% of residential EIRs and 56% of non-residential EIRs take longer than the 591-day maximum review period established by Prop 45.
Prop 45 would cut the average EIR timeline in half. Due to the enforcement of Prop 45’s 591-day limit on EIR certifications, the average EIR review period would decline by 639 days for residential EIRs and 603 days for non-residential EIRs.
Prop 45 would make EIR timelines more predictable. Under current law, roughly 17% of EIR reviews last longer than five years (see Figure 1). By capping this period at 591 days, Prop 45 reduces this review period uncertainty. Among the residential EIRs exceeding this time limit, the average review period was 1,674 days (4.6 years); under Prop 45, these projects’ average review period would decline by 1,082 days or roughly three years.
Non-EIR project reviews would also be completed more quickly. Projects receiving Mitigated Negative Declarations (MNDs), Negative Declarations (NDs) or CEQA exemptions currently have estimated average review periods of six to eight months. Depending on review type, Prop 45 is estimated to reduce these timelines by one to two months.

Other Prop 45 reforms would further reduce review period delays. In addition to its CEQA review period limits, Prop 45 also establishes time limits for other phases of project review, including 30 days for application completeness, 135 days for other discretionary approvals following CEQA review, and 300 days for judicial review. The measure also includes procedural reforms related to streamlined analysis of project alternatives, late-filed public comments, and judicial review. The economic and fiscal estimates in this report quantify only the impacts of Prop 45’s CEQA review timelines and therefore represent conservative lower-bound estimates. They do not include potential impacts from these additional timeline and procedural reforms.

Residential permitting would increase by 18.1% under Prop 45. As shown in Figure 2, based on Prop 45’s estimated impact on CEQA review timelines, the measure would increase annual permitting rates by an estimated 18.1%, or nearly 20,000 additional homes annually. The largest increase occurs among EIR projects, which account for 23.4% of units permitted under the status quo; EIR housing starts are estimated to increase 36.1%. Increases among the non-EIR project types range from 6.5% to 13.9%.

By reducing delay, Prop 45 is estimated to reduce non-residential EIR project costs by 3%, on average. II. Prop 45 Overview
Prop 45’s provisions fall into two broad categories: binding time limits controlling the duration essential project review periods (“timeline provisions”), and procedural reforms that provide options for simplifying a project’s environmental review and any related litigation (“procedural reforms”). 1
Application receipt to application completeness (30+ Days)
Within 30 calendar days of the submission of an essential project application, Prop 45 requires the public agency to determine whether the application is complete. Applicants have 90 days to amend and resubmit applications that are determined incomplete.
Application completeness to CEQA Determination (90 – 591 Days)
Once an application is deemed complete, any environmental review conducted by a lead agency under CEQA is subject to a CEQA review time limit that varies according to the type of CEQA review conducted. Prop 45 requires that EIR certification decisions be made within 365 business days (531 calendar days) of application completeness. 2 For projects receiving a mitigated negative declaration (MND) or Negative Declaration (ND), this determination must be made within 180 business days (262 calendar days) of application completeness. Notices of a project’s exemption from CEQA are required within 90 business days (131 calendar days).
If the lead agency fails to comply with the applicable CEQA review time limit, the applicant may request a public hearing. Within 60 calendar days of this request, the lead agency must complete its CEQA review and issue its determination. As a result, under Prop 45, the maximum timeline for an EIR certification, for example, would generally be 591 days (i.e., 531 days for the certification of an EIR plus this 60-day noncompliance period), while the maximum timeline for an Exempt project is 191 days.
Other Entitlement (135 days)
In addition to CEQA review, essential projects may also require other discretionary approvals. Under Prop 45, the public agencies responsible for these other entitlements must provide approvals within 90 calendar days of the completion of CEQA review. Because agencies that fail to meet this deadline must act within 45 days of an essential project applicant’s written request, Prop 45 effectively limits this review period to 135 days.
Litigation (300 days)
Prop 45 requires that legal challenges brought against essential projects be filed within 30 days of a lead agency’s CEQA determination and that courts resolve this litigation within 270 days using judicial streamlining procedures available for certain projects under existing state law.
