III. Residential Impacts
Project carrying costs, including interest on loans, land holding costs, consultant and legal fees, and construction cost inflation, accrue throughout the entitlement process, and incremental increases in these costs reduce project feasibility, causing projects to be delayed, downsized, or abandoned. Timeline uncertainty compounds this effect, as lenders and investors are more likely to advance projects when entitlement durations are predictable. The expected review timeline reductions under Prop 45 would therefore increase the number of financially feasible projects and raise rates of residential development. 3
Entitlement Time and Entitlement Volatility Elasticity
Prior studies of residential project review periods and development feasibility in California show that development activity is responsive to changes in both the average duration of the entitlement review period as well as changes in the uncertainty (or “volatility”) of this timeline.
Entitlement Time Elasticity
The entitlement time elasticity refers to the extent to which a reduction in the average duration of a project’s entitlement review generates an increase in the rate of homebuilding. Two prior studies in California have estimated this elasticity. First, a Terner Center analysis of housing project feasibility (https://ternercenter.berkeley.edu/research-and-policy/policy-dashboard-los-angeles/) assessed the impacts of various reforms of local zoning rules and entitlement procedures on the number of residential units developed in Los Angeles County. 4 Terner’s findings are based on model pro formas that were developed for each residential parcel in Los Angeles County based on the parcel’s location, status quo zoning designation, and empirical estimates of the costs incurred by developers during each phase of entitlement, permitting, and construction. The Terner analysis finds that a 25% reduction in entitlement timelines would be expected to increase annual housing starts by 9.8% (i.e., an entitlement period elasticity estimate of 0.392). 5 Consistent with the Terner Center’s finding, Gabriel and Kung’s (2024) analysis (https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=4873581) of City of Los Angeles entitlement and permitting data over the 2010-2022 period showed that a 25% reduction in average multifamily project approval time increased the number of residential units permitted annually by 11.4% (i.e., an approval time elasticity of 0.46). 6
For purposes of estimating Prop 45’s impact on residential EIR project development, this report conservatively adopts the Terner Center’s entitlement time elasticity of 0.39.
Entitlement Volatility Elasticity
In addition to the average entitlement duration, entitlement time uncertainty is itself a significant factor affecting residential project feasibility, as investors and developers require larger returns to compensate for added project risks. Gabriel and Kung quantify this uncertainty based on the standard deviation of the natural log of multifamily project approval times and refer to this measure as approval time “volatility.” 7 Based on multifamily development data in Los Angeles, the authors find that a decline of 25% in this log-form standard deviation increases residential project starts by 8.5% (i.e., a volatility elasticity of 0.327).

Prop 45 would make major changes to CEQA. But many CEQA reformers don’t support it
By Joe Garofoli (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/joe-garofoli/) , Political Columnist Oct 21, 2026
Key CEQA reformers are concerned that Prop 45 could lead to more suburban sprawl.
Santiago Mejia/S.F. Chronicle
Some California leaders who have spent years spearheading changes to the state’s landmark environmental protection law either haven’t taken a position on or are opposing Proposition 45, which would take even bigger chunks out of CEQA, the California Environmental Quality Act.
CEQA was created in 1970 under then-Gov. Ronald Reagan to protect the beauty and vibrancy of the state. It requires developers to disclose potential environmental impacts of their projects and work with communities to blunt those impacts. But for decades, the law has been weaponized to jam development by everyone from NIMBYs to construction unions to wealthy suburbanites. A 2024 study (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Report279.pdf) by the Little Hoover Commission found that on average, “litigation adds almost two years to project time frames. In the face of such lengthy delays, financing can vanish, stopping a project even if it would eventually have survived the CEQA process and been approved.” Preparing an environmental impact report can take a year or longer and cost up to $1 million.
Powerful labor interests have balked at changing CEQA, because unions have long used the law to extract wage concessions from developers. Wealthy suburbanites have used it to halt unwanted development. The same study found that 78% of CEQA litigation “may disproportionately challenge housing in higher-income neighborhoods.”

Prop 45 — backed by the California Chamber of Commerce, local chambers around the state, developers and affordable housing advocates — seeks to expedite development by imposing strict deadlines on certain categories of infrastructure projects described as “essential”: housing, water, clean energy, healthcare, public safety, wildfire mitigation, broadband internet access, education and transportation.
Yet some key CEQA reformers are concerned about its unintended consequences, in particular that its provisions to loosen regulations could lead to more suburban sprawl — developments far from urban centers that destroy forest or agricultural land and force residents to drive everywhere, increasing air pollution and greenhouse gas emissions, and exacerbating the climate crisis. Infill housing, meanwhile, is denser and typically enables residents to walk or take public transit to work. Many of California’s leading CEQA reformers oppose suburban sprawl and advocate for infill development, particularly near public transit.
State Sen. Scott Wiener, D-San Francisco, one of the architects of some of the Legislature’s most consequential CEQA reforms over the past decade, isn’t taking a position on the measure. Neither is one of his top allies, California YIMBY (https://cayimby.org/blog/proposition-45-2026/), which advocates for building more homes to ease California’s crippling housing crisis. Environmental advocate Tom Steyer supported (https://x.com/TomSteyer/status/1942757810686812370?s=20) CEQA reforms crafted in the Legislature but opposes (https://tomsteyer.substack.com/p/my-california-ballot-guide) Prop 45. It “goes way beyond any common-sense reforms to CEQA and is using the law to circumvent the public process and due process,” he wrote on Substack.
Other top Democrats have ducked taking a position.

“Let’s say some big data center developer comes in and takes care of some people in the Legislature with donations, and then all of a sudden they’re pushing for those guys to be qualified for this Proposition 45 benefit of not having to go through all the CEQA stuff, and then they get a fast-track deal,” Turnacliff said.
But other leading CEQA reformers are backing Prop 45, including Assembly Member Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland, who wrote (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/joegarofoli/article/california-ceqa-20244075.php?utm_campaign=CMS%20Sharing%20Tools%20(Premium)&utm_source=share-by-email&utm_medium=email) a bill signed by Newsom last year that exempted most infill housing projects from the environmental reviews required under CEQA.
“What Prop 45 represents is a thoughtful way to actually get the projects (completed) that are essential for our communities,” Wicks told reporters Monday at a housing-related campaign event for Becerra in El Cerrito. “It still requires (projects) to go through CEQA. It just puts important shot clocks on it.”
Housing Action Coalition, another frequent ally on CEQA reform legislation, is also breaking ranks to back Prop 45. The organization felt that there were gaps in some recent reform legislation in Sacramento — like the ability to quickly build housing on parking lots at dilapidated shopping mall sites — that weren’t covered by existing legislation, said Ali Sapirman, the group’s advocacy and policy manager. Even though the Housing Action Coalition typically doesn’t support legislation that could lead to sprawl, it is confident that existing CEQA laws could be used to stop unwanted sprawl projects.
“And those gaps are real in terms of numbers,” Sapirman said. “The permitting delays add more than $75,000 to the cost of a new home, and that was really critical to our members.”

“There’s a bunch of stuff that 45 could do that we’re like, ‘Well, that would not be a great outcome,’” said California YIMBY’s Lewis. “But there’s some stuff that it would do that could be a good outcome. We weighed those against each other, and we were like, yeah, they kind of cancel each other out. We’re not going to weigh in on this one.”

By The Editorial Board (https://www.sbsun.com/author/the-editorial-board/) | opinion@scng.com (mailto:opinion@scng.com)

Political leaders on both sides of California’s political spectrum have for years argued the “landmark” California Environmental Quality Act (https://oag.ca.gov/environment/ceqa) has become a well-intentioned mess that delays and halts necessary projects. Each year, lawmakers carve out narrow CEQA exemptions to jumpstart housing and other projects, but the law remains the main impediment to construction.
Serious reformers call for a far-reaching reform rather than a piecemeal approach where the new exemptions always come with strings attached. California voters will finally have a chance to approve a broad revamping of CEQA if they approve Proposition 45 (https://yesonprop45.com/?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24230162147&gbraid=0AAAABERV53DPhse1uF6kJe9gSwNKQkjnn&gclid=Cj0KCQjwh4TVBhCWARIsAG0czmoolxoIXHVW50jx8Fg8UEWwoKIObh-uv0AC-B4mfP7yt_31Pl2Q8uoaAiL4EALw_wcB), which was developed by the California Chamber of Commerce.
Despite claims by opponents (https://www.noprop45ca.com/get-the-facts?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24181535415&gbraid=0AAAABEh2tjegTvJRnKULDVxAsudB3h5RV&gclid=Cj0KCQjwh4TVBhCWARIsAG0czmqIH_J4cEgkiSg8QVsqgJGk_KtWNj31ICRl8y2ShzhVZ9KarZi3AT0aAqDyEALw_wcB), Prop. 45 does not gut a law that requires local agencies to assess the environmental impacts of major projects. Instead, it tweaks the law in sensible and fair-minded ways that provide quicker approval timelines, reduce meritless lawsuits and limit open-ended demands by local agencies.
CEQA applies to any project that requires a discretionary approval. The agency often requires developers to provide an Environmental Impact Report (EIR) (https://abundanthousingla.org/what-is-ceqa-why-it-needs-to-be-reformed-part-i/). CEQA allows virtually anyone to sue the approving agency by arguing the environmental analysis was inadequate. This comes on top of the myriad other local and state approvals.
It’s easy to see how this open-ended process (https://www.hklaw.com/en/case-studies/getting-in-its-own-way-behind-californias-ceqa-curtain) is abused. Unions threaten lawsuits to secure wage concessions. Angry neighbors will do so, also. No-growth groups have mastered the art of delaying, stopping and adding costs to new projects. Nearly half of CEQA lawsuits are filed against public projects. The lawsuits often target environmentally friendly projects, infill housing and transit.
Prop. 45 streamlines CEQA for projects it deems “essential” — housing, water systems, clean energy, health facilities, fire and police stations, forest clearing, education facilities and many transportation projects. Per the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=45&year=2026), it allows a developer to demand a hearing if an agency doesn’t meet its one-year EIR deadline. It requires agencies to specify all the information they need upfront rather than continually moving the goalposts.
The initiative (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=45&year=2026) stops agencies from constantly revising their review standards. It limits timeframes for public comments. It narrows court review so that lawsuits can only halt the part of the project under review rather than the entire project. It sets reasonable parameters on CEQA review rather than allowing the process to drag on for years.

Opponents point to the “high tens of millions of dollars” (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=45&year=2026) it will cost governments to comply with the rewritten rules, but every new regulation or revamping of an old one will require governments to spend money to implement the new procedures. It’s a small sum in the scheme of California budgets and could yield long-term fiscal benefits if it truly succeeds in streamlining more projects.
Opponents also complain about a loss of “local control,” (https://www.rstreet.org/commentary/local-control-is-a-fancy-term-for-big-government/) but CEQA is a state law and the locals have abused it to obstruct important projects. The initiative’s proper goal is to reduce red tape from all levels of government.
Some opponents argue the state’s previous CEQA exemption laws already fix the problems, but that’s clearly not the case. Narrowly crafted CEQA exemptions have not resulted in significant new building because they don’t go far enough.
We suspect most opponents of Prop. 45 and CEQA reform in general simply don’t want to give up any tools for obstructing projects they don’t like. But after decades of them abusing CEQA for their own ends, it’s time to streamline the CEQA process.
Vote “yes” on Proposition 45.

The California Environmental Quality Act has been used in such an abusive way for more than 50 years that then-Gov. Jerry Brown’s 2012 description of CEQA reform as “the Lord’s work” has gone from being seen as a good one-liner from an unusually witty politician to a profound observation about life in the Golden State.
There is a reason the Legislature has had to pass so many CEQA exemptions:
Many major, valuable projects would never have been built without this protection. The 1970 state law makes it too easy for third parties to block or stall proposals that they don’t like or want to be paid to support. This led directly to a 2017 analysis that documents CEQA’s central role in the state’s decades-old shortage of housing, massively driving up the cost of all types of shelter and impoverishing millions of residents.

Yes, of course, some CEQA lawsuits are defensible and necessary.
But when you see the range of organizations that have vowed support for Proposition 45 — a modest CEQA reform on the November ballot sponsored by the California Chamber of Commerce — it’s eye-opening.
The California Hospital Association, the California Farm Bureau, the California Senior Alliance and more than a half-dozen clean energy groups are among a vast list of institutions seeking relief from the migraines they face because of the broadly written, vague law.
Prop. 45 would impose a 365-day limit on official environmental reviews for projects ranging from broadband construction to building roads, homes and schools to wildfire mitigation. Courts would be given a maximum of 270 days to rule on CEQA suits after they are filed.
Contrary to claims that the changes would gut “the state’s strongest-in-the-nation environmental laws,” local governments would still have considerable authority in the approval process. Activists wouldn’t be muzzled.
This is reflected in the analysis of Prop. 45 from the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office.
The LAO’s biggest concern had to do with potentially substantial implementation costs for state and local governments, not weakened green regulations. And the analysis also noted the benefit to governments of new revenue from ventures no longer blocked by CEQA — and from having their own projects cost less.
Prop. 45 won’t transform the state’s regulatory maze overnight. But it would make California’s planning approval process fairer, less expensive and considerably more predictable.
Yes on 45.

Complex projects often require more extensive study, and unless technical studies are included in the application (see discussion regarding completeness review), it may be difficult to complete studies in a manner that allows the deadlines in the initiative to be attained. Simple examples include biological studies requiring species surveys tied to certain seasons, traffic studies that could rely on the inclusion of school-year data, and groundwater studies based on full-year operations. Further, controversial projects may generate hundreds or thousands of public comments needing response. In the case of an EIR, 365 business days equals roughly a year and a half. EIR practitioners are aware of the extreme challenges imposed by these time frames, especially if an applicant does not grant an extension.
Initial Practice Considerations for Time Limits under Proposition 45
The time limit provisions under Prop. 45 may be the most daunting components of this initiative and may raise the most perplexing uncertainties—including potential outcomes if it is not possible to complete CEQA documentation as required.
Lead agencies will be under extreme time pressure for any projects that generate substantial public interest and/or that are complex. They should understand all phases of CEQA compliance and the time involved and may need to adjust internal review time frames and review rounds for administrative draft documents.
We have addressed the need for ordinances or other mechanisms to establish “objective” thresholds and conduct completeness review. Lead agencies may also consider when project changes trigger a new review for completeness, as well as other rules that could help facilitate compliance with the time limits.
4: PRELIMINARY SCOPING PROCESS
Pursuant to Article 5, PRC Section 21024, Prop. 45 would create for qualifying essential projects an alternative scoping process to the notice of preparation and public scoping period in classic CEQA. The applicant may voluntarily choose to employ the preliminary scoping process. If the applicant does not choose this process, other scoping requirements of CEQA would continue to apply. The preliminary scoping process described in PRC Section 21024 must be completed in not more than 60 days.
An applicant would begin by providing written notice to the lead agency of its intent to complete the preliminary scoping process. The notice must present “a preliminary overview and description of the proposed essential project sufficient to inform the lead agency and the public of the anticipated features of the project.” Details like engineering plans, technical studies, or design drawings are not required. The written notice must include, to the extent known: (A) location, size, boundaries; (B) principal components and fundamental purpose; (C) general type of use, facility, infrastructure; (D) potentially affected resource areas; and (E) anticipated public agency permits or approvals. Beyond location, size, and boundaries; principal components; and type of use, facility, or infrastructure, other specifics about site plan, building height or mass, infrastructure dimensions, or other physical characteristics are not required.
After receiving the notice, the lead agency and the applicant are to hold at least two meetings to discuss the project and impacted resource areas. The lead agency will record all meetings. The lead agency must post the notice on a website so the public can submit comments by email. The applicant may, but need not, convene a public scoping meeting. The applicant must maintain a summary record of input but “shall not be required to respond to any input received.”
Benefits and Challenges of the Preliminary Scoping Provision
The benefit relates to improved efficiency of scoping with this process, in part because it focuses scoping deliberations between the applicant and the lead agency, including the need for at least two discussion meetings. Also, a maximum time frame is created for improved schedule certainty (no more than 60 days).
This process involves limitations compared with current CEQA requirements. CEQA scoping notifies and seeks important input about potential environmental effects to be studied from trustee and responsible agencies. In addition, it requires a scoping meeting for major projects (i.e., projects of statewide, regional, or areawide significance). A challenge of the preliminary scoping process is the loss of these important avenues of input about potential environmental impacts. Finally, with the allowance in this new preliminary scoping process that an applicant shall not be required to respond to scoping input, ambiguity may arise about how much the public input may ultimately influence environmental document contents. Nonetheless, applicants would be well advised to fully consider public input.
Initial Practice Considerations for Scoping under Proposition 45
Initial practice recommendations for scoping under Prop. 45 include seeking an applicant’s decision about its process choice as early as possible, determining if some other form of consultation with trustee and responsible agencies is needed, and reserving one of the applicant/lead agency meetings to consider public input and agree on environmental document contents at the end of the up-to-60-day scoping period.
5: DETERMINATION OF IMPACT SIGNIFICANCE
Currently, the determination of significance of environmental impacts under CEQA involves the use of quantitative thresholds (e.g., vehicle miles traveled, pounds per day of specified air emissions, exceedance of a certain decibel level) and qualitative thresholds (e.g., conflict with existing zoning for agricultural use, exposure to noxious odors, interfere substantially with sensitive species migratory corridors, physically divide a community, expose people to significant wildfire risks). Determination of significance is based on substantial evidence provided via technical expertise, modeling, field observations, and other sources.
Under proposed PRC Section 21022(a)(1), a public agency considering an essential project must “identify, evaluate, determine significance, and mitigate the impacts of an essential project based on compliance with existing laws.”
“Existing laws” is defined under proposed PRC Section 21028(r):
Laws in effect when the application is filed. These are “formally adopted legal requirements contained in statutes, regulations, rules, standards, or ordinances” in effect on the date the application was submitted. This definition effectively freezes the standards as of that date.
An exception for later life-safety rules. A later-adopted requirement can apply only if the lead agency finds compliance is needed to address a “specific, adverse life-safety impact.” That means a “significant, quantifiable, direct, and unavoidable” impact, based on “objective, identified and written public safety standards.”
Building code updates. Updates to the California Building Standards Code, including the Fire Code, apply if they take effect before that same cutoff.
Under proposed PRC Section 21022(a)(2), an agency may have “published, adopted, or routinely used” thresholds of significance prior to the submittal of an essential project reapplication or application. This section allows the applicant to elect to vest into these thresholds. Proposed PRC Section 21022(c) also allows the applicant to waive the above requirements in writing.
Benefits and Challenges for Impact Analysis
By limiting impact determinations to compliance with existing laws, interpretations of significance are largely limited. Issues that typically require professional judgment, such as whether a scenic vista is significantly affected or groundwater overdraft is substantial, either would need to be compared to objective legal standards where they can be created or seemingly would not be evaluated for significance.
With this limitation, which is seemingly beneficial in terms of certainty in impact determinations, a number of challenges are raised. Only a limited number of agencies have formally adopted CEQA thresholds of significance that are based on existing laws as proposed under Prop. 45. Typically, agencies use PRC Section 21083(b), State CEQA Guidelines Section 15065, State CEQA Guidelines Appendix G, recommended thresholds from agencies (e.g., air districts), or recommendations of experts based on substantial evidence. In some cases, customized thresholds of significance are also created by agencies to address environmental impacts unique to the project under evaluation.
The proposed provisions under PRC Section 21022(a)(2), in combination with PRC Section 21029, may make difficult impact determinations for certain topics, including aesthetics, agricultural resources, biological resources, cultural resources, energy, land use and planning, recreation, and wildfire, that are not easily addressed through existing laws.
Although the CEQA statute and the State CEQA Guidelines would meet the definition of an existing law under PRC Section 21028(r), the use of, for example, responses to Appendix G (Initial Study checklist) to determine significance may not be appropriate when they involve qualitative thresholds (even when supported by substantial evidence), such as if a project like a large transmission line would substantially affect a scenic vista. Such a determination may involve judgment and therefore not meet the definition of existing laws under proposed PRC Section 21028(r). In addition, recommended thresholds that are not formally adopted but are based on objective standards (e.g., numeric thresholds involving air pollution provided by air districts) may also not meet the definition of an existing law under PRC Section 21028(r).
Initial Practice Considerations for Impact Significance Determination under Proposition 45
One option is that agencies could formally adopt thresholds of significance for essential projects that meet the requirements of proposed PRC Section 21022(a)(2) and PRC Section 21029. However, formal adoption may be a lengthy process and would not likely be in place in time to address essential project applications that could be submitted immediately after November 3, 2026, should Prop. 45 be approved by the voters.
6: STANDARD OF REVIEW
CEQA generally requires a lead agency to prepare an EIR whenever substantial evidence supports a fair argument that a project may have a significant effect on the environment, even if other substantial evidence supports a contrary conclusion (State CEQA Guidelines Section 15064[f][1]). The fair argument standard is one of CEQA’s defining features because it sets a comparatively low threshold for requiring an EIR.
Prop. 45 substantially narrows judicial review of CEQA challenges to essential projects. Proposed Article 6, PRC Section 21026, lays out judicial review of essential project approvals. This section applies to all essential projects and provides that “a petitioner’s claims shall be limited to a public agency’s noncompliance with objective existing laws, and the scope of the court’s review shall be limited to whether the approval or authorization complies with objective existing laws,” and “for the purpose of this subdivision, ‘objective’ means involving no personal or subjective judgment and being uniformly verifiable by reference to an external and uniform benchmark or criterion available and knowable by both the applicant and the public agency before the application was submitted.” These provisions apply to EIRs and MNDs alike, raising the standards needed to overturn approval of these documents.
Benefits and Challenges of the Standard of Review Provision
The fair argument standard has long been a target of CEQA reform advocates because it sets a low bar for requiring an EIR, which is CEQA’s most comprehensive, time-consuming, and costly level of review. For the same reason, environmental advocates regard it as one of the most important tools for ensuring full analysis and disclosure before project approval. The fair argument standard has been well known for its ability to empower petitioners, whether an environmental or neighborhood group challenging an adjacent development, or a labor union or other economic interest using CEQA for leverage.
Prop. 45 eliminates the fair argument standard applied to adequacy of MNDs and places them on equal footing with EIRs. Further, by limiting review of either MNDs or EIRs to “noncompliance with objective existing laws,” litigation risk would be substantially reduced.
The challenges associated with the changes in standard of review reflect those discussed above for the “determination of significance” in that challenges may arise around both the need to adopt thresholds that conform to the initiative’s definition of existing laws and how such laws can or would be drafted to address issues typically more subjective or not based on such laws (like aesthetics, several biological resource issues, historic resources, etc.). Presumably, if no objective existing laws address these traditional CEQA issue areas, the analysis of them would not be subject to litigation challenge.
Initial Practice Considerations of the Standard of Review Provision under Proposition 45
If enacted, Prop. 45 could give lead agencies and applicants greater confidence in relying on NDs and MNDs for essential projects. Combined with the proposition’s shortened review timelines, abbreviated public comment periods, and accelerated judicial review, significant time and cost savings could result.
The same considerations for “determination of significance” surrounding the need for lead agencies to adopt standards of significance apply here.
7: ALTERNATIVES ANALYSIS
CEQA currently requires an EIR to evaluate a range of reasonable alternatives, including a mandatory no project alternative (State CEQA Guidelines Section 15126.6). The purpose is to identify feasible alternatives that would avoid or substantially lessen significant impacts while attaining most of the project’s basic objectives. This provision gives decision-makers options and lets them compare environmental tradeoffs.
Proposed Article 5, PRC Section 21025, allows a restriction on the range of alternatives. An applicant may voluntarily elect to use the preliminary scoping process (see prior discussion of this topic, above), which includes a streamlined alternatives analysis. PRC Section 21025 permits an applicant to develop a singular alternative to the project, subject to lead agency review and comment, that is presumed to lessen impacts. The applicant’s alternative thus becomes the only alternative, aside from the “no project” alternative, the EIR can evaluate—unless the applicant proposes additional alternatives for consideration.
The alternative must take into consideration input received during preliminary scoping and be compatible with the project’s “fundamental purpose.” To the extent practicable, it must also be compatible with applicable local zoning and land use policies. The alternative need not be located on a different site (proposed PRC Section 21025[a]). It may also include different or additional components than the proposed project. Such components may consist of on- or off-site physical improvements, or alternative operational parameters or programs designed to lessen impacts (proposed PRC Section 21025[b][2][B]). Prop. 45 does not define “fundamental purpose” or explain how that concept relates to CEQA’s well-developed framework for project objectives. It also allows applicants to propose additional alternatives at their discretion (proposed PRC Section 21025[f]). However, Prop. 45 offers little guidance on how those alternatives would fit into a process otherwise built around a single applicant alternative and the no project alternative.
The lead agency must certify whether the alternative meets the requirements of Article 5 after the applicant transmits the project alternative and no project alternative. The lead agency’s discretion regarding consideration of the alternatives appears limited to certification (see above). Prop. 45 does not address circumstances where the lead agency concludes the alternative(s) do not meet the requirements of Article 5.
Benefits and Challenges of the Alternatives Provision
The benefits of the alternatives provision are less obvious than those of the initiative’s other streamlining provisions. Developing a reasonable range of alternatives takes time. Alternatives are also best formulated once the analysis has progressed far enough to identify the significant impacts they are meant to address, and it may therefore be difficult to propose feasible alternatives that reduce significant effects during a preliminary process. Prop. 45 does attempt to address some challenges with the current CEQA process. For instance, the State CEQA Guidelines require evaluation of a reasonable range of alternatives but do not define what should be considered a reasonable range. Lead agencies thus sometimes require consideration of five to ten-plus alternatives, which can add time and cost to an EIR. However, while more certainty is provided by placing limits on the number of alternatives, this provision places responsibility for developing the alternative in the hands of the party with an economic interest in project approval rather than the entity, the lead agency, that is charged with reducing the significant effects of a project via mitigation or alternatives. Under the streamlined process, both the proposed alternative and the no project alternative would largely be developed before the environmental analysis has proceeded past scoping. A project’s significant impacts may not be well understood within 15 days after scoping closes. As a result, alternatives may have to be formulated before the issues they are meant to address have been fully identified.
Prop. 45 also says little about the lead agency’s discretion once the applicant submits its alternatives. Can a lead agency require substantial revisions if the proposed alternative does not meaningfully reduce significant impacts? Can it reject the applicant’s description of the no project alternative if it believes reasonably foreseeable conditions would differ materially? Beyond noting that the lead agency must certify that the applicant has met the procedural requirements of Article 5, the initiative does not address these questions.
Initial Practice Considerations for Alternatives under Proposition 45
Lead agencies may want to develop a clear set of criteria they expect in alternatives to the project, including substantial evidence to support the criteria (such as impact reduction) so that applicants have sufficient guidance to successfully achieve the alternatives certification. Lead agencies may also consider requiring an applicant to submit a preliminary assessment of potential alternatives as part of the application process.
8: TRIBAL CONSULTATION PROCESS
In Article 3, PRC Section 21016, the initiative describes an alternative process of tribal consultation for qualifying essential projects. All essential projects must follow the alternative tribal consultation process if they use the Prop. 45 streamlining provisions, per PRC Section 21015(d)(1).
The tribal consultation process pertains to consultation with “consulting tribes,” which are defined as tribes appearing on the most recent list of Federally Recognized Indian Tribes that are traditionally and culturally affiliated with the geographic area of the proposed essential project (PRC Section 21028[e][1]). Also, for essential projects using this process, the definition of “California Native American tribe,” as used in all other sections of CEQA, is changed to “consulting tribes,” per PRC 

[Showing characters 20000 to 40000 of 52208. Call web_fetch with offset 40000 to keep reading.]

Section 21028(e)(2). As a result, Prop. 45 replaces the Assembly Bill 52 (PRC Section 21080.3.1 et seq.) consultation process for essential projects, and California tribes not listed by the federal government are ineligible for the PRC Section 21016 consultation process.
The applicant starts the process by submitting project information to the lead agency and beginning an initial screening process, separate from (but presumably concurrent with) the preliminary scoping process. The lead agency is to complete a records search within 20 days of receipt of the project information, including the NAHC Sacred Lands File, California’s regional information center, and lead agency records. The lead agency must provide the project information and records search results to any consulting tribe with an invitation to “meet and confer.” If a consulting tribe does not respond to the invitation within 30 days, the initial screening process will be deemed complete. If tribal consultation is initiated, it is to follow the AB 52 process, with several modifications, including (1) only federally recognized tribes may consult; (2) measures to avoid or mitigate a significant impact to tribal cultural resources must be agreed in writing between the lead agency, the tribe, and the applicant; and (3) a lead agency may approve a project if tribal consultation has ended in good faith, agreed upon mitigation is adopted as a project condition, and infeasibility to avoid and preserve in place is documented with substantial evidence.
Benefits and Challenges of the Essential Project Tribal Consultation Process
Prop. 45’s tribal consultation process generally benefits the applicant through shorter time frames to complete consultation and the lead agency through control of process features. The lead agency produces the records search, which must occur in a 20-day period after receiving project information, faster than traditional records searches. The process assigns discretion to the lead agency to decide whether or not to use tribal methods and standards or traditional knowledge, with an explanation of its decision if it declines. The applicant also has more assigned authority to approve in writing mitigation measures resulting from consultation, along with a tribe and the lead agency.
The primary challenge relates to the exclusion of California Native American tribes recognized by the state but not by the federal government. A comparison of the Native American Heritage Commission’s list of California tribes and the federally recognized list confirms that approximately 60 tribes now able to consult under the AB 52 process lack federal recognition; these California tribes would not qualify for Prop. 45’s tribal consultation process. Also, compliance with the 20-day time frame for provision of a records search would be very difficult and likely often infeasible for smaller lead agencies without the availability of a professional archaeologist.
Initial Practice Considerations for Tribal Consultation under Proposition 45
AB 52 has benefited from a sufficiently prescribed process with action steps, templates of consultation tools, and tribal communication protocols that are well known and documented. Practitioners, lead agencies, the Native American Heritage Commission, and tribal representatives would need to quickly modify procedural guidance and templates to tailor them to the proposition’s process. Also, lead agencies need to determine how to expedite the records search process to meet the 20-day deadline. Finally, the state may need to consider how to address the needs of California tribes that qualify for AB 52 but are no longer eligible for Prop. 45’s tribal consultation process.
Conclusion
If Prop. 45 passes, it will no doubt trigger initial questions and confusion regarding definitions and process ambiguities, which likely will result in legal challenges even before the first essential project is processed. As implementation begins, it will necessitate updates to the State CEQA Guidelines and establishment of new lead agency processes, ultimately resulting in an initial flurry of incurred costs and project-specific challenges.
As described herein, Prop. 45’s strict timelines would undoubtedly put extra pressure on lead agency staff to expedite essential project review. Setting up processes for determining what are essential projects and how they should be processed alone could present a burden for public agencies that are already short-staffed and under-resourced. In particular, smaller agencies that rely on contract planners and attorneys may be especially hard hit by requirements to expedite agency review and usher projects through CEQA at an accelerated pace.
These process changes and associated staffing needs, along with the costs associated with developing new guidelines and standards, meeting tighter time limits, and responding to legal challenges, would result in as-yet-uncertain fiscal impacts. Some of these costs could be covered by fees paid by applicants, and once Prop. 45 compliance has ramped up, some costs may decline. But according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, initial costs for state and local governments would potentially exceed $100 million annually. While fiscal impacts in the longer term are uncertain, it is possible that faster project approvals could save local governments money, and higher tax revenues could be generated.
In sum, Prop. 45 includes provisions that mirror past reform proposals by sensible, educated CEQA practitioners, attorneys, and legislators, and its intent to expedite entitlement of “essential” projects is commendable. However, in casting their ballots this November, voters must consider not only the potential benefits of creating faster entitlement pathways for projects that may indeed be considered “essential” to the prosperity of our communities and our economy, but also the potential pitfalls of establishing a new process applicable to a subset of projects subject to CEQA. And while the CEQA statute most certainly leaves room for improvement, we should be mindful of integrating a revised compliance regime that can be amended only through a two-thirds majority of the legislature and only in ways that further the measure’s stated purposes.

Proposition 45: No Recommendation
September 23, 2026
Share
Share this page on Twitter (https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcayimby.org%2Fblog%2Fproposition-45-2026%2F&text=Proposition+45%3A+%3Cspan+class%3D%22dewidow%22%3ENo+Recommendation%3C%2Fspan%3E)
Share this page on Facebook (https://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fcayimby.org%2Fblog%2Fproposition-45-2026%2F&t=Proposition%2045:%20No%20Recommendation)
Share this page via Email (mailto:?subject=Proposition+45%3A+%3Cspan+class%3D%22dewidow%22%3ENo+Recommendation%3C%2Fspan%3E+-+California+YIMBY&body=https%3A%2F%2Fcayimby.org%2Fblog%2Fproposition-45-2026%2F)
by Max Dubler
Introduction
While Proposition 45 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/45/index.htm) meaningfully touches on housing, it will have a much more significant impact on non-housing projects. Pro-housing voters should consider the arguments for and against the measure and make their own decision based on their values.
Analysis
Background: The California Environmental Quality Act
Passed in 1970 and signed into law by then-Governor Reagan, the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA, say “SEE-kwah”) required government agencies to study and publicize the potential environmental impacts of public projects like dams, highways, and power plants, and gave the public the right to sue if they do not believe the impact analysis is sufficient. The scope of the law was massively expanded when the courts ruled that any project that requires public approval is a “public project.” This empowered a wide variety of interests to use the CEQA process to delay or block projects they don’t like.
Last year, the state legislature passed AB 130 (https://cayimby.org/legislation/ab-609/), which exempted (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/06/ceqa-urban-development-infill-budget/) “infill” housing, broadly defined [1] as homes in existing developed areas, from environmental review under CEQA. This was a major victory for California YIMBY, which has long sought this exemption and sponsored AB 609, which was incorporated into AB 130.
What does Prop 45 do?
Creates an alternative, opt-in process with strict “shot clocks” for environmental review (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-45/legal-text/#prop-45-local-timelines) for “essential” housing, water, transportation ( excluding high speed rail), clean energy, transmission, broadband, and healthcare infrastructure. Environmental review for these projects must be completed within 365 business days, or about a year and a half. There are shorter timelines for determining application completeness (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-45/legal-text/#prop-45-completeness) (30 days) and lesser levels of environmental review (180 days for a negative declaration or a mitigated negative declaration).
Creates a 90-day shot clock for “any and all” public agency approvals required for essential projects besides CEQA, including building permits, Coastal Development Permits, and utility approvals.
Requires tribal consultation for all projects, AB 130 labor standards for housing projects (except 100% affordable projects under 85’), and Section 21183.5 labor standards (https://law.justia.com/codes/california/code-prc/division-13/chapter-6-5/section-21183-5/) for other projects that use this environmental review pathway.
Limits public comment on environmental reviews to 45 days (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-45/legal-text/#prop-45-public-comment).
Limits the scope of “alternative projects” that must be analyzed (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-45/legal-text/#prop-45-alternatives) in the environmental review process to one alternative proposed by the applicant and a “no project” alternative.
Creates a new evidentiary standard for environmental impacts (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-45/legal-text/#prop-45-impacts) requiring that they only be found significant if they violate objective, quantifiable standards already in existing law (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-45/legal-text/#prop-45-judicial-scope) when a project is proposed, and freezes those standards on the date a project application is filed (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-45/legal-text/#prop-45-impacts). This would eliminate public agencies’ broad discretion to explore project alternatives and negotiate environmental mitigations.
Curtails (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-45/legal-text/#prop-45-remedies) courts’ ability to block projects in their entirety. If a legal challenge to a project’s environmental review is successful, the remedy is limited to the specific issue identified in the lawsuit. The courts can’t order an agency to rescind its approval of the broader project.
Broadly, Prop 45 tightens up the environmental review process. It will make it easier to build infrastructure and other large scale projects by curtailing potential litigants’ ability to slow down and block construction by filing lawsuits challenging projects’ environmental impact analyses.
How does this affect housing?
Prop 45 would affect housing in two major ways: first, it would make it easier to build housing projects [2], mostly new subdivisions, that do not qualify for the AB 130 infill exemption, as well as the infrastructure necessary to service those housing projects. Second, it would significantly speed public agency approvals for housing projects that use this environmental review process.
The labor provisions in AB 130, the existing CEQA infill exemption, would apply (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-45/legal-text/#prop-45-housing-labor) to projects that use the Prop 45 environmental review process unless (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-45/legal-text/#prop-45-mandatory-parts) they are also using a different streamlining law that mandates prevailing wages or a project labor requirement, in which case they would have to abide by those requirements.
While Prop 45 will speed public agency approvals for all housing, it will also make it easier to build car-dependent sprawl housing and the freeways and water infrastructure necessary to serve that sprawl.
What does California YIMBY think of this?
While this measure does affect housing, it’s not primarily about housing. Rather, it’s about reining in an out of control CEQA process (https://www.theatlantic.com/ideas/archive/2021/03/signature-environmental-law-hurts-housing/618264/) that has ballooned far beyond what the legislature intended in 1970 and made building large projects slow and expensive (https://www.mercurynews.com/2025/04/20/ceqa-california-high-speed-rail/?share=aft0p2r22rr2itegarfi).
Prop 45 would reform CEQA by bringing policy ideas that have worked to streamline housing permitting—shot clocks, objective standards that vest at the time of an application, limited agency discretion to expand the scope of review, narrow remedies, etc—to the environmental review process.
Whether this is a good idea depends on how you weigh the tradeoffs: is permitting new wind and solar energy infrastructure faster worth making it easier to build freeways? Should we make it easier to build transmission lines to carry that clean energy to consumers, even if it means potentially impacting wildlife habitat? Zooming out, is litigation about the public disclosure of environmental impacts (https://history.yale.edu/publications/public-citizens-attack-big-government-and-remaking-american-liberalism) really the best way to weigh the environmental costs of large projects against their potential public benefits and ensure that communities have a voice in what’s built near them?
These are big fundamental questions about growth, sustainability, and the proper structure of democratic decision-making.
Narrowing the focus to housing, the central question here is how you feel about sprawl. California YIMBY works to make it easier to build new homes in our existing cities and towns, where we already have infrastructure to serve them. As we have said before (https://cayimby.org/news-events/statement-in-support-of-the-east-solano-plan/):
“When it comes to solving our housing crisis, our focus remains on making it easier to build housing in existing cities—near quality jobs and public services. Toward this end, we have worked to liberalize (https://cayimby.org/reports/california-adu-reform-a-retrospective/) zoning, streamline (https://cayimby.org/legislation/sb-330/) permitting, and reduce (https://cayimby.org/legislation/ab-2097/) costs. We believe we can (and must) solve the housing and climate crises simultaneously. That means building communities with denser housing and alternatives to automobile dependence.”
That said, we support building well-designed new cities (https://cayimby.org/news-events/statement-in-support-of-the-east-solano-plan/) and we realize that some greenfield development will necessarily be part of solving our housing shortage. Given the scale of the housing crisis, we need all the new housing we can get. Further, lots of people want single family homes on larger lots; and they should be able to have them, to the extent that is sustainable and feasible.
Still, our friends in the environmental movement have raised significant substantive concerns (https://www.greenbelt.org/blog/ceqa-baca-initiative/) about this measure. Most relevant to housing voters: we should not be building new homes in the fire-prone wildland urban interface (https://cayimby.org/blog/the-impact-of-land-use-planning-on-wildfire-risk-a-study-in-southern-california/) because doing so puts people in harm’s way (https://cayimby.org/blog/how-the-northwests-wildfire-crisis-is-a-sprawl-crisis/) and exacerbates our insurance crisis (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-07-22/californians-are-subsidizing-mansion-wildfire-insurance-as-fair-risk-explodes). The fact that Prop 45 makes it easier to build freeways but not high speed rail also gives us pause.
The bottom line: there are good reasons to support this measure and good reasons to oppose it. Housing voters should consider it in light of broader concerns about climate and sustainability.
Recommendation: Neutral
Further Reading
Ballotpedia analysis (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_45,_Changes_to_Environmental_Review_Process_for_Certain_Projects_Initiative_(2026)), “yes” endorsement from Circulate Planning and Policy (https://www.circulatesd.org/why_circulate_supports_prop_45), “no” endorsement from Greenbelt Alliance (https://www.greenbelt.org/blog/ceqa-baca-initiative/), annotated measure text from GrowSF (https://growsf.org/voter-guide/san-francisco-voter-guide-november-2026-election/measures/prop-45/legal-text/), Legislative Analyst’s Office analysis (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=45&year=2026), Public Citizens: The Attack on Big Government and the Remaking of American Liberalism (https://history.yale.edu/publications/public-citizens-attack-big-government-and-remaking-american-liberalism) (book)
Notes
[1] AB 130 defines an “infill” project as one where the project site meets any of the following criteria:
(A) Has been previously developed with an urban use.
(B) At least 75 percent of the perimeter of the site adjoins parcels that are developed with urban uses.
(C) At least 75 percent of the area within a one-quarter mile radius of the site is developed with urban uses.
(D) For sites with four sides, at least three out of four sides are developed with urban uses and at least two-thirds of the perimeter of the site adjoins parcels that are developed with urban uses.
”Urban use” means any current or previous residential or commercial development, public institution, or public park that is surrounded by other urban uses, parking lot or structure, transit or transportation passenger facility, or retail use, or any combination of those uses.
[2] The measure’s definition of “essential housing projects” is extremely broad, encompassing residential projects; mixed-use projects; transitional housing, emergency shelters, and supportive housing; farmworker housing; group living accommodations like monasteries; student housing of all types; senior housing; new subdivisions; and adaptive reuse of commercial buildings.

Prop
45
CA
Prop
45
|
Statute
Modifies Environmental Review for Certain Projects
Changes the California Environmental Quality Act to streamline the environmental review of eight categories of housing and certain transportation, energy, health, public safety, education, and water projects designated as essential.
SPUR's Recommendation
The SPUR Board of Directors could not reach a supermajority consensus position on this measure. SPUR agrees that CEQA creates excessive risk, cost, uncertainty, and delay and has consistently supported targeted reforms for infill housing, clean energy, and climate resilience. However, Prop. 45 would make broader changes that conflict with SPUR’s vision for urban growth. The measure could accelerate desirable projects, such as infill housing near transit and zero-emission energy infrastructure, but it could also streamline development that contributes to sprawl or environmental harm, including subdivisions on the urban edge and polluting energy facilities. Given weak growth controls and lower land costs at the urban edge, Prop. 45's provisions could encourage development patterns that undermine the measure’s benefits and SPUR’s mission. Prop. 45 could reduce frivolous litigation and delays by strengthening evidentiary standards and establishing deadlines. However, its timelines could strain local governments, and potential lawsuits could discourage legitimate planning decisions. Finally, the law would be difficult to modify, requiring voter approval or a two-thirds legislative majority.
The SPUR Board of Directors supports removing excessive risk, uncertainty, and delay from building infill housing, public transit, drinking water, hospitals, schools, and truly zero-emission infrastructure in the right places, but it remains deeply concerned about this measure’s potential negative impacts.
No Recommendation
What Prop. 45 Would Do
Proposition 45 would amend the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to streamline environmental review for eight categories of projects it deems “essential,” regardless of location or scale, as well as any related public, private, or utility infrastructure. It would limit the scope of environmental analysis, create shorter, enforceable timelines, narrow court discretion, and provide project applicants with new enforcement remedies.
“Essential” projects are described as:
Housing projects , defined as residential units, emergency shelters, transitional housing, supportive housing, farmworker housing, mixed-use developments, student housing, group living accommodations, and senior housing
Clean energy projects that produce, generate, or store electricity derived from renewable or sustainable resources, including but not limited to solar, wind, geothermal, fuel cells, small hydroelectric generation, digester gas, biomass, landfill gas, ocean wave, ocean thermal, or tidal current, and associated transmission lines
Water projects, including those that directly or indirectly provide water to a public water system
Public health projects , defined as medical treatment facilities
Public safety projects, defined as first-responder facilities or wildfire reduction projects undertaken by a public agency, including home hardening and vegetation management and electric utility line replacement, hardening, or undergrounding
Broadband Internet access projects, defined as projects to provide mass market retail Internet service to customers, such as data centers
Transportation projects, including public streets, highways, bridges, transit projects, and electric vehicle charging and refueling infrastructure
Education facilities, including their acquisition and expansion
Projects eligible for streamlining would include new construction, improvements, maintenance, repair, or replacement projects. Projects not eligible for streamlining under this measure include jail or detention facilities, new oil or natural gas production facilities, the California high-speed rail system, and the Delta conveyance project.
Prop 45 would make the following key changes to CEQA environmental review:
Enforceable timelines for environmental review: Currently, the timeline for certifying an environmental review depends on the project’s complexity and the staff workload at the responsible public agency (the “lead agency”). Prop. 45 would establish the following enforceable timelines for the certification of an environmental review:
30 days to determine whether an application is complete
180 days to approve a negative declaration (when a project has no environmental impacts) or mitigated negative declaration (when a project’s environmental impacts can be mitigated)
365 days to certify an environmental impact report
If a lead public agency misses these deadlines or imposes unlawful conditions on the project, applicants may file a legal complaint within 90 days to compel a decision and may require the lead agency to convene its highest-ranking governing body to vote on the project application.
Public comment: Prop. 45 would cap public comment periods for essential projects at 45 days for draft environmental impact reports and 20 days for negative or mitigated negative declarations.
Scope of environmental review: The measure would narrow the scope of the environmental impact report for essential projects and give project applicants greater discretion. Key changes include:
Optional scoping: Makes the scoping phase of environmental impact reports optional. If the project applicant pursues scoping, the lead agency must complete it within 60 days, including the mandatory 30-day public comment period.
Limited alternatives: Restricts the review to a single project alternative selected by the applicant, shifting planning responsibility from the lead agency to the developer.
Legal challenges: Makes several changes to reduce frivolous legal challenges and risk of delays.
Filing limitations: Requires lawsuits to be filed within 30 days of project approval.
Substantial evidence: Increases the standard of review from “fair argument” to “substantial evidence,” creating a higher standard for challenging the lead agency’s decision and reducing frivolous lawsuits.
Judicial “shot clock” : Requires courts to resolve lawsuits within 270 days.
Judicial discretion: Directs courts to require applicants to correct rejected portions of an environmental impact report but not to redo the entire report.
The Backstory
The California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA), enacted in 1970, requires state and local public agencies to evaluate, disclose, and mitigate the potential environmental impacts of public and private projects that require government approval, use public funds, and could physically change the environment. CEQA currently applies to most projects, except some types of infill housing and transportation projects within existing cities and within walking distance to transit.
CEQA is a foundation of California environmental protection, helping preserve natural resources and prevent harmful projects in disadvantaged communities. However, its review and litigation processes can also add significant time and cost to housing and infrastructure projects and have been used to block infill housing, transit, and other projects.
In recent years, California has sought to preserve CEQA’s protections while addressing the state’s significant need for affordable housing and climate-friendly transportation options by streamlining or exempting certain infill housing, affordable housing, and sustainable transportation projects through legislative action. Despite these reforms, the housing affordability crisis has worsened. Prop. 45 would pursue broader CEQA reforms directly through the ballot.
The California Chamber of Commerce placed the measure on the ballot through a voter signature initiative. It requires a simple majority (50% plus one vote) to pass and would take effect immediately. If enacted, amendments would require a two-thirds vote of the state legislature.
Equity Impacts
Prop. 45 would pose three main negative equity impacts. First, it could streamline projects that increase pollution and toxic exposures in environmental justice communities — those with an unfair share of pollution, health risks, and climate hazards — including certain renewable energy facilities and ancillary infrastructure such as highway expansions.
Second, it would limit required consultation with federally recognized tribes, excluding more than 50 state-recognized tribes and disempowering many tribes that lack sufficient documentation to become federally recognized.
Third, it would cap public comment periods (45 days for full environmental impact reports), which may be insufficient for large or complex projects. A short comment period tends to favor those commenters who are well-organized and well-resourced.
Pros
Prop. 45 could reduce project delays and costs by addressing routine administrative burdens, resolving legal ambiguity, providing greater certainty, and potentially speeding housing approvals and construction.
Expedited review could accelerate safety projects such as undergrounding power lines, helping prevent loss of life and property damage while controlling ratepayer costs.
Requiring substantial evidence of harm could raise the legal standard and make frivolous lawsuits easier to dismiss, potentially speeding up approval and construction.
Cons
The measure’s broad scope could streamline environmentally harmful projects or worsen conditions in environmental justice communities, regardless of location or scale.
Streamlining low-density, greenfield, hazard-prone, and auto-oriented development could encourage sprawl, including through highway expansions, gas pipelines, and fueling stations.
Allowing lawsuits over project denials and conditions could undermine local planning powers, increase litigation risk, and discourage agencies from regulating projects with significant impacts.
Strict review timelines could burden resource-constrained agencies, particularly smaller cities, and increase litigation risk. Strict public comment timelines may make it harder for people with fewer resources to participate.
Allowing environmental reviews to analyze only one applicant-selected alternative could limit consideration of better options.
Requiring a two-thirds legislative vote for amendments could make the law difficult to adapt or improve.
No Recommendation

How Much Do Approval Delays Add to the Cost of a California Home?
Updated October 16, 2026
Approval delays add more than $75,000 to the cost of building a typical new single-family home in California. The calculation below uses an average construction cost of $400 per square foot, an average new-home size of 2,401 square feet (the U.S. Census Bureau’s Western U.S. average), and the 8% increase in total development costs that California’s extended development timelines cause. Prop 45 (https://yesonprop45.com/get-the-facts/) sets enforceable deadlines for agency decisions and court challenges to cut those delays.

2 | LITTLE HOOVER COMMISSION
Dedicated to Promoting Economy and
Efficiency in California State Government
The Little Hoover Commission, formally known as the Milton
Marks “Little Hoover” Commission on California State Government
Organization and Economy, is an independent state oversight agency.
By statute, the Commission is a bipartisan board composed of
five public members appointed by the governor, four public
members appointed by the Legislature, two senators and
two assemblymembers.
In creating the Commission in 1962, the Legislature declared
its purpose:
...to secure assistance for the Governor and itself in
promoting economy, efficiency and improved services in the
transaction of the public business in the various departments,
agencies and instrumentalities of the executive branch of
the state government, and in making the operation of all
state departments, agencies and instrumentalities, and
all expenditures of public funds, more directly responsive
to the wishes of the people as expressed by their elected
representatives...
The Commission fulfills this charge by listening to the public,
consulting with the experts and conferring with the wise. In the
course of its investigations, the Commission typically empanels
advisory committees, conducts public hearings and visits
government operations in action.
Its conclusions are submitted to the Governor and the Legislature
for their consideration. Recommendations often take the form
of legislation, which the Commission supports through the
legislative process.

DEAR GOVERNOR AND MEMBERS OF THE LEGISLATURE:
In March of 2023, the Little Hoover Commission launched a study to review California’s bedrock environmental
law – the California Environmental Quality Act.
California’s environmental landscape has incalculably benefited from CEQA, which requires agencies to review
proposed projects to assess potential impacts to the environment and mitigate those impacts to the degree
feasible. This law must be upheld now and for the protection of generations to come.
However, during the Commission’s study, we concluded that, like any law, CEQA is not perfect.
In this report, we examine the current state of CEQA and whether reforms are necessary. We offer targeted,
limited suggestions to improve the law’s functioning and to ensure it is accomplishing its purpose.
The Commission respectfully submits this work and stands prepared to help you take on this challenge.
