CEQA: TARGETED REFORMS FOR CALIFORNIA’S CORE ENVIRONMENTAL LAW | 5
Executive Summary
For more than half a century, the California
Environmental Quality Act has been a bedrock of
environmental protection, and has played a role
in countless environmental victories, including the
protection of old-growth Redwoods, lands near Lake
Tahoe, and the San Francisco Bay. Often, CEQA’s
protections have been most profound in the most
disadvantaged and vulnerable communities, where
negative environmental impacts have often been
greatest in the past.
But it is also true that CEQA, like any law, can have
damaging, often unintended, consequences. It is an
expensive and lengthy process that can add years to
project timeframes. It can be used for purposes that
have little relationship to environmental protection.
Its strong bias toward the status quo means that
it can be used to block projects that would help
improve the environment.
Additionally, policymakers must weigh the
value of goals that can sometimes be in tension
or competition, such as the importance of
environmental protection versus the merit of
building more housing.
CEQA Litigation
Most CEQA projects do not result in litigation. On
average, about 200 CEQA lawsuits are filed each year
in California, or about two percent of all projects
subject to CEQA review. At the same time, research
suggests that when CEQA litigation does occur, it
often targets residential projects, which are needed
as California seeks to lessen its high housing costs.
According to research by both the law’s defenders
and detractors, housing projects are the most
common single type of project challenged by CEQA
litigation.
CEQA as Proxy
CEQA debates often serve as proxy battles for a
variety of related but distinct policy contests. In
particular, CEQA tends to be the battlefield for
debates over land-use and local control. This adds
an additional challenge to analyzing CEQA, in that it
can be difficult to disentangle CEQA from other policy
debates.
Legislative Action on
CEQA
Recent legislative efforts to reform CEQA have
been extensive, including changes signed into
law by Governor Newsom just this past summer.
Among other things, these recent reforms seek to
extend and expand judicial streamlining in hopes
of compressing litigation timelines. The recency of
these reforms suggests some degree of caution
in assessing the law at this moment, and thus
our Commission refrains from making specific
recommendations regarding compressed timelines
for CEQA litigation. We believe the state should wait
to measure the success of recent reforms before
embarking on major additional changes. At the same
time, the introduction just in the past few years of
roughly 200 bills that would have changed CEQA—
measures that are listed in this report—suggests that
many policymakers believe some reform to CEQA is
needed.
Recommendations
We believe that CEQA should be retained as a
strong form of environmental protection. Its value is
especially apparent in disadvantaged communities
that often have a history of environmental
degradation. However, we also recommend targeted
and limited reforms.
6 | LITTLE HOOVER COMMISSION
Strengthen standing
requirements.
The state should establish the same standing
requirement to file a suit under CEQA as exists under
the National Environmental Policy Act, the federal law
after which CEQA was in many respects modeled.
“Data Dumps” and “Late Hits.”
The submission of public input should be limited
to the public comment periods, and lead agencies
should not be required to consider information
submitted after the end of the public comment
period, although there should also be an exception
for information that could not have been known
during the public comment period.
Create a broad, simplified
exemption for infill housing.
The state should exempt all infill housing from CEQA
review.
Provide for additional judicial
training.
The Legislature should provide funding sufficient to
extend CEQA judicial training from two days to a full
week.
Deference to statute and CEQA
guidelines.
The Legislature should strongly reaffirm existing
statutory language that courts should defer to the
procedural and substantive requirements of statute
and the CEQA Guidelines.
Significance thresholds and
mitigations.
The state should establish clear parameters
for significance thresholds and for analysis and
mitigation of impacts.
Study Items
The Legislature should commission in-depth studies
of several areas of potential CEQA reform: the
creation of CEQA courts, the translation of CEQA
documents, the potential for a bonding requirement
for CEQA litigation, the use of vehicle miles traveled
(VMT) analysis, and whether there should be a period
of time during which analytical models are “locked
in,” and in which newly developed alternative models
need not be used.
CEQA: TARGETED REFORMS FOR CALIFORNIA’S CORE ENVIRONMENTAL LAW | 7
CEQA: Targeted Reforms for
California’s Core Environmental Law
Introduction
For more than half a century, the California
Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) has been a
bedrock of environmental protection. In a state with
unparalleled environmental endowments, but also a
history of serious environmental degradation, CEQA
has provided substantial protection of the state’s
natural resources.
At root, the value of CEQA is displayed in the fact that
its fundamental requirement—that public agencies
evaluate the environmental impact of proposed
projects, disclose those impacts to the public, and
mitigate them to the degree feasible—now seems
almost inherent to good governance. It may be
difficult for many Californians to imagine a state in
which government agencies could take substantial
actions without even considering the impact on the
environment, but that is the California that existed
before CEQA. In its more specific impacts, the
benefits of CEQA have been concrete.1 CEQA litigation
has played a role in protecting some of California’s
most famous environmental treasures:
◊ Protecting old-growth Redwoods in Humboldt
County.
◊ Preserving the Martis Valley near Lake Tahoe.
◊ Ensuring the protection of the Owens Valley, along
the eastern side of the Sierra.
◊ Stopping significant threats to the San Francisco
Bay.
Often, CEQA’s protections have been most
profound in the most disadvantaged and vulnerable
communities, those where negative environmental
impacts have often been greatest in the past. For
example, CEQA litigation also played a role in:
◊ Stopping the installation of oil wells in the middle
of a residential community in Arvin, a small
community at the Southern end of the San Joaquin
Valley.
◊ Requiring extensive mitigation measures designed
to reduce emissions and improve safety at a
pesticide plant in Pittsburg, in the Bay Area.
Any fair and thorough assessment of CEQA must
include these benefits the law has brought to
California. California’s extraordinary environment
deserves extraordinary protection, and CEQA has
been a bedrock of that protection.
But there are also critical evaluations of CEQA, and
these too must be considered. These assessments
include:
◊ CEQA can be an expensive and lengthy process,
especially for large or complicated projects. This
is true even if there is not litigation. Preparation
of an Environmental Impact Report under CEQA
can take a year or longer and cost hundreds of
thousands of dollars, or even, in some cases, more
than $1 million.2 One study of CEQA litigation
found that on average, litigation adds almost two
years to project timeframes. In the face of such
lengthy delays, financing can vanish, stopping a
project even if it would eventually have survived
the CEQA process and been approved.
◊ CEQA can be used for purposes that have little
relationship to environmental protection, such
as efforts to preclude development opposed by
nearby residents, to target competing businesses,
or to ensure that certain labor standards are
included in a given project.
◊ CEQA has a strong bias toward the status quo,
and generally assumes that change is harmful to
8 | LITTLE HOOVER COMMISSION
the environment and that maintaining the status
quo is environmentally benign or beneficial. This
means that CEQA can be used to block projects
that would help improve the environment.
Aside from these direct impacts of CEQA both pro
and con, policymakers must weigh the value of
competing public values, such as the importance
of environmental protection versus the merit of
building more housing. In some cases both can be
accomplished simultaneously, but at other times,
these goals exist in mutual tension and balance.
Cognizant of these the various assessments of CEQA,
and of the importance of the law’s impact on many
aspects of California’s governance, the Little Hoover
Commission began a series of hearings to consider
input from stakeholders, academic researchers,
policymakers, and others regarding the current
impact of CEQA, and whether changes to the law are
needed. Beginning in March of 2023, the Commission
held five hearings on CEQA. We took testimony from
24 invited witnesses and heard public comment from
many additional stakeholders. Commission staff
interviewed dozens of people involved in the CEQA
debate, including legal practitioners, environmental
experts, business interests, the environmental justice
community, organized labor, academic experts,
and many others. Staff also received hundreds
of pages of written comment… and reviewed
relevant research from many sources. This report
summarizes the Commission’s findings and, in line
with the Commission’s statutory charge, makes
recommendations to the Legislature and governor
for CEQA reforms.
How CEQA Functions
CEQA declares that it is the policy of the state to,
“develop and maintain a high-quality environment
now and in the future, and take all action
necessary to protect, rehabilitate, and enhance the
environmental quality of the state.” The law also
declares that it is state policy to, “Create and maintain
conditions under which man and nature can exist in
productive harmony to fulfill the social and economic
requirements of present and future generations.”3
CEQA requires public agencies considering a
discretionary project—a project they may approve
or reject as they see fit—to study the proposal for
potential environmental impacts, analyze the scale of
those impacts, disclose the project’s environmental
impacts to the public, and mitigate them to the
extent feasible.
Signed into law by Governor Ronald Reagan in the
fall of 1970, CEQA was part of a broad response to
the growth of the modern environmental movement
(the first Earth Day had occurred earlier that year,
for example) and to the passage of the National
Environmental Policy Act, which was signed into law
on New Year’s Day, 1970. Like its federal model, CEQA
was a response to the realization that inadequate
attention had been paid to the environmental
consequences of development decisions.
CEQA has changed considerably over its lifespan.
What began as a 4-page statute is now almost 160
pages. The administrative CEQA Guidelines that
explain the operation of the law and interpret 50
years of judicial rulings stretch for a further 150
pages, with an additional 50 pages of appendices.
The growth and increasing complexity of CEQA is the
product of both judicial action and legislative statute,
and of the interplay between the two.
Through most of its history, the growth and
application of CEQA has been driven as much, and
perhaps more, by court rulings as by statutory
change. Within a few years of CEQA becoming law,
two key court cases dramatically expanded the
scope of CEQA. In Friends of Mammoth v. Board of
Supervisors of Mono County (1972), the California
Supreme Court extended CEQA to cover private
activities that required permits from public
agencies. No Oil, Inc. v. City of Los Angeles (1974)
CEQA: TARGETED REFORMS FOR CALIFORNIA’S CORE ENVIRONMENTAL LAW | 9
then established that agencies must prepare an
Environmental Impact Report (EIR), “whenever it
can be fairly argued…that the project may have a
significant environmental impact.” Subsequent court
rulings have expanded the number and variety of
environmental impacts that must be analyzed under
CEQA and guide how impacts are analyzed and
reported.
The Legislature, in turn, has also shaped CEQA’s
growth and development. In part in response
to the perceived burden of CEQA review, the
Legislature has created an array of CEQA exemptions
and streamlining measures. Meanwhile, state
government has also revised CEQA to advance policy
priorities. For example, with the goal of reducing car-
related greenhouse gas emissions, the Legislature
in 2013 passed SB 743, which changed how
transportation impacts are evaluated under CEQA,
moving from an analysis of how projects will affect
traffic congestion to analyzing how they will impact
vehicle miles traveled (VMT).
The CEQA Process
Implementation of CEQA is governed by the CEQA
Guidelines, administrative guidelines developed by
the Governor’s Office of Planning and Research (OPR)
and issued by the Natural Resources Agency. The
CEQA Guidelines reflect statutory requirements and
further incorporate court decisions with respect to
interpreting and implementing statute.
CEQA generally proceeds through a 3-step process
(Appendix A to this background memo includes OPR’s
full flowchart for the CEQA process). The public entity
carrying out the project or responsible for approving
the project is the “lead agency.” In the case of private
projects, the relationship between the project
applicant and the lead agency can vary: sometimes
the lead agency may drive the environmental
review; sometimes the applicant may carry out
the review subject to lead agency approval of the
review documents; and sometimes lead agency and
applicant will collaborate in the review process.
1. DOES CEQA APPLY?
First, the relevant public agency must determine if
the proposed activity is a project subject to CEQA;
that is, is it a “whole action” subject to the public
agency’s discretionary approval that has potential
to either cause a direct physical change in the
environment or to cause a foreseeable indirect
change in the environment.
If the project is ministerial—that is, if agency
authorization is required so long as the project meets
specified requirements—then CEQA does not apply.
In addition, a project may be exempt from CEQA
under a range of statutory or categorical exemptions.
If an exemption applies, the agency may file a Notice
of Exemption (NOE). (Lead agencies may require
a project to go through CEQA review even if an
exemption could apply, especially if they believe that
the exemption might be subject to legal challenge).

- Located in urban areas on non-environmentally-sensitive sites

- Consistent with applicable general plan and zoning standards and must meet minimum density requirements
- Meet heightened design and, if located within 500 feet of a freeway, certain air filtration and heating, ventilation, and air conditioning requirements

Proposition 45 is backed by the California Chamber of Commerce and supported by a long list of homebuilders whose vision for California's future comes from the past.
'This is the Chamber of Commerce saying, 'We need to bring back the kinds of growth that California had in the 1960s,'' said Christopher Elmendorf, a law professor at the University of California, Davis, who studies land-use regulations.

Modifies Environmental Review for Certain Projects.
Initiative Statute.
## Analysis of Measure
### Proposal
Proposition 45 creates new procedures for reviewing certain types of projects that it defines as “essential.”
Figure 1 lists the types of projects eligible for the new procedures.
The proposition (1) tightens time limits for CEQA review, permits, and court challenges; (2) changes parts of the CEQA review process; and (3) changes the court’s review process for CEQA lawsuits.
The proposition gives eligible project applicants the option of using the new procedures or existing procedures.
***Tightens Time Limits for Review and Court Challenges of Eligible Projects.*** Proposition 45 creates more binding time limits for state and local governments to do both CEQA and permitting reviews.
This includes time limits for determining if a project application is complete, finishing the EIR, and granting other types of approvals and permits.

# Endorsement: CEQA is a mess. Prop 45 is even messier
Proposition 45 would significantly expedite the CEQA review process for eight categories of projects and potentially make it easier to build  environmentally ruinous projects.
...
Proposition 45, placed on the November ballot via signatures gathered by the California Chamber of Commerce, would significantly expedite the CEQA review process for eight categories of projects its authors deem “essential”: housing, water (other than the Delta tunnel), clean energy (excepting nuclear power), healthcare, public safety, wildfire mitigation, broadband internet access, education and transportation (other than high-speed rail).
...
First, it establishes a litany of strict deadlines — some of which are technically already in CEQA but rarely enforced.
Government agencies, for example, would have 30 days to determine whether a project application is complete, 365 days to conduct an environmental review and decide whether to certify it and 90 days to decide on permits.
If agencies fail to meet these deadlines, applicants could trigger a public hearing within 60 days, at which time a final decision must be made.
Applicants can sue if agencies don’t follow these procedures.

Why Circulate Planning & Policy Supports Prop 45
California's cost of living is out of control because our outdated system for approving essential projects is too slow, too bureaucratic, and too costly—making it harder to build the housing, transit, and other infrastructure our communities depend on. These unnecessary delays drive up costs for families, businesses, and taxpayers while making California less affordable for everyone.
That's why Circulate supports Prop 45, the Building an Affordable California Act (https://yesonprop45.com/) on the November 2026 ballot.
Prop 45 creates clear, enforceable timelines for environmental review, agency permitting, and judicial review for eligible projects. Rather than allowing projects to become trapped in years of bureaucratic delay and costly litigation, Prop 45 establishes accountability from application through final court decisions. By creating certainty throughout the approval process, the measure is expected to accelerate essential projects by 2 to 10 or more years, reducing costs and delivering benefits to Californians sooner.
Just as importantly, Prop 45 does not eliminate environmental review or weaken environmental protections. Every eligible project must still comply with the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) and all applicable federal, state, and local environmental laws and regulations. The measure simply ensures that environmental review, permitting decisions, and any legal challenges are completed within reasonable, enforceable deadlines instead of dragging on indefinitely.
For too long, unnecessary delays have increased the cost of nearly everything Californians rely on. Permitting delays can add years to building timelines, forcing families to wait even longer to realize the benefits of affordable housing. Further, permitting delays alone add more than $75,000 to the cost of a new home. Prop 45 cuts unnecessary red tape, lowers project costs, and helps deliver the infrastructure Californians need faster. This means California will be able to more quickly deliver affordable housing that strengthens our communities and economy.
Prop 45 also preserves local control. Cities and counties retain their authority to approve or deny projects, and Californians continue to have meaningful opportunities to participate throughout the project approval process. The measure creates a process that is faster, fairer, and more predictable—not one that sacrifices accountability or environmental protections.
More than 145 organizations (https://yesonprop45.com/our-coalition/) representing affordable housing, healthcare, water providers, agricultural producers, clean energy leaders, social justice advocates, and small business leaders support Prop 45 because California cannot afford to keep delaying the essential projects that improve quality of life and make our state more affordable.
California deserves a permitting system that protects the environment and delivers the infrastructure families, workers, businesses, and communities need.
Learn more about Prop 45 at: www.YesOnProp45.com (http://www.yesonprop45.com/)

Vote No on Prop 45: Rolling Back CEQA Is A Proposition Californians Can’t Afford
October 29, 2026 (https://www.greenbelt.org/2026/10/29/)
CEQA (https://www.greenbelt.org/tag/ceqa/), Voter Guide (https://www.greenbelt.org/tag/voter-guide/)
Updated on October 29 to include links. Originally published on January 16, 2026.
For advocates working at the intersection of environmental protection and climate-smart growth, theCalifornia Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) (https://www.greenbelt.org/land-use-planning-dictionary/california-environmental-quality-act/) has long been a source of both pride and frustration. While it has been a critical tool to protect our natural and working lands, its procedural delays have often been used to stall projects essential to a low-carbon future: dense infill (https://www.greenbelt.org/land-use-planning-dictionary/infill-development/) housing and transit-oriented development (https://www.greenbelt.org/land-use-planning-dictionary/transit-oriented-development/) in our existing communities.
In July 2025, however, at the urging of Governor Newsom, the California legislature passed some of the most impactful changes to CEQA (https://www.greenbelt.org/blog/ceqa-reform-explainer/) since its inception. Taken together, the two bills (AB 130 and SB 131) provide robust statutory CEQA exemptions for infill housing and housing element rezonings, require the state to map infill areas where exemptions would apply, and narrow the scope of the administrative record, helping to curtail anti-housing litigation.
Read my Op-Ed in the East Bay Times on why Prop 45 is a ruse handing shortcuts to polluters disguised as relief. (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/09/12/opinion-vote-no-prop-45-would-take-away-our-best-defense-against-corporate-polluters/amp/)
Check out some highlights of Greenbelt Alliance’s commentary in local and regional press:
Prop. 45: Will California Vote to Trade Environmental Regulation for Quicker Housing Development? – Forum KQED (https://www.kqed.org/forum/2010101915583/prop-45-will-california-vote-to-trade-environmental-regulation-for-quicker-housing-development)
Will Prop. 45 Fix California’s Housing Crisis or Roll Back a Valuable Environmental Law? – Political Breakdown KQED (https://www.kqed.org/news/12101722/will-prop-45-fix-californias-housing-crisis-or-roll-back-a-valuable-environmental-law)
Why are pro-housing groups split on Proposition 45? – CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/10/yimby-prop-45-ceqa/)
Sonoma County stakeholders, cities eye Prop. 45’s potential to broadly reform California’s bedrock environmental law – The Press Democrat (https://www.pressdemocrat.com/2026/10/26/prop-45-california-sonoma-county-housing-environment/)
Despite these monumental changes that address the barriers to critical infill development, California’s business lobby and sprawl developers were left unsatisfied. Now, they are proposing a ballot initiative that would make far more radical changes to the law. After gathering enough signatures to qualify for the November ballot, this is now called Proposition 45.
While the rhetoric of the measure (initially called Building an Affordable California Act, or BACA (https://advocacy.calchamber.com/2025/12/17/calchambers-ceqa-reform-boosting-californias-economy-and-state-budget/) ) seems to be aligned with urbanist goals and those of the broader abundance and affordability movements, the actual policy details and mechanics of the initiative—and the progress we’ve already achieved in the legislature (https://www.greenbelt.org/blog/2025-legislative-priorities/) last year—suggest that the costs it brings far outweigh any potential benefits.
Below, we outline seven reasons why the measure should be rejected (click to read more):
1. Major Reforms Have Already Been Enacted
For years, a primary objective for California’s urbanists was to stop the abuse of environmental law against projects that genuinely help the environment: dense, transit-oriented housing.
In a landmark shift for the state, that goal has largely been realized. Following years of advocacy by urbanists, the legislature passed a clean statutory CEQA exemption for infill housing. AB 130, which Greenbelt Alliance was proud to support (https://www.greenbelt.org/blog/ceqa-reform-ca/), is already being utilized across California, allowing builders to move forward with climate-friendly housing in high-opportunity areas like Palo Alto or Beverly Hills without the threat of being endlessly delayed by the environmental review process. While there is room for technical refinements, the fundamental issue at hand—the misuse of environmental laws to delay environmentally-friendly housing projects—has largely been addressed.
2. Everything is “Essential”
As the saying goes, “the devil is in the details”, and that’s certainly true for the BACA initiative. While modest on the surface, BACA creates a completely new set of rules for what it calls “essential” projects. So what, exactly, is an “essential project”?
The list is incredibly broad. Under Article 2, Section 21013, “essential projects” include housing, water, transportation, clean energy, transmission, broadband, and healthcare infrastructure. In practice, this definition encompasses a wide range of large-scale developments. For example, new freeways and existing freeway expansions would qualify as “essential transportation” projects; large greenfield sprawl developments would be treated as “essential” housing projects; and new dams and reservoirs would qualify as “essential” water projects. The definition even includes all “related and ancillary infrastructure,” meaning that highway interchanges, utility extensions, and water pipelines that enable sprawl developments also receive streamlined approval. All of these are enormous projects in terms of size and scale, with major potential environmental impacts. Yet, just like an apartment building in an urban area, under BACA, they would qualify for a significantly truncated review process.
In effect, this new CEQA process mirrors the fundamental flaw of its predecessor. While the old system failed to exempt low or no-impact projects from excessive review, the new one errs in the opposite direction, fast-tracking high-risk developments with significant potential for harm.
3. All Timelines Are Not Created Equal
The BACA initiative imposes strict timelines for this new class of projects that it deems “essential”: the environmental review process can take no more than one year. On the surface, a one-year limit on an Environmental Impact Report (EIR) seems reasonable. And for certain projects, like an apartment building on a parking lot in downtown San Francisco, or a townhome development in an LA suburb, it would be.
However, the measure’s definition of “essential” includes highways, dams, large-scale subdivisions, and other major projects. The environmental review required for projects at this scale cannot be done in a single year. Surveying hundreds if not thousands (or even tens of thousands) of acres of undisturbed and undeveloped land for species nesting patterns and habitat, water pollution impacts, and other environmental concerns physically cannot be accomplished within the timeframe laid out in the initiative. By forcing these projects into such a condensed timeline, we will be creating a system that overlooks genuine environmental harm in favor of speed.
For projects with unambiguous environmental benefits, such as housing developments within already urbanized areas, such speed makes sense. Many of the project types considered by this measure do not have the same clear, unambiguous benefits.
4. Restrictive Alternatives
One of CEQA’s most critical tools for preventing environmental harm is its alternative analysis provision, which allows for the identification of better project locations and designs. Currently, CEQA requires agencies to analyze a “reasonable range of alternatives” that could reduce environmental impacts, including different sites, reduced intensity options, and designs that avoid sensitive resources. This is how agencies can say, “this housing should be built downtown on a parking lot instead of on farmland,” or “this highway expansion has an alternative transit solution.”
BACA restricts this to just three options: the proposed project, one alternative designed by the applicant themselves (which doesn’t even need to be at a different location), and “no project.” The applicant’s alternative can be a slightly modified version of their original proposal on the same site. This eliminates the core mechanism for steering projects away from environmentally sensitive locations toward more appropriate sites, exactly the tool needed to prevent sprawl, protect open space, and ensure development happens in the right places.
5. The Evidentiary Standard
Maybe the most radical change incorporated in the ballot measure is to CEQA’s standard of review. Right now, CEQA allows a lead agency (generally a city or county) to use its own discretion to explore project alternatives and negotiate environmental mitigations. BACA proposes to eliminate this by requiring that environmental impacts only be found significant if they violate objective, quantifiable standards already in existing law when the project was proposed, which doesn’t sound inherently unreasonable!
However, the measure doesn’t actually require jurisdictions to adopt such standards; instead, it exploits their absence. If numerical thresholds don’t already exist for resources like oak woodlands, groundwater, or wildlife corridors, impacts to them essentially can’t be found significant regardless of severity. A genuine objective standards approach would mandate jurisdictions adopt protective thresholds and update them as science improves. This measure rewards weak standards, freezes them at application date, and prevents improvements based on new knowledge.
6. Ballot Box Permanence
Finally, one of the greatest flaws of the measure is its rigidity. Should it pass, BACA would require a 2/3rds vote of the legislature to amend.
California has a long, storied history with ballot box governance, where initiatives become impossible to adjust as new problems arise. The 2/3rds requirement virtually guarantees the law could never be changed, regardless of what issues may arise. An unchangeable measure, with foreseeable negative impacts for the state, may have lasting consequences for generations.
Some of the project types included in this measure, such as clean energy or transmission infrastructure, may benefit from the types of streamlining being considered if careful, targeted changes were made. Rather than a broad, clunky initiative that will be extremely difficult to change, we should advocate for those reforms through the legislative cleanup process already underway.
7. The Costs Are Just Too High
California faces converging affordability crises: insurers fleeing the state, utility rates climbing, and municipal budgets straining under unsustainable costs. All of these issues stem from the same source: decades of sprawling outward, often into fire-prone areas, leaving us with infrastructure we cannot afford to maintain and risks we cannot afford to insure.
BACA will accelerate these failures by trading short-term speed for permanent costs. By gutting CEQA’s alternatives analysis—the primary tool for steering projects away from costly, high-risk locations—this limits agencies to the developer’s preferred site, one alternative the developer designs themselves, and “no project.” It freezes environmental standards at the date of application, rewarding jurisdictions with weak protections. And it requires agencies to approve permits within strict timelines regardless of fiscal consequences, because most cities lack the quantitative standards BACA requires to find fiscal impacts “significant.”
The result: even if we build some things faster today, we’ll be paying the tab forever. Even more homes in fire zones will continue to destabilize our insurance markets. More infrastructure extensions will push up our utility rates. More sprawling subdivisions that generate less revenue than they cost to maintain will ensure even higher taxes. BACA promises affordability through speed but delivers the opposite: cheaper to build, but financially ruinous to sustain.
At a time when people are struggling to make ends meet, and when the federal government is doing all it can to roll back our environmental protections, the last thing we need is to double down on the failed policies we have tried for decades and know do not work.
Proposition 45 will hurt the environment and your wallet.
Greenbelt Alliance strongly opposes Proposition 45 and urges voters to vote NO on 45 this November.

Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. California voters considering Proposition 45 (https://calmatters.org/newsletter/prop-45-yimby/) will decide the fate of a sweeping infrastructure measure that opponents warn could render the state’s brand-new data center laws virtually toothless. That would make it far easier for developers to force unwanted facilities into local communities, potentially undermining a growing wave of bans, moratoriums, and anti-data-center resolutions (https://calmatters.org/economy/technology/2026/10/california-data-centers-hit-with-local-regulation-flood/) at the city and county level. Data center backers insist the ballot measure will do nothing for them — even as some data center beneficiaries are spending big backing Prop. 45. Supporters have framed Prop. 45 as a tool to accelerate critical infrastructure projects (https://calmatters.org/environment/2026/10/prop-45-california-ceqa-explained/), like housing and schools, and the measure does not directly name data centers among the sorts of projects it considers critical. But some legal scholars and environmental advocates say that the proposition’s technical language creates a loophole. By expediting environmental reviews under the California Environmental Quality Act (https://calmatters.org/environment/2026/10/prop-45-california-ceqa-explained/) for broad categories of projects — including broadband internet facilities and any additional infrastructure required to get them up and running — the measure could quietly allow data centers to bypass recent state safeguards and local scrutiny. Julia Stein, a legal scholar and deputy director at UCLA School of Law’s Emmett Institute on Climate Change and the Environment, warns that the measure acts as a “blunt force instrument when it comes to streamlining” because of how wide its secondary umbrella extends. “What Prop. 45 does is designate an entire class of projects that would be subject to streamlining, and then it also says that projects ancillary to those projects — so something that you might need to do in the course of the development of the project that’s exempted itself — would fall within that same streamlining bubble,” Stein said. Telecommunications projects are explicitly streamlined under the proposition, “and there’s an argument that the development of data centers might be necessary for projects like that,” Stein added. MORE ON DATA CENTERS California cities pull the plug on data centers after state regulations don’t scale up fast enough (https://calmatters.org/economy/technology/2026/10/california-data-centers-hit-with-local-regulation-flood/) October 22, 2026 October 22, 2026 Other projects, like high-speed rail, are explicitly excluded from streamlining under the proposition — but data centers are not on that list, either. Stein and three other environmental law scholars told CalMatters that this opens the door for legal challenges. “The fact that they excluded some projects but have not expressly excluded data centers, a court would probably actually interpret that not as an unintentional oversight, but rather as intent to include data centers in the initiative,” said Matt McKerley, an attorney with Shute, Mihaly and Weinberger. Further, opponents argue that the proposition’s language, which includes a clause that it would supersede other related laws, would override measures like the recently-passed Senate Bill 887 (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb887), which made it harder to fast-track environmental review for data centers. Industry representatives say these objections to Prop. 45 are misplaced. The Data Center Coalition, an industry group supporting Prop. 45, insists their facilities fall outside the initiative’s scope, which focuses largely on housing development (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/10/yimby-prop-45-ceqa/) ad other infrastructure like roads and bridges. Get California’s most essential headlines without feeling overwhelmed. Email address By clicking subscribe, you agree to the terms (https://calmatters.org/about/policies-and-standards/). Sign up for free Δ “The Data Center Coalition has reviewed Proposition 45 and concluded that data centers are not eligible for Prop. 45’s streamlining, nor are they a covered entity under any part of the measure,” said Khara Boender, the coalition’s Director of Government Affairs—West. Industry representatives also point to a recent legal opinion memo (https://yesonprop45.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/legopinion_DataCenter.pdf) from California’s Office of Legislative Counsel, which provides legal services to members of the Legislature. The memo argues that Prop. 45’s statutory definitions do not apply to data centers. Amelia Matier, from the Yes on 45 campaign, echoed that take, saying, “Data centers are not included in Prop 45.” She added: “The defenders of California’s unaffordable status quo are desperate to distract voters with lies because they cannot defend the costly delays and red tape driving up prices for working families. ” Opponents of the measure include the California Labor Federation, Western Center on Law & Poverty, and various environmental advocacy groups that have spent more than $31 million dollars pushing back against the measure. Despite maintaining that data centers fall outside the proposition’s reach, tech and utility interests benefiting from California’s computing boom are putting massive financial weight (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-45-modifies-environmental-review-certain-projects-initiative-statute) behind its passage. Proponents have poured over $40 million into the Yes on Prop. 45 campaign, including $3.05 million from utility giant PG&E and $500,000 from warehouse and data center developer Prologis — a cash influx that opponents argue reveals who truly expects to profit if the measure passes. The debate over Prop. 45’s data center impact comes at a pivotal moment in California’s AI infrastructure boom. Gov. Gavin Newsom recently signed seven landmark data center laws (https://calmatters.org/economy/technology/2026/09/new-california-laws-data-centers/) aimed at forcing operators to disclose water usage, pay for their own grid upgrades, and undergo environmental review. Yet local communities aren’t waiting for state regulations to take effect. Amid rising fears of rate hikes, grid overload, and water depletion, grassroots opposition has erupted across California. At least 26 cities and counties have proposed or passed moratoriums, bans, or strict limits aimed to stop data center development (https://calmatters.org/economy/technology/2026/10/california-data-centers-hit-with-local-regulation-flood/) in their communities. Nina Robertson, a deputy managing attorney in Earthjustice’s California regional office, said the ambiguity written into the ballot text would trigger immediate legal battles over local permitting authority. “And who’s going to bear the cost of that litigation?” Robertson asked. “It’s going to be the local governments.” Read more from CalMatters Text Get breaking news on your phone. By Katherine Ortiz, CalMatters

California voters considering Proposition 45 will decide the fate of a sweeping infrastructure measure that opponents warn could render the state’s brand-new data center laws virtually toothless.

BACA makes the ballot
Initiative to drastically change CEQA appears to have enough signatures to make ballot
It looks like the California Chamber of Commerce has enough signatures (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/04/27/could-a-change-to-environmental-law-reduce-california-costs/) to put on the November ballot their initiative (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0023A1%20%28%26quot%3BEssential%20Projects%26quot%3B%29.pdf) that would drastically change the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). Given that, I’m re-upping the analyses I did earlier this year on the measure: Part 1 (https://legal-planet.org/2026/02/25/what-does-the-building-an-affordable-california-act-do/) (overview), Part 2 (https://legal-planet.org/2026/02/26/what-does-baca-do-part-ii/) (sweeping scope of the initiative in terms of laws affected), Part 3 (https://legal-planet.org/2026/02/26/what-does-baca-do-part-iii/) (broad vested rights created by the initiative), Part 4 (https://legal-planet.org/2026/02/27/what-does-baca-do-part-iv/) (approval changes that apply to all California law), Part 5 (https://legal-planet.org/2026/02/27/what-does-baca-do-part-v/) (limits on the types of impacts that would be considered under CEQA), Part 6 (https://legal-planet.org/2026/02/28/what-does-baca-do-part-vi/) (changes to the scope and alternatives analyses under CEQA), Part 7 (https://legal-planet.org/2026/03/01/what-does-baca-do-part-vii/) (the broad scope of projects covered by the initiative), Part 8 (https://legal-planet.org/2026/03/01/what-does-baca-do-part-viii/) (the initiative makes future changes very difficult), Part 9 (https://legal-planet.org/2026/03/02/what-does-baca-do-part-ix/) (the gaps in state environmental law the initiative would produce), Part 10 (https://legal-planet.org/2026/03/02/what-does-baca-do-part-x/) (the issues with CEQA that reforms should tackle).
While the name given the proponents to the initiative is “Building an Affordable California Act”, on the ballot the title will be: “Modifies Environmental Review for Certain Projects.” The full measure is here (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0023A1%20%28%26quot%3BEssential%20Projects%26quot%3B%29.pdf). The title of the initiative and ballot summary prepared by the state Attorney General is here (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/Title%20and%20Summary%20%2825-0023A1%29.pdf). (That title and summary will be the first part of what voters see in their ballot guides when they come out this fall.)

A summary of BACA
An overview of my analyses of Proposition 45
I’ve written a lot on the Cal Chamber sponsored initiative to dramatically change CEQA, BACA, which is Proposition 45 on this year’s ballot. Here are some key takeaways from what I’ve written, as well as links to the relevant blog posts.
First, BACA will not just apply to CEQA. It broadly expands vested rights (https://legal-planet.org/2026/02/26/what-does-baca-do-part-iii/) and imposes strict time limits for all permitting in the state (https://legal-planet.org/2026/02/27/what-does-baca-do-part-iv/) for covered projects. It’s possible that it prevents ever increasing or changing regulatory standards for a covered project, even after it is constructed and is in operation (https://legal-planet.org/2026/02/26/what-does-baca-do-part-iii/). And it will significantly weaken a range of substantive environmental protections (https://legal-planet.org/2026/03/02/what-does-baca-do-part-ix/) in California, such as for endangered species habitat and cumulative air pollution.
Second, BACA will not just apply to clean energy, mass transit, and housing projects (https://legal-planet.org/2026/03/01/what-does-baca-do-part-vii/). It applies to freeways and roads, to dams and irrigation projects, and to logging projects. It may well cover any development project that eliminates natural habitat in California (on the grounds of reducing fire risk). It may well include (https://legal-planet.org/2026/06/24/baca-and-data-centers-part-i/) data (https://legal-planet.org/2026/06/25/baca-and-data-centers-part-ii/) centers (https://legal-planet.org/2026/09/10/more-on-baca-and-data-centers/).
Third, for all intents and purposes, BACA basically repeals CEQA for covered projects. Proponents may be able to unilaterally limit the scope of CEQA review and determine what alternatives are to be considered (https://legal-planet.org/2026/02/28/what-does-baca-do-part-vi/). CEQA loses any independent review or mitigation requirements (https://legal-planet.org/2026/02/27/what-does-baca-do-part-v/), and simply becomes a checklist for compliance with other laws. And judicial enforcement is sharply limited, even for compliance with those other laws.
Fourth, there is significant uncertainty about how BACA will work. In particular, provisions of the initiative may cause it to be interpreted much more broadly (https://legal-planet.org/2026/02/26/what-does-baca-do-part-ii/) than an initial read of the text indicates, and it overrides any conflicting laws (https://legal-planet.org/2026/02/26/what-does-baca-do-part-ii/).
Fifth, BACA will be extremely difficult to amend if it is enacted (https://legal-planet.org/2026/03/01/what-does-baca-do-part-viii/). Any changes require a 2/3 majority in the state legislature.
Sixth, BACA does address some real concerns (https://legal-planet.org/2026/03/02/what-does-baca-do-part-x/) with how CEQA works, including the ability of project opponents to play Calvinball and develop new claims of harms that must be analyzed and mitigated, with moving targets for what alternatives should be assessed and what standards apply for mitigation. I’ve outlined (https://legal-planet.org/2026/05/12/reforming-ceqa-part-i/) a range (https://legal-planet.org/2026/05/12/reforming-ceqa-part-2/) of (https://legal-planet.org/2026/05/13/reforming-ceqa-part-3/) reforms (https://legal-planet.org/2026/05/13/reforming-ceqa-part-4/) to (https://legal-planet.org/2026/05/14/reforming-ceqa-part-5/) CEQA (https://legal-planet.org/2026/05/14/reforming-ceqa-part-6/) that I think would address those concerns but with less collateral damage than BACA would produce.
Seventh, there are a number of constraints (https://legal-planet.org/2026/07/29/the-limits-of-implementation-for-baca/) on how broadly BACA will be implemented in practice. Union labor or prevailing wage requirements may limit how many projects use BACA (except for housing, which is exempt from those requirements). Local zoning and planning rules in place at the time a project is proposed would also continue to restrict what is possible.
Eighth, BACA will probably undermine the planning process in California (https://legal-planet.org/2026/07/28/baca-and-planning/), and incentivize more piecemeal analysis and approval of individual projects, likely increasing the cumulative environmental impacts of development.
Finally, in particular BACA will likely contribute to eliminating most endangered species habitat protections (https://legal-planet.org/2026/09/13/the-end-of-endangered-species-habitat-protections-in-california/) in California, a state that claims to be an environmental leader.

EIR Projects: Status Quo CEQA Review Durations
The status quo CEQA Review period duration for EIRs is estimated based on analysis of CEQA document timelines across a sample of 539 residential EIR projects that submitted data to the state’s CEQANet portal (https://ceqanet.lci.ca.gov/) after January 1, 2020 (the “EIR Project Sample”). 10 Figure 6 shows the distribution of CEQA Review durations across the 539 residential EIR projects included in the analysis sample. While the median CEQA Review duration was 715 days (or just under two years), the average NOP-NOD period was 1,141 days (or roughly three years). Forty-one percent of projects were certified within the maximum 591-day period allowed under Prop 45. 11 Twenty-seven percent of the sampled projects’ review periods lasted between 591 days and three years. Nearly one in six residential EIR reviews in the sample took more than five years to complete, including 6% that took more than a decade.

Prop 45 Would Cut Roughly Three Years from the Longest Residential EIR Timelines
Estimating Prop 45’s impact on the average residential EIR entitlement timeline requires calculating the difference between (a) the status quo average entitlement duration for the EIR project sample and (b) the average period across these projects if Prop 45’s 591-day CEQA review time limit were enforced against EIR projects with review durations exceeding this maximum. Similarly, Prop 45’s impact on entitlement volatility depends on the change in the standard deviation of project entitlement periods under the 591-day limit.
Figure 7 summarizes the calculation of the change in the average entitlement duration under Prop 45. Under the status quo, the average entitlement period is an estimated 1,276 days (i.e., 1,141 days of CEQA review plus 135 days of other entitlement review). Of the 539 projects in the EIR sample, 221 had their EIRs certified in fewer than 591 days, and the average total entitlement period for this cohort (509 days) is assumed to remain the same under Prop 45. For the remaining 318 projects with CEQA reviews exceeding the Prop 45 time limit, the average status quo entitlement period is 1,809 days, of which 1,674 days is CEQA review. Prop 45’s 591-day limit would reduce the total entitlement period to 726 days, on average (as it would reduce the CEQA review phase from 1,674 days to Prop 45’s 591-day limit). As a result, Prop 45 would cut the average entitlement timeline across all residential EIR projects roughly in half, from 1,276 days to 637 days. For projects exceeding Prop 45’s time limit, the reduction would be even greater: 1,082 days, or roughly three years.

Economic and Fiscal Impacts of Increased Residential Construction
Prop 45’s Impact on Housing Affordability
By adding nearly 200,000 homes over ten years, Prop 45 would increase housing supply and put downward pressure on rents and home prices. Based on the state Department of Finance (DOF) estimates of the total statewide housing stock (https://dof.ca.gov/forecasting/demographics/estimates/e-5-population-and-housing-estimates-for-cities-counties-and-the-state-2020-2026/) (15.06 million units as of 2026) and status quo permitting rates (i.e., 108,269 units annually), the increase in residential construction under Prop 45 would increase the state’s housing stock by 1.21% after 10 years. 18 According to a recent Pew Research Center analysis, a 10% increase in a metropolitan region’s rental supply resulted in a 5.4% reduction in the region’s rents relative to nationwide rent cost trends (i.e., a “supply-price effect” of 0.54). 19 Based on this effect, Prop 45’s supply impact would reduce average rents and home prices by 0.66% (i.e., 1.21% × 0.54).
Macroeconomic Benefits of New Housing
In addition to Prop 45’s expected impact on housing costs in California, new housing also generates spillover economic and fiscal benefits that exceed the housing affordability impacts shown above. Empirical studies of supply-constrained housing markets have shown that unlocking new housing supply in high-cost regions promotes economic growth by enabling more workers to access the higher-paying jobs concentrated in these areas. 20 This expansion of the regional labor supply, in turn, attracts more firms to the area. Housing construction in high-demand regions additionally provides several quality-of-life benefits, including reduced commute times and household overcrowding. 21
Fiscal Impacts of Increased Residential Development
Increases in residential development generate additional tax revenues for state and local governments on a one-time basis during the construction period and on an ongoing annual basis once the new units are complete. Construction period tax revenues include personal income taxes (PIT) generated by income earned by construction workers and firm owners, corporation taxes generated by the corporate profits from this activity, and sales taxes on construction materials and equipment. Ongoing property tax revenues are generated annually once a new unit is added to the local property tax roll.

IV. Non-Residential Impacts
By shortening non-residential project review timelines, Prop 45 would lower costs incurred by public agencies and California utility ratepayers or consumers. Longer project review periods increase total project costs through two primary channels. First, because the costs of pre-development activities, including planning, engineering, design, and environmental review, are incurred before construction begins, longer review periods impose higher carrying costs on sponsors (i.e., the “pre-development cost of capital”). Second, because construction costs have historically outpaced general inflation in California, delaying the start of construction imposes higher real construction costs on project developers (i.e., “construction cost inflation”).
Pre-Development Cost Impact
Project sponsors require a minimum annual rate of return on pre-development capital investments. The impact of these capital costs on total project budgets depends on the project sponsor type as well as the share of project expenses incurred during the pre-development period.
Public Agency and Private Sector Pre-Development Costs of Capital
For private sponsors, the cost of capital reflects the annual internal rate of return (IRR) required by a project’s investors or lenders. Because of the high risk of project failure during the planning and approval process, 27 higher rates of return are demanded on pre-development stage capital than capital invested in shovel-ready projects. Because clean energy projects account for roughly 63% of total IOU and private sector essential project expenditures, and 100% of the annual essential construction spending incurred by California’s ratepayers, this report relies on market study estimates of the IRR typically earned on pre-development utility-scale solar project investments. 28 Based on this research, the real private sponsor cost of capital is an estimated 16%. 29
Though public agencies may not require or earn investment returns on their infrastructure spending, these entities may incur financing costs to the extent bonds are issued to fund these initial capital investments. In either case, given the time value of money, governments discount projects’ future benefits or costs when conducting benefit-cost analyses (i.e., for every year that a project or program’s benefits are delayed, their expected values are reduced by the chosen discount rate). 30 Given the large share of public spending on transportation projects, this report adopts a discount rate of 4% as the effective public agency cost of capital. 31
Impact of Pre-Development Capital Costs Across Essential Project Categories
The per-year pre-development cost for each essential project category and project sponsor type is calculated by applying the discount rate or IRR (an annual percentage) to the percentage share of project expenses committed during pre-development (i.e., the pre-development cost share).
As shown in Figure 17, based on federal survey data and research materials, this cost share is estimated to range from 3% (for clean energy projects) to 25% (for broadband). 32 As a result, a one-year reduction in the average transportation project review period, for example, is estimated to reduce total project costs by 0.6% if the sponsor is a public agency (i.e., 15% × 4%) and by 2.4% if the sponsor is a private firm (i.e., 15% × 16%).

Introduction
The California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) was enacted unanimously
by a bipartisan legislature and signed by then-Governor Ronald Reagan in
1970. CEQA is a catchall statute requiring state and local agencies to consider
environmental impacts before approving or undertaking a construction
project, plan or regulation applicable to a construction project or the physical
environment. CEQA is older than the Endangered Species Act, Clean Air and
Clean Water acts, California Coastal Act, National Historic Preservation Act,
and thousands of other federal and state laws and regulations that ostensibly
protect the environment and public health. Any person or entity that
disagrees with an agency’s decision to approve or undertake a project that
is subject to CEQA can file a lawsuit in state court. CEQA trial and appellate
court proceedings typically take about five years to complete, and while
litigation is pending, most approved projects are stalled.
Jennifer Hernandez has practiced environmental and land use law in California
for 40 years; teaches environmental justice, land use and environmental law in
California law schools; serves on the boards of several nonprofit environmental
and other organizations; and has published several books and scores of articles
on CEQA, land use housing, climate and other topics. While the author is grateful
for the research assistance provided by the Independent Institute and other
Holland & Knight attorneys, the opinions and recommendations in this study are
the author’s and should not be attributed to any other person or organization, to
Holland & Knight or any client of the firm, or to the Independent Institute.
CEQA increasingly has been criticized as a major
reason California can’t build enough housing,
water, and transportation infrastructure or public
service facilities – including important projects
approved and funded by taxpayers – because all
projects subject to CEQA must also comply with
myriad other laws to protect human health and the
environment, only projects approved by elected and
appointed officials can be challenged, and litigation
delays increase project costs and sometimes derail
projects altogether. In 2024, California's preeminent
government oversight agency, the Little Hoover
Commission, issued a landmark report describing
CEQA's past successes and present challenges –
and recommended significant reforms.1 In 2025, the
California Assembly Select Committee on Permitting
Report likewise acknowledged challenges posed by
CEQA in achieving the state's housing, infrastructure
and climate goals.2 The need to reform CEQA and its
national equivalent, the National Environmental Policy
Act (NEPA), was even acknowledged by Democratic
Party candidates in the 2024 national election.
CEQA reform debates are highly politicized
because powerful stakeholders exploit CEQA
lawsuits and lawsuit threats to leverage economic
or environmental settlements and judicial outcomes
that cannot otherwise be realized by laws and
regulations. Often missing from political debates is
how CEQA is applied in practice – including which
projects are being sued and how those lawsuits are
resolved. For the past decade, we have been filling
that gap with actual CEQA litigation information.
This report includes 11 years of previously
unreported data about the judicial outcomes of
CEQA appeals. It concludes with analysis of how
California Proposition 45 on the November 2026
ballot offers voters the opportunity to accomplish
what decades of legislative efforts have not –
meaningful, structural CEQA reform.

Why are pro-housing groups split on Proposition 45?
by
Ben Christopher (https://calmatters.org/author/ben-christopher/)

In summary
Proposition 45 is intended to make it easier to build. But some pro-housing groups worry it will only lead to more sprawl.
Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called.
For nearly a decade, California’s Yes In My Backyard activists and other pro-development advocates have wanted to overhaul California’s signature environmental law to clear the way for more housing construction.
Now Proposition 45 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-45-environmental-review/) is on the ballot. Supporters say it would, among other things, overhaul that law, known as the California Environmental Quality Act, or CEQA, to clear the way for — you guessed it — more housing construction.
So why are YIMBYs divided?
Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/buffy-wicks-165044), an Oakland Democrat and one of the movement’s most stalwart champions in the Legislature, is for it. So is the bulk of the building industry (https://yesonprop45.com/our-coalition/), including many major for- and non-profit developers.
Bay Area pro-housing advocates Eastbay for Everyone (https://eastbayforeveryone.org/2026/03/05/streamlining-sprawl-is-not-pro-housing/) and the Greenbelt Alliance (https://www.greenbelt.org/blog/ceqa-baca-initiative/), two typical allies of Wicks, are emphatically against it.
In the uncommitted middle lies the lion’s share of California YIMBYism: Abundant Housing Los Angeles (https://www.abundanthousingla.org/endorsements-pac#endorsements), SPUR (https://www.spur.org/voter-guide/2026-11/ca-prop-45-environmental-review-ceqa), and both California YIMBY (https://cayimby.org/blog/proposition-45-2026/) and YIMBY Action (https://yimbyaction.org/prop45-recap) — the movement’s two flagship advocacy organizations — have all taken neutral positions.
“It’s been a weird campaign so far,” said Ali Sapirman, advocacy manager at the Housing Action Coalition, an urban building industry group that supports the measure. “The housing community has been a little bit fractured.”
Those fissures aren’t over whether more homes should be built across California. Instead, it mostly boils down to a question of where .
“The central question here is how you feel about sprawl,” Max Dubler of California YIMBY wrote in the group’s non-endorsement statement (https://cayimby.org/blog/proposition-45-2026/), referring to low-density housing development at the edge of metro areas. Though some exurban growth “will necessarily be part of solving our housing shortage,” he expressed concern about making it easier to build “car-dependent sprawl housing and the freeways and water infrastructure necessary to serve that sprawl.”
To sprawl or not to sprawl
For nearly a decade, the Legislature has been on a tear (https://www.spur.org/publications/research/2026-06-30/california-housing-laws), passing “streamlining” bills aimed at speeding up the regulatory approval of new construction. Almost all of those laws have only applied to projects in places where homes and other infrastructure already exist.
Prioritizing so-called infill development helped wrangle together a coalition of developers and construction labor unions (https://calmatters.org/politics/2025/07/california-construction-unions-housing/), but also a diverse swath of Democratic-leaning advocates whose interest in seeing more apartments and condos goes beyond the cause of affordability alone. That includes climate activists who want to see less commuter car traffic; transit, bicycle and pedestrian advocates who want more riders and walkers and urbanists who want Los Angeles to more closely resemble Barcelona (https://la.streetsblog.org/2022/07/07/some-urban-observations-from-my-barcelona-vacation).
In breaking from that urban focus, Prop. 45 is driving a wedge inside that coalition.

If passed, the measure would speed up the review process required under CEQA (pronounced “see-kwah”) for all types of housing projects. That includes transit-adjacent downtown condo towers, but also freshly paved subdivisions at the metropolitan fringe.
The measure is “a doubling down on essentially 75 years of land-use patterns that we know haven’t worked,” said Jordan Grimes, legislative director with Greenbelt Alliance, which opposes the measure. “It’s a return to the sprawl era.”
Not everyone in the movement necessarily sees that as a bad thing. Among those who want California to build its way out of its current housing shortage (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/09/california-housing-shortage/), opinions differ (https://www.nytimes.com/2025/04/10/magazine/suburban-sprawl-texas.html) over whether more environmentally-friendly (https://ternercenter.berkeley.edu/research-and-policy/role-of-new-housing-in-reducing-climate-pollution/) infill development alone is up to the task.
“I’m an ‘all of the above’ person when it comes to housing,” said Wicks, explaining her support of the measure. “I think we need housing of all different types, shapes, and sizes.”
An earlier version of this rift first emerged earlier this decade when a handful of Bay Area tech investors announced plans to build a brand new city on Solano County farmland in 2023 under the banner of California Forever (https://www.nytimes.com/2023/08/25/business/land-purchases-solano-county.html). Some YIMBY commentators applauded the plan as a welcome injection of much-needed supply (https://www.latimes.com/opinion/story/2025-12-01/california-forever-regulatory-streamlining). Others decried it as sprawl dressed in urbanist clothing (https://sfstandard.com/2024/06/21/california-forever-east-solano-plan-yimby/).
With Prop. 45, that regional debate is now playing out at a statewide scale.
Housing front and center
Prop. 45 is about much more than housing policy (https://calmatters.org/environment/2026/10/prop-45-california-ceqa-explained/).
CEQA requires public agencies to review the possible environmental consequences of the decisions they make, including the permitting of private projects. For decades industry groups, developers and, more recently, housing supply boosters have said the law makes it too easy for project opponents to jam up worthwhile projects by repeatedly demanding additional analysis.
“The clock is endless and the number of people and entities who can challenge you are also endless,” said Linda Mandolini of Eden Housing, an affordable housing developer.
Prop. 45 would not exempt any projects from environmental review outright. But for projects deemed “essential,” it would narrow the focus of these reviews and require them to wrap up within 365 business days. Any resulting litigation would also face a shot clock; Judges would have 270 business days to resolve them. Such lawsuits would also be made harder to sustain in court. Aside from housing, essential projects include roads, hospitals, schools, clean energy projects, water and broadband infrastructure.
But housing has loomed large in the electoral debate. The Yes on 45 campaign has touted the support of affordable housing developers (https://yesonprop45.com/2026/10/02/affordable-housing-leaders-unite-behind-prop-45-to-lower-housing-costs-and-build-the-homes-californians-need/) and housing advocates (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Xg8AW0KK6tY), while pointing to housing affordability (https://www.kqed.org/news/12100915/housing-fix-or-data-center-loophole-this-ballot-measure-would-overhaul-ceqa) concerns as the initial impetus for the measure.
It’s easy to see why. Environmental challenges to often innocuous-seeming housing projects have regularly generated headlines for years, helping to cement the idea among lawmakers and many voters that CEQA is a major cause of the state’s housing woes.
Environmental justice groups and their allies have spent years fighting against that argument in the Legislature. Though Prop. 45 does not exempt “essential” projects from environmental review outright — it just shortens and hems in the process — these groups have now lined up to oppose it for much the same reason: They reject the premise that CEQA needs fixing.
But for opponents like Grimes, who supported many recent streamlining bills, the argument that the law is holding up desperately needed residential construction is a year out of date. Last year, the governor signed Assembly Bill 130 (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260ab130), a Wicks-authored measure that exempted most infill housing (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/06/ceqa-urban-development-infill-budget/) from the CEQA.
Since becoming law in July 2025, developers have used it to entitle 17,913 units of housing, according to the Office of Land Use and Climate Innovation, a state agency.
“When you look at what’s left to do on urban housing, there are absolutely still barriers,” said Grimes, whose organization applauded last year’s exemption (https://www.greenbelt.org/blog/ceqa-reform-ca/). “CEQA just isn’t one of them.”
The task of the No on 45 campaign, he said, is to convince enough voters that “we’ve actually solved this problem.”
Are we done here?
Many developers and affordable housing advocates, even those working in urban areas, dispute that CEQA is no longer a major obstacle.
Last year’s exemption does not exempt projects larger than 20 acres, which means supersized (https://www.sfchronicle.com/sf/article/s-f-stonestown-development-19577137.php) urban (https://nypost.com/2026/05/26/lifestyle/westminster-mall-demolished-for-bolsa-pacific-mega-complex/) redevelopment (https://www.cbsnews.com/sanfrancisco/news/development-at-cupertinos-old-vallco-shopping-mall-site-finally-moves-ahead/) projects are still subject to the old process.
Prop. 45 also applies shot clocks to other permits (https://legal-planet.org/2026/02/27/what-does-baca-do-part-iv/) issued later in the development process and which regularly slow a project more than environmental review.
And while state laws like last year’s infill carveout may grant certain developers the right to ignore CEQA, there is nothing to stop a deep-pocketed opponent from suing anyway. Putting time limits on those lawsuits could be the difference between a project succeeding and being delayed to death, said Mandolini.
She points to the planned 130-unit affordable housing project that Eden Housing has been trying to and failing to build in the Bay Area suburb of Livermore since 2018 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/projects/2026/livermore-affordable-housing-timeline/) as an example. In 2021, a nonprofit funded by a handful of well-heeled Livermore residents sued the city, arguing that it hadn’t done enough environmental analysis on a housing development that would be built on a former grocery store parking lot behind a row of downtown restaurants. A lower court ruled that the group’s CEQA arguments were “almost utterly without merit.” An appellate court agreed. The state Supreme Court allowed that ruling to stand.
But by then two years had passed.
“Every year you lose in litigation is real money for real projects and another year that 130 families don’t get to live in that housing,” said Mandolini. “It’s a great way to kill a project.”
Even an infill project.
But among some pro-housing supporters of the proposition, the infill versus sprawl debate isn’t much of a debate at all.
“We’re not an urbanist organization,” said Mahdi Manji with the Inner City Law Center, a legal aid provider and housing advocacy group in Los Angeles’ Skid Row. The group supports Prop. 45 and doesn’t mind the concept of more housing far from the city’s core. “To the extent it results in housing that is a little more affordable in Lancaster and Palmdale, a lot of our clients live out in Lancaster and Palmdale.”

California (https://legal-planet.org/topics/california/)
BACA makes the ballot
Initiative to drastically change CEQA appears to have enough signatures to make ballot
It looks like the California Chamber of Commerce has enough signatures (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/04/27/could-a-change-to-environmental-law-reduce-california-costs/) to put on the November ballot their initiative (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0023A1%20%28%26quot%3BEssential%20Projects%26quot%3B%29.pdf) that would drastically change the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). Given that, I’m re-upping the analyses I did earlier this year on the measure: Part 1 (https://legal-planet.org/2026/02/25/what-does-the-building-an-affordable-california-act-do/) (overview), Part 2 (https://legal-planet.org/2026/02/26/what-does-baca-do-part-ii/) (sweeping scope of the initiative in terms of laws affected), Part 3 (https://legal-planet.org/2026/02/26/what-does-baca-do-part-iii/) (broad vested rights created by the initiative), Part 4 (https://legal-planet.org/2026/02/27/what-does-baca-do-part-iv/) (approval changes that apply to all California law), Part 5 (https://legal-planet.org/2026/02/27/what-does-baca-do-part-v/) (limits on the types of impacts that would be considered under CEQA), Part 6 (https://legal-planet.org/2026/02/28/what-does-baca-do-part-vi/) (changes to the scope and alternatives analyses under CEQA), Part 7 (https://legal-planet.org/2026/03/01/what-does-baca-do-part-vii/) (the broad scope of projects covered by the initiative), Part 8 (https://legal-planet.org/2026/03/01/what-does-baca-do-part-viii/) (the initiative makes future changes very difficult), Part 9 (https://legal-planet.org/2026/03/02/what-does-baca-do-part-ix/) (the gaps in state environmental law the initiative would produce), Part 10 (https://legal-planet.org/2026/03/02/what-does-baca-do-part-x/) (the issues with CEQA that reforms should tackle).
While the name given the proponents to the initiative is “Building an Affordable California Act”, on the ballot the title will be: “Modifies Environmental Review for Certain Projects.” The full measure is here (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0023A1%20%28%26quot%3BEssential%20Projects%26quot%3B%29.pdf). The title of the initiative and ballot summary prepared by the state Attorney General is here (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/Title%20and%20Summary%20%2825-0023A1%29.pdf). (That title and summary will be the first part of what voters see in their ballot guides when they come out this fall.)

A summary of BACA
An overview of my analyses of Proposition 45
I’ve written a lot on the Cal Chamber sponsored initiative to dramatically change CEQA, BACA, which is Proposition 45 on this year’s ballot. Here are some key takeaways from what I’ve written, as well as links to the relevant blog posts.
First, BACA will not just apply to CEQA. It broadly expands vested rights (https://legal-planet.org/2026/02/26/what-does-baca-do-part-iii/) and imposes strict time limits for all permitting in the state (https://legal-planet.org/2026/02/27/what-does-baca-do-part-iv/) for covered projects. It’s possible that it prevents ever increasing or changing regulatory standards for a covered project, even after it is constructed and is in operation (https://legal-planet.org/2026/02/26/what-does-baca-do-part-iii/). And it will significantly weaken a range of substantive environmental protections (https://legal-planet.org/2026/03/02/what-does-baca-do-part-ix/) in California, such as for endangered species habitat and cumulative air pollution.
Second, BACA will not just apply to clean energy, mass transit, and housing projects (https://legal-planet.org/2026/03/01/what-does-baca-do-part-vii/). It applies to freeways and roads, to dams and irrigation projects, and to logging projects. It may well cover any development project that eliminates natural habitat in California (on the grounds of reducing fire risk). It may well include (https://legal-planet.org/2026/06/24/baca-and-data-centers-part-i/) data (https://legal-planet.org/2026/06/25/baca-and-data-centers-part-ii/) centers (https://legal-planet.org/2026/09/10/more-on-baca-and-data-centers/).
Third, for all intents and purposes, BACA basically repeals CEQA for covered projects. Proponents may be able to unilaterally limit the scope of CEQA review and determine what alternatives are to be considered (https://legal-planet.org/2026/02/28/what-does-baca-do-part-vi/). CEQA loses any independent review or mitigation requirements (https://legal-planet.org/2026/02/27/what-does-baca-do-part-v/), and simply becomes a checklist for compliance with other laws. And judicial enforcement is sharply limited, even for compliance with those other laws.
Fourth, there is significant uncertainty about how BACA will work. In particular, provisions of the initiative may cause it to be interpreted much more broadly (https://legal-planet.org/2026/02/26/what-does-baca-do-part-ii/) than an initial read of the text indicates, and it overrides any conflicting laws (https://legal-planet.org/2026/02/26/what-does-baca-do-part-ii/).
Fifth, BACA will be extremely difficult to amend if it is enacted (https://legal-planet.org/2026/03/01/what-does-baca-do-part-viii/). Any changes require a 2/3 majority in the state legislature.
Sixth, BACA does address some real concerns (https://legal-planet.org/2026/03/02/what-does-baca-do-part-x/) with how CEQA works, including the ability of project opponents to play Calvinball and develop new claims of harms that must be analyzed and mitigated, with moving targets for what alternatives should be assessed and what standards apply for mitigation. I’ve outlined (https://legal-planet.org/2026/05/12/reforming-ceqa-part-i/) a range (https://legal-planet.org/2026/05/12/reforming-ceqa-part-2/) of (https://legal-planet.org/2026/05/13/reforming-ceqa-part-3/) reforms (https://legal-planet.org/2026/05/13/reforming-ceqa-part-4/) to (https://legal-planet.org/2026/05/14/reforming-ceqa-part-5/) CEQA (https://legal-planet.org/2026/05/14/reforming-ceqa-part-6/) that I think would address those concerns but with less collateral damage than BACA would produce.
Seventh, there are a number of constraints (https://legal-planet.org/2026/07/29/the-limits-of-implementation-for-baca/) on how broadly BACA will be implemented in practice. Union labor or prevailing wage requirements may limit how many projects use BACA (except for housing, which is exempt from those requirements). Local zoning and planning rules in place at the time a project is proposed would also continue to restrict what is possible.
Eighth, BACA will probably undermine the planning process in California (https://legal-planet.org/2026/07/28/baca-and-planning/), and incentivize more piecemeal analysis and approval of individual projects, likely increasing the cumulative environmental impacts of development.
Finally, in particular BACA will likely contribute to eliminating most endangered species habitat protections (https://legal-planet.org/2026/09/13/the-end-of-endangered-species-habitat-protections-in-california/) in California, a state that claims to be an environmental leader.
