A summary of BACA
An overview of my analyses of Proposition 45
I’ve written a lot on the Cal Chamber sponsored initiative to dramatically change CEQA, BACA, which is Proposition 45 on this year’s ballot. Here are some key takeaways from what I’ve written, as well as links to the relevant blog posts.
First, BACA will not just apply to CEQA. It broadly expands vested rights (https://legal-planet.org/2026/02/26/what-does-baca-do-part-iii/) and imposes strict time limits for all permitting in the state (https://legal-planet.org/2026/02/27/what-does-baca-do-part-iv/) for covered projects. It’s possible that it prevents ever increasing or changing regulatory standards for a covered project, even after it is constructed and is in operation (https://legal-planet.org/2026/02/26/what-does-baca-do-part-iii/). And it will significantly weaken a range of substantive environmental protections (https://legal-planet.org/2026/03/02/what-does-baca-do-part-ix/) in California, such as for endangered species habitat and cumulative air pollution.
Second, BACA will not just apply to clean energy, mass transit, and housing projects (https://legal-planet.org/2026/03/01/what-does-baca-do-part-vii/). It applies to freeways and roads, to dams and irrigation projects, and to logging projects. It may well cover any development project that eliminates natural habitat in California (on the grounds of reducing fire risk). It may well include (https://legal-planet.org/2026/06/24/baca-and-data-centers-part-i/) data (https://legal-planet.org/2026/06/25/baca-and-data-centers-part-ii/) centers (https://legal-planet.org/2026/09/10/more-on-baca-and-data-centers/).
Third, for all intents and purposes, BACA basically repeals CEQA for covered projects. Proponents may be able to unilaterally limit the scope of CEQA review and determine what alternatives are to be considered (https://legal-planet.org/2026/02/28/what-does-baca-do-part-vi/). CEQA loses any independent review or mitigation requirements (https://legal-planet.org/2026/02/27/what-does-baca-do-part-v/), and simply becomes a checklist for compliance with other laws. And judicial enforcement is sharply limited, even for compliance with those other laws.
Fourth, there is significant uncertainty about how BACA will work. In particular, provisions of the initiative may cause it to be interpreted much more broadly (https://legal-planet.org/2026/02/26/what-does-baca-do-part-ii/) than an initial read of the text indicates, and it overrides any conflicting laws (https://legal-planet.org/2026/02/26/what-does-baca-do-part-ii/).
Fifth, BACA will be extremely difficult to amend if it is enacted (https://legal-planet.org/2026/03/01/what-does-baca-do-part-viii/). Any changes require a 2/3 majority in the state legislature.
Sixth, BACA does address some real concerns (https://legal-planet.org/2026/03/02/what-does-baca-do-part-x/) with how CEQA works, including the ability of project opponents to play Calvinball and develop new claims of harms that must be analyzed and mitigated, with moving targets for what alternatives should be assessed and what standards apply for mitigation. I’ve outlined (https://legal-planet.org/2026/05/12/reforming-ceqa-part-i/) a range (https://legal-planet.org/2026/05/12/reforming-ceqa-part-2/) of (https://legal-planet.org/2026/05/13/reforming-ceqa-part-3/) reforms (https://legal-planet.org/2026/05/13/reforming-ceqa-part-4/) to (https://legal-planet.org/2026/05/14/reforming-ceqa-part-5/) CEQA (https://legal-planet.org/2026/05/14/reforming-ceqa-part-6/) that I think would address those concerns but with less collateral damage than BACA would produce.
Seventh, there are a number of constraints (https://legal-planet.org/2026/07/29/the-limits-of-implementation-for-baca/) on how broadly BACA will be implemented in practice. Union labor or prevailing wage requirements may limit how many projects use BACA (except for housing, which is exempt from those requirements). Local zoning and planning rules in place at the time a project is proposed would also continue to restrict what is possible.
Eighth, BACA will probably undermine the planning process in California (https://legal-planet.org/2026/07/28/baca-and-planning/), and incentivize more piecemeal analysis and approval of individual projects, likely increasing the cumulative environmental impacts of development.
Finally, in particular BACA will likely contribute to eliminating most endangered species habitat protections (https://legal-planet.org/2026/09/13/the-end-of-endangered-species-habitat-protections-in-california/) in California, a state that claims to be an environmental leader.

EIR Projects: Status Quo CEQA Review Durations
The status quo CEQA Review period duration for EIRs is estimated based on analysis of CEQA document timelines across a sample of 539 residential EIR projects that submitted data to the state’s CEQANet portal (https://ceqanet.lci.ca.gov/) after January 1, 2020 (the “EIR Project Sample”). 10 Figure 6 shows the distribution of CEQA Review durations across the 539 residential EIR projects included in the analysis sample. While the median CEQA Review duration was 715 days (or just under two years), the average NOP-NOD period was 1,141 days (or roughly three years). Forty-one percent of projects were certified within the maximum 591-day period allowed under Prop 45. 11 Twenty-seven percent of the sampled projects’ review periods lasted between 591 days and three years. Nearly one in six residential EIR reviews in the sample took more than five years to complete, including 6% that took more than a decade.

Prop 45 Would Cut Roughly Three Years from the Longest Residential EIR Timelines
Estimating Prop 45’s impact on the average residential EIR entitlement timeline requires calculating the difference between (a) the status quo average entitlement duration for the EIR project sample and (b) the average period across these projects if Prop 45’s 591-day CEQA review time limit were enforced against EIR projects with review durations exceeding this maximum. Similarly, Prop 45’s impact on entitlement volatility depends on the change in the standard deviation of project entitlement periods under the 591-day limit.
Figure 7 summarizes the calculation of the change in the average entitlement duration under Prop 45. Under the status quo, the average entitlement period is an estimated 1,276 days (i.e., 1,141 days of CEQA review plus 135 days of other entitlement review). Of the 539 projects in the EIR sample, 221 had their EIRs certified in fewer than 591 days, and the average total entitlement period for this cohort (509 days) is assumed to remain the same under Prop 45. For the remaining 318 projects with CEQA reviews exceeding the Prop 45 time limit, the average status quo entitlement period is 1,809 days, of which 1,674 days is CEQA review. Prop 45’s 591-day limit would reduce the total entitlement period to 726 days, on average (as it would reduce the CEQA review phase from 1,674 days to Prop 45’s 591-day limit). As a result, Prop 45 would cut the average entitlement timeline across all residential EIR projects roughly in half, from 1,276 days to 637 days. For projects exceeding Prop 45’s time limit, the reduction would be even greater: 1,082 days, or roughly three years.

Economic and Fiscal Impacts of Increased Residential Construction
Prop 45’s Impact on Housing Affordability
By adding nearly 200,000 homes over ten years, Prop 45 would increase housing supply and put downward pressure on rents and home prices. Based on the state Department of Finance (DOF) estimates of the total statewide housing stock (https://dof.ca.gov/forecasting/demographics/estimates/e-5-population-and-housing-estimates-for-cities-counties-and-the-state-2020-2026/) (15.06 million units as of 2026) and status quo permitting rates (i.e., 108,269 units annually), the increase in residential construction under Prop 45 would increase the state’s housing stock by 1.21% after 10 years. 18 According to a recent Pew Research Center analysis, a 10% increase in a metropolitan region’s rental supply resulted in a 5.4% reduction in the region’s rents relative to nationwide rent cost trends (i.e., a “supply-price effect” of 0.54). 19 Based on this effect, Prop 45’s supply impact would reduce average rents and home prices by 0.66% (i.e., 1.21% × 0.54).
Macroeconomic Benefits of New Housing
In addition to Prop 45’s expected impact on housing costs in California, new housing also generates spillover economic and fiscal benefits that exceed the housing affordability impacts shown above. Empirical studies of supply-constrained housing markets have shown that unlocking new housing supply in high-cost regions promotes economic growth by enabling more workers to access the higher-paying jobs concentrated in these areas. 20 This expansion of the regional labor supply, in turn, attracts more firms to the area. Housing construction in high-demand regions additionally provides several quality-of-life benefits, including reduced commute times and household overcrowding. 21
Fiscal Impacts of Increased Residential Development
Increases in residential development generate additional tax revenues for state and local governments on a one-time basis during the construction period and on an ongoing annual basis once the new units are complete. Construction period tax revenues include personal income taxes (PIT) generated by income earned by construction workers and firm owners, corporation taxes generated by the corporate profits from this activity, and sales taxes on construction materials and equipment. Ongoing property tax revenues are generated annually once a new unit is added to the local property tax roll.

IV. Non-Residential Impacts
By shortening non-residential project review timelines, Prop 45 would lower costs incurred by public agencies and California utility ratepayers or consumers. Longer project review periods increase total project costs through two primary channels. First, because the costs of pre-development activities, including planning, engineering, design, and environmental review, are incurred before construction begins, longer review periods impose higher carrying costs on sponsors (i.e., the “pre-development cost of capital”). Second, because construction costs have historically outpaced general inflation in California, delaying the start of construction imposes higher real construction costs on project developers (i.e., “construction cost inflation”).
Pre-Development Cost Impact
Project sponsors require a minimum annual rate of return on pre-development capital investments. The impact of these capital costs on total project budgets depends on the project sponsor type as well as the share of project expenses incurred during the pre-development period.
Public Agency and Private Sector Pre-Development Costs of Capital
For private sponsors, the cost of capital reflects the annual internal rate of return (IRR) required by a project’s investors or lenders. Because of the high risk of project failure during the planning and approval process, 27 higher rates of return are demanded on pre-development stage capital than capital invested in shovel-ready projects. Because clean energy projects account for roughly 63% of total IOU and private sector essential project expenditures, and 100% of the annual essential construction spending incurred by California’s ratepayers, this report relies on market study estimates of the IRR typically earned on pre-development utility-scale solar project investments. 28 Based on this research, the real private sponsor cost of capital is an estimated 16%. 29
Though public agencies may not require or earn investment returns on their infrastructure spending, these entities may incur financing costs to the extent bonds are issued to fund these initial capital investments. In either case, given the time value of money, governments discount projects’ future benefits or costs when conducting benefit-cost analyses (i.e., for every year that a project or program’s benefits are delayed, their expected values are reduced by the chosen discount rate). 30 Given the large share of public spending on transportation projects, this report adopts a discount rate of 4% as the effective public agency cost of capital. 31
Impact of Pre-Development Capital Costs Across Essential Project Categories
The per-year pre-development cost for each essential project category and project sponsor type is calculated by applying the discount rate or IRR (an annual percentage) to the percentage share of project expenses committed during pre-development (i.e., the pre-development cost share).
As shown in Figure 17, based on federal survey data and research materials, this cost share is estimated to range from 3% (for clean energy projects) to 25% (for broadband). 32 As a result, a one-year reduction in the average transportation project review period, for example, is estimated to reduce total project costs by 0.6% if the sponsor is a public agency (i.e., 15% × 4%) and by 2.4% if the sponsor is a private firm (i.e., 15% × 16%).

Introduction
The California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) was enacted unanimously
by a bipartisan legislature and signed by then-Governor Ronald Reagan in
1970. CEQA is a catchall statute requiring state and local agencies to consider
environmental impacts before approving or undertaking a construction
project, plan or regulation applicable to a construction project or the physical
environment. CEQA is older than the Endangered Species Act, Clean Air and
Clean Water acts, California Coastal Act, National Historic Preservation Act,
and thousands of other federal and state laws and regulations that ostensibly
protect the environment and public health. Any person or entity that
disagrees with an agency’s decision to approve or undertake a project that
is subject to CEQA can file a lawsuit in state court. CEQA trial and appellate
court proceedings typically take about five years to complete, and while
litigation is pending, most approved projects are stalled.
Jennifer Hernandez has practiced environmental and land use law in California
for 40 years; teaches environmental justice, land use and environmental law in
California law schools; serves on the boards of several nonprofit environmental
and other organizations; and has published several books and scores of articles
on CEQA, land use housing, climate and other topics. While the author is grateful
for the research assistance provided by the Independent Institute and other
Holland & Knight attorneys, the opinions and recommendations in this study are
the author’s and should not be attributed to any other person or organization, to
Holland & Knight or any client of the firm, or to the Independent Institute.
CEQA increasingly has been criticized as a major
reason California can’t build enough housing,
water, and transportation infrastructure or public
service facilities – including important projects
approved and funded by taxpayers – because all
projects subject to CEQA must also comply with
myriad other laws to protect human health and the
environment, only projects approved by elected and
appointed officials can be challenged, and litigation
delays increase project costs and sometimes derail
projects altogether. In 2024, California's preeminent
government oversight agency, the Little Hoover
Commission, issued a landmark report describing
CEQA's past successes and present challenges –
and recommended significant reforms.1 In 2025, the
California Assembly Select Committee on Permitting
Report likewise acknowledged challenges posed by
CEQA in achieving the state's housing, infrastructure
and climate goals.2 The need to reform CEQA and its
national equivalent, the National Environmental Policy
Act (NEPA), was even acknowledged by Democratic
Party candidates in the 2024 national election.
CEQA reform debates are highly politicized
because powerful stakeholders exploit CEQA
lawsuits and lawsuit threats to leverage economic
or environmental settlements and judicial outcomes
that cannot otherwise be realized by laws and
regulations. Often missing from political debates is
how CEQA is applied in practice – including which
projects are being sued and how those lawsuits are
resolved. For the past decade, we have been filling
that gap with actual CEQA litigation information.
This report includes 11 years of previously
unreported data about the judicial outcomes of
CEQA appeals. It concludes with analysis of how
California Proposition 45 on the November 2026
ballot offers voters the opportunity to accomplish
what decades of legislative efforts have not –
meaningful, structural CEQA reform.

In summary
Proposition 45 is intended to make it easier to build. But some pro-housing groups worry it will only lead to more sprawl.
Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called.
For nearly a decade, California’s Yes In My Backyard activists and other pro-development advocates have wanted to overhaul California’s signature environmental law to clear the way for more housing construction.
Now Proposition 45 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-45-environmental-review/) is on the ballot. Supporters say it would, among other things, overhaul that law, known as the California Environmental Quality Act, or CEQA, to clear the way for — you guessed it — more housing construction.
So why are YIMBYs divided?
Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/buffy-wicks-165044), an Oakland Democrat and one of the movement’s most stalwart champions in the Legislature, is for it. So is the bulk of the building industry (https://yesonprop45.com/our-coalition/), including many major for- and non-profit developers.
Bay Area pro-housing advocates Eastbay for Everyone (https://eastbayforeveryone.org/2026/03/05/streamlining-sprawl-is-not-pro-housing/) and the Greenbelt Alliance (https://www.greenbelt.org/blog/ceqa-baca-initiative/), two typical allies of Wicks, are emphatically against it.
In the uncommitted middle lies the lion’s share of California YIMBYism: Abundant Housing Los Angeles (https://www.abundanthousingla.org/endorsements-pac#endorsements), SPUR (https://www.spur.org/voter-guide/2026-11/ca-prop-45-environmental-review-ceqa), and both California YIMBY (https://cayimby.org/blog/proposition-45-2026/) and YIMBY Action (https://yimbyaction.org/prop45-recap) — the movement’s two flagship advocacy organizations — have all taken neutral positions.
“It’s been a weird campaign so far,” said Ali Sapirman, advocacy manager at the Housing Action Coalition, an urban building industry group that supports the measure. “The housing community has been a little bit fractured.”
Those fissures aren’t over whether more homes should be built across California. Instead, it mostly boils down to a question of where .
“The central question here is how you feel about sprawl,” Max Dubler of California YIMBY wrote in the group’s non-endorsement statement (https://cayimby.org/blog/proposition-45-2026/), referring to low-density housing development at the edge of metro areas. Though some exurban growth “will necessarily be part of solving our housing shortage,” he expressed concern about making it easier to build “car-dependent sprawl housing and the freeways and water infrastructure necessary to serve that sprawl.”
To sprawl or not to sprawl
For nearly a decade, the Legislature has been on a tear (https://www.spur.org/publications/research/2026-06-30/california-housing-laws), passing “streamlining” bills aimed at speeding up the regulatory approval of new construction. Almost all of those laws have only applied to projects in places where homes and other infrastructure already exist.
Prioritizing so-called infill development helped wrangle together a coalition of developers and construction labor unions (https://calmatters.org/politics/2025/07/california-construction-unions-housing/), but also a diverse swath of Democratic-leaning advocates whose interest in seeing more apartments and condos goes beyond the cause of affordability alone. That includes climate activists who want to see less commuter car traffic; transit, bicycle and pedestrian advocates who want more riders and walkers and urbanists who want Los Angeles to more closely resemble Barcelona (https://la.streetsblog.org/2022/07/07/some-urban-observations-from-my-barcelona-vacation).
In breaking from that urban focus, Prop. 45 is driving a wedge inside that coalition.

If passed, the measure would speed up the review process required under CEQA (pronounced “see-kwah”) for all types of housing projects. That includes transit-adjacent downtown condo towers, but also freshly paved subdivisions at the metropolitan fringe.
The measure is “a doubling down on essentially 75 years of land-use patterns that we know haven’t worked,” said Jordan Grimes, legislative director with Greenbelt Alliance, which opposes the measure. “It’s a return to the sprawl era.”
Not everyone in the movement necessarily sees that as a bad thing. Among those who want California to build its way out of its current housing shortage (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/09/california-housing-shortage/), opinions differ (https://www.nytimes.com/2025/04/10/magazine/suburban-sprawl-texas.html) over whether more environmentally-friendly (https://ternercenter.berkeley.edu/research-and-policy/role-of-new-housing-in-reducing-climate-pollution/) infill development alone is up to the task.
“I’m an ‘all of the above’ person when it comes to housing,” said Wicks, explaining her support of the measure. “I think we need housing of all different types, shapes, and sizes.”
An earlier version of this rift first emerged earlier this decade when a handful of Bay Area tech investors announced plans to build a brand new city on Solano County farmland in 2023 under the banner of California Forever (https://www.nytimes.com/2023/08/25/business/land-purchases-solano-county.html). Some YIMBY commentators applauded the plan as a welcome injection of much-needed supply (https://www.latimes.com/opinion/story/2025-12-01/california-forever-regulatory-streamlining). Others decried it as sprawl dressed in urbanist clothing (https://sfstandard.com/2024/06/21/california-forever-east-solano-plan-yimby/).
With Prop. 45, that regional debate is now playing out at a statewide scale.
Housing front and center
Prop. 45 is about much more than housing policy (https://calmatters.org/environment/2026/10/prop-45-california-ceqa-explained/).
CEQA requires public agencies to review the possible environmental consequences of the decisions they make, including the permitting of private projects. For decades industry groups, developers and, more recently, housing supply boosters have said the law makes it too easy for project opponents to jam up worthwhile projects by repeatedly demanding additional analysis.
“The clock is endless and the number of people and entities who can challenge you are also endless,” said Linda Mandolini of Eden Housing, an affordable housing developer.
Prop. 45 would not exempt any projects from environmental review outright. But for projects deemed “essential,” it would narrow the focus of these reviews and require them to wrap up within 365 business days. Any resulting litigation would also face a shot clock; Judges would have 270 business days to resolve them. Such lawsuits would also be made harder to sustain in court. Aside from housing, essential projects include roads, hospitals, schools, clean energy projects, water and broadband infrastructure.
But housing has loomed large in the electoral debate. The Yes on 45 campaign has touted the support of affordable housing developers (https://yesonprop45.com/2026/10/02/affordable-housing-leaders-unite-behind-prop-45-to-lower-housing-costs-and-build-the-homes-californians-need/) and housing advocates (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Xg8AW0KK6tY), while pointing to housing affordability (https://www.kqed.org/news/12100915/housing-fix-or-data-center-loophole-this-ballot-measure-would-overhaul-ceqa) concerns as the initial impetus for the measure.
It’s easy to see why. Environmental challenges to often innocuous-seeming housing projects have regularly generated headlines for years, helping to cement the idea among lawmakers and many voters that CEQA is a major cause of the state’s housing woes.
Environmental justice groups and their allies have spent years fighting against that argument in the Legislature. Though Prop. 45 does not exempt “essential” projects from environmental review outright — it just shortens and hems in the process — these groups have now lined up to oppose it for much the same reason: They reject the premise that CEQA needs fixing.
But for opponents like Grimes, who supported many recent streamlining bills, the argument that the law is holding up desperately needed residential construction is a year out of date. Last year, the governor signed Assembly Bill 130 (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260ab130), a Wicks-authored measure that exempted most infill housing (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/06/ceqa-urban-development-infill-budget/) from the CEQA.
Since becoming law in July 2025, developers have used it to entitle 17,913 units of housing, according to the Office of Land Use and Climate Innovation, a state agency.
“When you look at what’s left to do on urban housing, there are absolutely still barriers,” said Grimes, whose organization applauded last year’s exemption (https://www.greenbelt.org/blog/ceqa-reform-ca/). “CEQA just isn’t one of them.”
The task of the No on 45 campaign, he said, is to convince enough voters that “we’ve actually solved this problem.”
Are we done here?
Many developers and affordable housing advocates, even those working in urban areas, dispute that CEQA is no longer a major obstacle.
Last year’s exemption does not exempt projects larger than 20 acres, which means supersized (https://www.sfchronicle.com/sf/article/s-f-stonestown-development-19577137.php) urban (https://nypost.com/2026/05/26/lifestyle/westminster-mall-demolished-for-bolsa-pacific-mega-complex/) redevelopment (https://www.cbsnews.com/sanfrancisco/news/development-at-cupertinos-old-vallco-shopping-mall-site-finally-moves-ahead/) projects are still subject to the old process.
Prop. 45 also applies shot clocks to other permits (https://legal-planet.org/2026/02/27/what-does-baca-do-part-iv/) issued later in the development process and which regularly slow a project more than environmental review.
And while state laws like last year’s infill carveout may grant certain developers the right to ignore CEQA, there is nothing to stop a deep-pocketed opponent from suing anyway. Putting time limits on those lawsuits could be the difference between a project succeeding and being delayed to death, said Mandolini.
She points to the planned 130-unit affordable housing project that Eden Housing has been trying to and failing to build in the Bay Area suburb of Livermore since 2018 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/projects/2026/livermore-affordable-housing-timeline/) as an example. In 2021, a nonprofit funded by a handful of well-heeled Livermore residents sued the city, arguing that it hadn’t done enough environmental analysis on a housing development that would be built on a former grocery store parking lot behind a row of downtown restaurants. A lower court ruled that the group’s CEQA arguments were “almost utterly without merit.” An appellate court agreed. The state Supreme Court allowed that ruling to stand.
But by then two years had passed.
“Every year you lose in litigation is real money for real projects and another year that 130 families don’t get to live in that housing,” said Mandolini. “It’s a great way to kill a project.”
Even an infill project.
But among some pro-housing supporters of the proposition, the infill versus sprawl debate isn’t much of a debate at all.
“We’re not an urbanist organization,” said Mahdi Manji with the Inner City Law Center, a legal aid provider and housing advocacy group in Los Angeles’ Skid Row. The group supports Prop. 45 and doesn’t mind the concept of more housing far from the city’s core. “To the extent it results in housing that is a little more affordable in Lancaster and Palmdale, a lot of our clients live out in Lancaster and Palmdale.”

What does BACA do? Part III
Proposed CEQA ballot initiative would prevent changing environmental standards very early in the development process.
This is the third in a series of blog posts on the California Chamber of Commerce’s proposed ballot initiative (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0023A1%20%28%26quot%3BEssential%20Projects%26quot%3B%29.pdf) amending the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). The first blog post is here (https://legal-planet.org/2026/02/25/what-does-the-building-an-affordable-california-act-do/). The second blog post is here (https://legal-planet.org/2026/02/26/what-does-baca-do-part-ii/).
The most sweeping change in the initiative is buried in the lead-in to an innocuously titled section, proposed new Section 21023 “Other Public Agency Actions for Essential Projects.”
Here is the key text, in the beginning of 21023(a)
“If an essential project requires any other public agency action that is not expressly addressed by other provisions of this chapter, the public agency shall make a final written decision thereon based on compliance with existing laws.”
What this means is that any approval – even if it has nothing to do with CEQA – must be made pursuant to “compliance with existing laws.” What does “existing laws” mean? That term is defined in proposed new Section 21028(r)(1):
“Formally adopted legal requirements contained in statutes, regulations, rules, standards, or ordinances that existed and were in effect on the date an application for an essential project was submitted to a public agency.”
Thus, only the law in place at the time an application is submitted to an agency can be applied to review of a project. This is what lawyers call “vested rights” – a constraint on the ability of the government to change the rules for a project after a certain point in time. California recognizes vested rights, but in general the trigger for vested rights in California is substantially later in time than the submission of an application. And for good reason.
Early vested rights provide certainty and predictability for project proponents. Those are good things. But they come with costs.
First, it prevents the government from responding to changed circumstances. For instance, if the environmental review of a project identifies a new harm not currently covered in existing written standards, there is nothing the government can do to prevent that harm. This may be particularly an issue when a proponent proposes a dramatically new type of project, or is proposing a project in a location without preexisting environmental data.
The initiative does provide a very limited exception to address this issue, but only “to mitigate or avoid a specific, adverse life-safety impact, meaning a significant, quantifiable, direct, and unavoidable life-safety impact, including life-safety impacts associated with new or emerging technologies, materials, or grid-integration systems, and that is based on objective, identified and written public safety standards, policies, or conditions.” (Proposed new Section 21028(r)(2)). If you’re a newly discovered endangered species population, for instance, you may well be out of luck. Or if there is uncertainty about the potential impacts, perhaps because there is not clear information about the risks of the new technology involved, the government may well be unable to act as well.
Second, it may facilitate strategic behavior by project proponents. 21028(r)(1) does not define “submitted” – but it seems to mean when an applicant has submitted an application, any kind of application, to the public agency. (Such a broad interpretation would, of course, be based on Section 21029, which calls for the initiative to be broadly interpreted to allow for approval of covered projects.) So what is to stop an applicant from submitting a proposal with minimal information to a public agency to freeze the relevant law? Sure, the public agency can say the application is incomplete – the initiative has a limited timeframe for the agency to provide such a response, where CEQA is involved – but there is nothing to stop the applicant from dawdling in their response, or providing only a partial response (requiring another reply by the agency), and so freezing the relevant law for an extended period of time. We might even see properties with submitted applications get increased value because of their vested rights.
The vested rights here do not appear to depend on whether CEQA applies to a project. And indeed the scope section for the proposed initiative, proposed new Section 21013, says it applies to all “essential” projects, period, not just to the “essential” projects going through a CEQA process. Thus, these are vested rights for all state and local approval of all covered projects in the state. That breadth belies the claims of the initiative text that it does not “diminish the authority of any public agency to approve or disapprove an essential project.” (Section 21014(a)).
And note that because the initiative states that it overrides any conflicting law, it necessarily overrides any contrary vested rights doctrine in state law for any other statute.
Finally, it is possible the vested rights in the initiative extend beyond the initial approval of the project, and prohibit increasing regulatory standards for any covered project after it is constructed, during its operation. The vested rights provision in 21023(a) covers “any other public agency action that is not expressly addressed by other provisions of this chapter.” Action is not defined in the initiative. But it might include any public agency action that applies at any time to the essential project – proposed new Section 21023(a) on its own terms provides no time limit to its coverage. If that is the case (and again, remember we are to broadly apply the initiative under Section 21029(a) “to afford the fullest possible weight to the interest of . . . essential projects”), then any subsequent regulatory decision for a covered project is bound by vested rights. In other words, the agency and state legislature could never update or make more stringent the regulatory standards that apply to a covered project, in perpetuity . It is a permanent lock-in of all regulatory standards. That would be a drastic – and probably untenable – change in law. Cutting against this interpretation is that overall Section 21023 sets decision timeframes for the “other public agency action” based on the timeframe for the original decision about CEQA applicability or review for the project. Section 21023(a)(1). However, one could also read this provision as implicitly prohibiting any adverse subsequent public agency action with respect to the project, if that action would occur after the deadlines set in Section 21023(a)(1). That would mean that public agencies could not (except at the request of the applicant) make additional regulatory decisions with respect to a covered project after its initial approval – basically achieving the same result of freezing in relevant law.
Of course, this broad vested rights provision is not flagged at all in the preamble to the initiative (which asserts it does not affect existing state environmental laws).

What does BACA do? Part IX
Proposed CEQA ballot initiative might create unexpected, large gaps in existing environmental protections in California.
This is the ninth in a series of blog posts on the California Chamber of Commerce’s proposed ballot initiative (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0023A1%20%28%26quot%3BEssential%20Projects%26quot%3B%29.pdf) amending the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). The first blog post is here (https://legal-planet.org/2026/02/25/what-does-the-building-an-affordable-california-act-do/). The second blog post is here (https://legal-planet.org/2026/02/26/what-does-baca-do-part-ii/). The third blog post is here (https://legal-planet.org/2026/02/26/what-does-baca-do-part-iii/). The fourth blog post is here (https://legal-planet.org/2026/02/27/what-does-baca-do-part-iv/). The fifth blog post is here (https://legal-planet.org/2026/02/27/what-does-baca-do-part-v/). The sixth blog post is here (https://legal-planet.org/2026/02/28/what-does-baca-do-part-vi/). The seventh blog post is here (https://legal-planet.org/2026/03/01/what-does-baca-do-part-vii/). The eighth blog post is here (https://legal-planet.org/2026/03/01/what-does-baca-do-part-viii/).
CEQA has over time become a key component of a range of environmental protections in California. As I’ve discussed before (https://legal-planet.org/2025/07/07/filling-the-gaps-from-ceqa-reform/), that means that if you significantly trim back on CEQA, the result may be a range of (unintended?) consequences in terms of reducing environmental legal protections under other laws, because those laws were drafted based on a reliance that CEQA review provided both procedural and substantive protections for important environmental resources. Thus, eliminating CEQA might result in substantial gaps in our current environmental protection structure in California.
The problem is that it’s not entirely clear what those gaps might be, at least not without a thorough review of the existing structure of current California environmental law. As an example, I’ll use the California Endangered Species Act (CESA), which I know fairly well, and thus have some (but not complete!) confidence to assess what the consequences of CEQA repeal might be.
CESA protects a range of endangered and threatened species in California. Some (but not all!) of those species are also protected against the federal Endangered Species Act (ESA). And many of those species are threatened by habitat destruction. One would think then, that CESA would provide clear protection for those species from habitat destruction. That would not necessarily be a correct conclusion though.
As it turns out (see this blog post (https://legal-planet.org/2025/04/24/the-california-esa-and-habitat-protection/)), whether CESA prevents the destruction of habitat for a CESA-listed species is not clear. State agencies have been acting as if that is the case – but that is in part because, regardless of what CESA says, CEQA does protect the habitat of CESA-listed species. Under the current CEQA guidelines, a project that would “substantially reduce the number or restrict the range of an endangered, rare or threatened species” necessarily has a significant effect on the environment, such that full CEQA review would be required. That in turn triggers the mitigation requirements under CEQA. Those requirements are not absolute – they apply to the extent “feasible” as determined by the agency. But they are a substantial protection. So the lack of explicit coverage of habitat destruction under CESA has not been an issue.
That would change if this initiative is enacted. As I discussed earlier, it is plausible that the mandatory findings of significance under the CEQA Guidelines would not count for determining significance for projects covered by the initiative. That in turn means that there probably is not “existing law” (defined in the initiative under Section 21028(r)(1) as “[f[ormally adopted legal requirements”) that protects CESA-listed species habitat, and that in turn means that impacts on that habitat would not be significant under the initiative, and so would not trigger mitigation requirements. In other words, the CEQA protections for endangered species habitat would be gone. Of course, perhaps CESA still provides protections here – either by interpreting the existing CESA language to cover habitat modification, or alternatively by amending CESA. But that’s a gamble I personally would not want to take.
And note that even if the mandatory findings of significance do count as existing law, they may well not satisfy the objective standard in the initiative that is necessary for judicial review of agency compliance with the revised CEQA procedures – in other words, an agency could still eliminate endangered species habitat without any possibility of litigation under CEQA.
(By the way, you may wonder if CESA-listed species that are also protected under the federal ESA would still have their habitat protected under the ESA. Not if the Trump Admnistration has its way and repeals the relevant provision of the ESA regulations! (https://legal-planet.org/2025/04/23/whats-the-harm/))
This is but one example. My guess is that there are many more in state environmental law where the loss of CEQA will destabilize the protections provided to a range of important resources: clean water, clean air, wetlands, endangered species, and more. For instance, it is possible that without CEQA, there might be substantial additional conversion of agricultural lands to other uses. As another example, air quality districts often use thresholds of significance for determining whether cumulative air quality impacts from projects are substantial. But, as noted above, it is not clear that those thresholds of significance will actually be relevant going forward for projects covered by this initiative. And since CEQA is generally the primary tool to address cumulative environmental impacts under California environmental law, that might mean that cumulative air quality impacts will no longer be regulated under state environmental law. That could be a huge issue for communities near major industrial sources, freeways, and ports, often with high proportions of Latino and African-American residents and low incomes, communities that face significantly worse air quality than most communities in the state.
And the potential gaps in underlying protection are important because, if CEQA review is going to be much lighter (if it exists at all) for a whole lot of projects, then those other protections will matter a whole more. Understanding the on-the-ground impact of this initiative requires understanding how state environmental law will operate with much less CEQA review, and that is very unclear.
What about the possibility that local land-use regulations might restrict the scope of what development is enabled by the initiative? Even if CEQA review is sped up (or essentially eliminated) by the initiative, wouldn’t local land-use regulations provide a check on what might occur?
The answer is . . . maybe. But probably less than one might expect. That is first because local governments vary greatly in their attitude towards individual projects, and their underlying zoning will vary a lot as well. So making generalizations here is hard. In major urban and suburban areas, there is a lot of single-family only zoning that will constrain development – but there are also areas without that zoning. In addition, as I noted earlier, the initiative appears to apply to rezoning decisions by local governments that apply to covered projects. Thus, while the local government may still have to do a rezone (or other zoning decision) to allow a project to proceed, the traditional CEQA review process would not apply to that rezoning decision – the new one would. And as noted throughout these blog posts, that might have sweeping implications.
Overall, the problem is really the uncertainty. But given the lock-in provision of the initiative, which prohibits the legislature from making amendments without a 2/3 majority, the legislature will be hamstrung in its ability to respond to any unintended consequences of this initiative.

The November elections are around the corner and an important voter initiative will be on the ballot: Building an Affordable California Act (BACA, also known as Proposition 45). BACA would fundamentally change how environmental review under the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) is conducted for qualifying “essential projects” by (i) providing for greater predictability via vested CEQA standards, (ii) establishing accelerated CEQA review timelines, and (iii) reducing CEQA litigation risks.
BACA would not create a new CEQA exemption or limit a public agency’s authority to approve or disapprove a qualifying project. Rather, it would establish a streamlining mechanism that would expedite CEQA review and entitlement processing for qualifying projects.
BACA, which is sponsored by the California Chamber of Commerce, requires approval by a majority of the voters. Recent polling shows that approximately 73% of likely voters support this initiative.
Which Projects Would Qualify?
BACA would apply to a broad range of “essential projects,” including:
Most housing developments, including student and senior housing
Public streets and highways
Solar, wind, and geothermal energy facilities
Public water system infrastructure
Educational facilities
Broadband internet access projects
The essential project categories also include any ancillary public, private, and utility infrastructure and public service facilities, such as electric, telecommunication, gas, water, wastewater, stormwater, transit, police, fire, and transportation improvements. BACA would also expressly allow for phased project applications. If a project application was submitted prior to BACA’s effective date and has not yet been approved, it could be withdrawn and resubmitted to invoke BACA’s benefits.
Because the statutory definition of “essential project” is broad, questions remain regarding the scope of qualifying projects.
Labor and Tribal Consultation Requirements
Generally, essential projects that utilize BACA would be subject to prevailing wage requirements, with the exception of housing development projects at or below 85 feet in height. Essential projects would also be subject to specified tribal consultation requirements.
Significant Changes
1. CEQA Standards Would be Vested
BACA would effectively freeze the applicable CEQA standards for essential projects. Public agencies would be required to evaluate and mitigate impacts based on compliance with standards that “existed and were in effect on the date an application for an essential project was submitted.”
2. CEQA Review Would be Based on “Existing Laws”
BACA would require public agencies to evaluate and mitigate environmental impacts for essential projects based on “existing laws,” which include formally adopted legal requirements contained in statutes, regulations, rules, standards, or ordinances. As discussed below, judicial review of essential projects would be based on compliance with “objective existing laws.” Therefore, it is expected that public agencies would be limited to imposing existing laws that are objective in the first instance, even though that is not specified. “Objective” laws involve no personal or subjective judgment and are uniformly verifiable by reference to an external and uniform benchmark or criterion.
Currently, public agencies often rely on guidance documents, scientific standards, technical studies, and agency expertise that are subjective and/or uncodified, meaning they likely would not qualify as “existing laws” under BACA. If BACA passes, we anticipate that public agencies will codify their preferred objective environmental standards, including thresholds of significance, to ensure they are enforceable under this new framework. The “existing laws” standard may reduce the scope of available significance thresholds and potential environmental impacts under CEQA for essential projects.
3. Project Review and Judicial Timelines Would be Accelerated
BACA would establish and reinforce mandatory timelines for CEQA compliance, some of which are already codified under existing law:
Certification of an Environmental Impact Report (EIR) within 365 business days after an application is deemed complete.
Adoption of a Negative Declaration (ND) or Mitigated Negative Declaration (MND) within 180 business days after an application is deemed complete.
Completion of other CEQA compliance (e.g., exemption determination) within 90 business days after an application is deemed complete.
If these deadlines are not met, BACA provides that the applicant must have the option to request a review meeting or hearing, which must be held within 60 days. Importantly, the public agency would be required to approve or deny the project – not just the CEQA document for the project – during that meeting or hearing. BACA also provides that any failure to meet the foregoing deadlines could be challenged in court.
Other applicable timelines include the following:
Application completeness determination within 30 calendar days of submission. If that deadline is missed, the project application would automatically be deemed complete. This requirement should also benefit essential projects not subject to CEQA compliance (e.g., projects approved ministerially).
Preliminary CEQA scoping within 60 calendar days.
Determine whether a project requires an EIR, ND, MND, CEQA exemption, or other CEQA document within 30 days after the application is deemed complete.
Public comment periods for an ND/MND and EIR would be fixed at 20 days and 45 days, respectively, with no opportunity for extensions or tolling.
Legal actions challenging an essential project would need to be completed within 270 days, including both original and appellate proceedings.
4. The EIR Alternatives Analysis Would be Narrowed
BACA would substantially narrow the required alternatives analysis for essential projects. Typically, CEQA requires that an EIR address a reasonable range of alternatives. Under BACA, applicants could opt into a preliminary scoping process, after which they would be able to develop a single project alternative that is “compatible with the proposed essential project’s fundamental purpose.” The EIR would only need to analyze the project, the no-project alternative, and the alternative developed by the applicant.
5. Judicial Review Would be Narrowed
Under BACA, a petitioner challenging an essential project may only assert claims relating to noncompliance with “objective existing laws,” and a court may only evaluate whether the project approvals comply with such laws. This requirement is expected to reduce the range of CEQA claims available to project opponents by focusing litigation on objective legal compliance rather than public agency judgment or subjective environmental standards.
Additionally, BACA provides that a court may only evaluate whether an essential project “is supported by substantial evidence in light of the whole record.” This appears to supplant the less-deferential fair argument standard for a ND/MND.
6. Judicial Remedies Would be Significantly Limited
BACA would also substantially reduce the remedies available to CEQA petitioners. Most notably, courts would no longer be authorized to rescind project approvals for essential projects in the event of a successful legal challenge. Instead, judges would only be able to direct public agencies to correct the deficiencies in the project approvals. The “noncomplying part, phase, or activity” would be prohibited from moving forward while the public agency takes remedial action, but the remainder of the project would technically be allowed to proceed.
This represents a major departure from the current state of affairs, where courts often set aside project approvals due to CEQA noncompliance. By eliminating that possibility, BACA would likely reduce the effectiveness of CEQA challenges to essential projects.
7. The Administrative Record Would be Limited
BACA would also narrow the scope of the administrative record for legal challenges to essential projects. “Late hit” electronic and written comments received less than 48 hours before the public hearing would not be included in the administrative record, meaning those comments could not serve as a basis for legal claims against the essential project. Verbal testimony made at a public hearing would still be included.
What this Means for Developers
If approved, BACA would be one of the most consequential reforms to CEQA in decades. It would provide developers with greater certainty during the entitlement and CEQA compliance phases of the development cycle.
Notably, BACA contains many provisions that are subject to interpretation. The breadth of the “essential project” categories, the scope of the “existing laws” framework, and the interaction between BACA and existing land use and environmental statutes are expected to generate ambiguity regarding the reach of the initiative. These topics will need to be vetted and may be the subject of future litigation. BACA provides that it should be interpreted “to afford the fullest possible weight to the interest of, and the approval and realization of, essential projects.” Additionally, courts may not interpret BACA to impose additional procedural or substantive requirements upon essential projects that are not enumerated in the text of the initiative itself.
Developers should evaluate how BACA could affect their entitlement strategy, application timing, and CEQA compliance. CEQA Reform Qualifies for the Ballot: What to Know About the Building an Affordable California Act
July 15, 2026 - E-Alerts (https://www.rutan.com/category/e-alerts/)
Back to Top

On June 25, 2026, the Building an Affordable California Act (“BACA”), a statewide measure sponsored by the California Chamber of Commerce, officially qualified for the November 2026 General Election ballot. The initiative will appear on California ballots this November as Prop 45. If passed by voters, BACA would reform the California Environmental Quality Act (“CEQA”) to create a broad category of “essential projects” that are entitled to a narrower environmental review process, the option to engage in a streamlined project alternatives analysis and more limited judicial review in the event of a project challenge. Early polling shows BACA garnering significant support among California voters, with 73 percent of likely voters indicating their support for the measure in a recently released poll.
BACA Streamlines Environmental Review for Essential Projects
BACA applies only to developments that qualify as “essential projects.” Specifically included are “essential housing projects,” which the law defines as housing projects including residential units only, residential mixed-use projects, commercial-to-residential conversions, subdivisions consisting of residential units or unimproved residential lots, and a number of specific housing categories including transitional housing, student housing, and senior housing. Other types of essential projects include qualifying water, clean energy, public health, public safety, broadband Internet access, education facility, and transportation projects. Essential projects utilizing BACA’s CEQA review provisions, except for housing projects under 85 feet above grade, must pay prevailing wages to all construction workers.
BACA would modify certain procedures and time limits for environmental review of essential projects. First, agencies will have 30 days to determine whether an essential project application is complete. If the agency fails to meet the completeness deadline, then the essential project application will automatically be deemed complete.
Once an agency has determined whether the project will require an Environmental Impact Report (“EIR”), Mitigated Negative Declaration (“MND”) or negative declaration, or than an exemption applies, the measure imposes various deadlines for the agency to make a final determination, which run from the date the application is deemed complete: 365 business days to certify an EIR, 180 business days to adopt a negative declaration, and 90 business days to make a final exemption determination. If the agency fails to meet these deadlines in making a final determination, the applicant has the option of requesting a meeting or hearing, which the agency would be required to hold within 60 days and either approve or deny the project at the meeting, and thereafter maintains an express right to challenge the agency’s failure in court. The measure also converts the existing minimum public comment periods for CEQA documents into fixed maximums that can only be extended by court order – 20 days for an MND or negative declaration and 45 days for an EIR.
Many of these deadlines are not entirely new. Existing law already generally requires agencies to determine application completeness within 30 days and complete EIRs and MNDs within certain timelines. What BACA changes is that its deadlines run in business days rather than calendar days, apply to all essential project approvals — including legislative approvals such as general plan amendments and zone changes, which current deadlines do not reach — and, most significantly, are enforceable in court.
BACA Allows for a Streamlined Alternatives Analysis and Mandates Narrower Review of Project Impacts
In addition to the new deadlines, BACA allows essential project applicants to opt-in to a preliminary scoping process that once completed allows for a simplified project alternatives analysis. In place of CEQA’s standard requirement to study a “reasonable range” of project alternatives, the streamlined analysis need only address three options: the proposed project itself, a no-project alternative, and single on-site project alternative.
Notably, BACA requires public agencies to evaluate a project’s environmental impacts – including the significance of the impacts and potential ways to mitigate them – based on the project’s compliance with “existing laws.” Under BACA’s definition of existing laws, this restricts the agency in evaluating the project’s compliance with formally adopted written standards that existed and were in effect when the project application was submitted. This appears to be a significant change, because under CEQA as it exists today, an agency has substantial discretion to determine whether a project’s impacts are significant and may resort to many different sources of information in making those determinations, some of which might qualify as “existing laws” but many of which likely don’t. For example, currently, agencies can develop thresholds to determine whether a project’s impacts are significant on a project-by-project basis; and even if no written legal standards exist concerning a particular type of impact, agencies often rely on new scientific studies, new information raised in public comments, and agency standards developed after the project was submitted in defining project impacts. Under BACA, an agency’s discretion to formulate project-specific thresholds or to rely on non-objective or post-submittal information appears to be sharply curtailed, which may reduce the number of project impacts an agency may determine as significant in the course of the review process.
BACA Limits Judicial Review of Essential Projects
BACA also limits the scope of judicial review of essential project approvals. Opponents who challenge an approval of an essential project under BACA would be limited to challenging the approval on the grounds that the lead agency did not comply with existing laws and objective standards in place at the time the application was submitted. And regardless of the level of environmental review undertaken on an essential project – e.g., whether an EIR versus an MND was prepared – a court reviewing a challenge to a project approval is required to determine “only” whether the approval is supported by substantial evidence. This appears aimed at displacing the more petitioner-friendly “fair argument” standard that currently governs challenges to MNDs and negative declarations.
Finally, even if a court finds that an agency’s approval of an essential project was defective, the court may not rescind the entire approval. Instead, the court is limited to enjoining only the part of the development impacted by the agency’s non-compliance until it is corrected.
Looking Ahead to November
BACA will head to the November ballot with a significant financial and organizational head start, bolstered by a strong showing in initial polling. A public opinion poll released by the Public Policy Institute of California in July showed 73 percent of likely California voters supporting the measure. Some notable supporters of the measure include the California Building Industry Association, the California Hospital Association, NAACP California and Pacific Gas & Electric, and of course its sponsor, the California Chamber of Commerce. The measure has also attracted a notable Democratic endorsement from Assemblymember Buffy Wicks, the author of the Legislature’s landmark 2025 infill housing CEQA exemption. The Committee to Build an Affordable California, the CalChamber-led campaign committee, reported nearly $13.8 million in contributions through the first quarter of 2026 — including $10 million from Building a Better California, a committee funded largely by Silicon Valley donors, and $2 million from Edison International.
However, opposition is beginning to organize. The State Building and Construction Trades Council and the Sierra Club of California have announced their opposition. The lead opposition committee, One Voice for California, has raised over $4 million from the Trades Council and environmental advocacy organizations since the committee was opened last month. Notably, while several other initiatives were withdrawn from the November ballot in eleventh-hour deals with the Legislature and rival interest groups, no such compromise emerged on BACA.

Prop 45 FAQ: Frequently Asked Questions
Updated October 26, 2026
What is Prop 45?
Prop 45 is a proposed ballot measure (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/45/analysis.htm) that modernizes California’s outdated approval process to build essential projects faster and more affordably. Prop 45 achieves this through ten key reforms (https://yesonprop45.com/read-the-measure/):
Enforceable Timelines: Agencies must approve or deny project applications within 365 days (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=45&year=2026). If they miss the deadline, applicants can request a public hearing or workshop , where a final decision must be made within 60 days .
Objective Standards for Agencies: Agencies must base their review on clear, written rules—like local ordinances, environmental laws or zoning standards—that were in place when the application was submitted.
Guaranteed Public Input: Establishes a firm 45-day public comment period with written responses to all timely comments—ensuring public participation and accountability.
Streamlined, Smarter Alternatives: Narrows the “alternatives” requirement to two: one feasible alternative project design that reduces environmental impacts, and one describing a “no project” scenario.
Judicial Shot Clock: Courts must fully resolve legal challenges within 270 days.
Fix What’s Broken: If one part of an environmental review document is rejected, only that section must be fixed—allowing the rest of the project to move forward on schedule.
Objective Standards for Courts: Courts may only overturn project approvals if agencies ignore clear, written rules—like zoning or environmental standards—that were in place when the application was submitted.
Evidence-Based Review: Courts must uphold a project’s approval if the agency’s decision was supported by substantial evidence.
Strong Worker Protections: Projects built under Prop 45 must meet California’s strongest-in-the-nation labor standards, including fair pay and safe job sites.
Tribal Protections: Protects and strengthens government-to-government consultation by ensuring early tribal engagement, incorporating Tribal Traditional Knowledge, and enhancing confidentiality protections.
By streamlining the permitting process and reducing frivolous lawsuits, these reforms will ensure California is building the essential projects that are critical for our quality of life and our economy—reducing costs and helping make our state more affordable.
Learn more:
What the Building an Affordable California Act Means, Practically (https://yesonprop45.com/2026/01/22/what-the-building-an-affordable-california-act-means-practically/), a legal analysis by Hanson Bridgett attorneys Sean Marciniak and Niran Somasundaram
Why is Prop 45 needed?
Prop 45 reforms California’s outdated approval system so California can build faster and lower costs. California’s cost of living is out of control because we’re failing to deliver the basics. Our outdated system for approving essential projects (https://www.hklaw.com/-/media/files/insights/publications/2026/09/hernandez_2026ceqastudy.pdf)—including housing, water systems, clean energy, roads, schools, and hospitals—is too slow, too bureaucratic, and too costly. Delays drive up costs, and those costs are passed on to renters, homebuyers, people paying electricity and water bills, and taxpayers. Delays also mean higher wildfire risk (https://www.latimes.com/environment/story/2025-11-25/cal-fire-approach-to-socals-wildfire-crisis-could-make-things-worse-court-says), more traffic congestion, overcrowded schools, aging hospitals, and slower progress toward California’s climate goals.
Learn more:
ICYMI: New 11-Year Study Finds CEQA Litigation Increasingly Tying Up Housing and Essential Infrastructure, with Housing the No. 1 Target (https://yesonprop45.com/2026/09/24/icymi-new-11-year-study-finds-ceqa-litigation-increasingly-tying-up-housing-and-essential-infrastructure-with-housing-the-no-1-target/) (Yes on 45 press release on the Holland & Knight study)
After 50 Years, California Voters Have a Chance to Fix CEQA (https://yesonprop45.com/2026/09/08/after-50-years-california-voters-have-a-chance-to-fix-ceqa/) (Beyond Green Jim Crow)
What kinds of projects does Prop 45 apply to?
Prop 45 applies only to essential projects (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=45&year=2026) Californians need to lower costs, improve our quality of life and keep our economy moving. The projects eligible for streamlining are:
Housing: New single-family homes, apartments, senior and student housing, supportive and farmworker housing, and conversion of commercial buildings for residential use.
Public Health: Hospitals, community clinics, and medical office facilities that expand access to care.
Clean Energy: Solar, wind, geothermal, clean hydrogen, battery storage, fuel cells, clean carbon capture, upgrades to the electric grid, transmission lines, and EV charging networks.
Water Infrastructure: Water-quality treatment, groundwater recharge, water recycling and desalination plants, dams, stormwater capture, and other projects that deliver safe drinking water and strengthen California’s drought resilience.
Education Facilities: K–12 schools, community colleges, public and private nonprofit colleges and universities, including CSU/UC campuses, labs, and student support facilities.
Public Safety & Wildfire Resilience: Fire and police stations, vegetation management, undergrounding utilities, home hardening, and fuel break maintenance.
Transportation: Road repairs, bridges, public transit expansions, bike and pedestrian safety projects, and electric vehicle infrastructure.
Broadband & Digital Access: Fiber-optic and wireless broadband projects connecting underserved and rural communities.
Learn more:
What the Building an Affordable California Act Means, Practically (https://yesonprop45.com/2026/01/22/what-the-building-an-affordable-california-act-means-practically/), a legal analysis by Hanson Bridgett attorneys Sean Marciniak and Niran Somasundaram
How will Prop 45 help bring down the cost of living?
By creating enforceable timelines, streamlining approvals, and reducing frivolous lawsuits, Prop 45 helps build essential projects faster and more affordably. Lengthy delays (https://yesonprop45.com/case-studies/) force Californians to wait longer and pay more for needed housing, energy, water, and other essential infrastructure. For example, permitting delays add more than $75,000 to the cost of a new home (https://yesonprop45.com/cost-of-delay-per-home/) and billions to the cost of hospitals, water systems, roads, bridges, and clean energy projects (https://yesonprop45.com/report-2026-09-25-economic-and-fiscal-impacts-of-proposition-45/). Those higher costs are ultimately paid by renters, homebuyers, utility customers, and taxpayers.
Learn more:
NEW REPORT: Prop 45 Will Deliver 200,000 More Homes and Save Taxpayers and Ratepayers Billions (https://yesonprop45.com/2026/09/30/new-reportprop-45-will-deliver-200000-more-homes-and-save-taxpayers-and-ratepayers-billions/) (Yes on 45 press release)
Affordable Housing Leaders Unite Behind Prop 45 to Lower Housing Costs and Build the Homes Californians Need (https://yesonprop45.com/2026/10/02/affordable-housing-leaders-unite-behind-prop-45-to-lower-housing-costs-and-build-the-homes-californians-need/) (Yes on 45 press release)
Does Prop 45 weaken environmental laws?
No . Prop 45 does not weaken or eliminate any environmental law (https://www.hansonbridgett.com/publications/260730_2100_hb-letter-prop-45). Prop 45 simply modernizes the process—setting clear timelines, preventing frivolous lawsuits, and ensuring reviews are faster, more transparent, and focused on results. California can build the clean energy, housing, and infrastructure projects we need without sacrificing our air, water, or natural resources (https://yesonprop45.com/2026/08/20/https-advocacy-calchamber-com-2026-08-20-the-three-lies-prop-45-opponents-keep-telling-and-telling/).
Learn more:
Opinion: Vote ‘yes.’ Prop. 45 changes construction timelines, not our standards (https://yesonprop45.com/2026/09/12/opinion-vote-yes-prop-45-changes-construction-timelines-not-our-standards/), by Jennifer Capitolo, Executive Director, California Water Association (East Bay Times)
Does Prop 45 reduce local control or public input?
No . Under Prop 45, local governments keep full authority (https://www.hansonbridgett.com/publications/260730_2100_hb-letter-prop-45) to approve, deny or condition projects in their communities. Prop 45 simply ensures those decisions are made within one year—not after years of delay. Prop 45 preserves public participation through a 45-day public comment period and written responses to all timely comments. Communities continue to decide what gets built, where it gets built, and under what conditions—with a faster, fairer, and more accountable process.
Learn more:
Why Prop 45 Is Good for Menifee and Surrounding Region (https://yesonprop45.com/2026/08/31/why-prop-45-is-good-for-menifee-and-surrounding-region/), by Katie Luna (The Valley Business Journal)
How does Prop 45 strengthen tribal consultation rights?
Prop 45 protects and strengthens tribal consultation by requiring early engagement with California Indian tribes before project applications are submitted, incorporating Tribal Traditional Knowledge, and enhancing confidentiality protections—all while fully respecting tribal sovereignty and the government-to-government consultation process (https://yesonprop45.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Prop-45-Tribal-Fact-Sheet-8.19.26.pdf).
Learn more:
What the Building an Affordable California Act Means, Practically (https://yesonprop45.com/2026/01/22/what-the-building-an-affordable-california-act-means-practically/), a legal analysis by Hanson Bridgett attorneys Sean Marciniak and Niran Somasundaram
What worker protections are included in Prop 45?
Under Prop 45, every essential project must meet California’s strongest labor standards—including fair pay, safe working conditions, and skilled-and-trained workforce requirements. Essential housing projects must meet California’s strong labor standards under AB 130 (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260ab130), and all other essential projects must comply with ELDP-level labor requirements (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PRC&sectionNum=21183).
Learn more:
What the Building an Affordable California Act Means, Practically (https://yesonprop45.com/2026/01/22/what-the-building-an-affordable-california-act-means-practically/), a legal analysis by Hanson Bridgett attorneys Sean Marciniak and Niran Somasundaram
Does Prop 45 eliminate the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA)?
No . CEQA (https://oag.ca.gov/environment/ceqa) remains fully in place under Prop 45. Prop 45 simply streamlines how CEQA is applied to essential projects by setting clear timelines, enforceable rules to provide predictability and accountability, and establishing a faster, evidence-based process for litigation. Prop 45 ensures CEQA works as it was intended—to protect the environment, not to block progress on essential projects.
Learn more:
Opinion: Vote ‘yes.’ Prop. 45 changes construction timelines, not our standards (https://yesonprop45.com/2026/09/12/opinion-vote-yes-prop-45-changes-construction-timelines-not-our-standards/), by Jennifer Capitolo, Executive Director, California Water Association (East Bay Times)
How does Prop 45 help the environment?
Prop 45 accelerates the very projects that will help California protect the environment and fight climate change. By cutting red tape for clean energy, water, and wildfire prevention (https://yesonprop45.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Prop-45-Environmental-Fact-Sheet-8.19.26.pdf), it reduces pollution, protects water supplies, and lowers carbon emissions. Prop 45 helps California build a cleaner, safer, and more sustainable future—faster.
Learn more:
Clean Energy Leaders Unite Behind YES on Prop 45 (https://yesonprop45.com/2026/03/26/clean-energy-leaders-unite-behind-building-an-affordable-california-act/) (Yes on 45 press release)
Former U.S. Energy Secretary Jennifer Granholm Endorses Prop 45 to Accelerate Clean Energy Development & Lower Cost of Living for Families (https://yesonprop45.com/2026/09/03/former-u-s-energy-secretary-jennifer-granholm-endorses-prop-45-to-accelerate-clean-energy-development-lower-cost-of-living-for-families/) (Yes on 45 press release)
We don’t improve public safety by delaying public safety projects (https://yesonprop45.com/2026/08/01/californians-have-a-rare-chance-to-rein-in-ceqa-and-support-housing-2/), by Ruben Grijalva, former State Fire Marshal and director of CAL FIRE (Orange County Register)
Could Prop 45 lead to unchecked development?
No . Prop 45 applies only to essential projects and keeps in place every existing protection for California’s most sensitive and protected lands. Every project must meet local zoning, land-use, and public review requirements (https://www.hansonbridgett.com/publications/260730_2100_hb-letter-prop-45). Prop 45 simply ensures those reviews happen on a clear, predictable schedule—delivering accountability and transparency, not exemptions or shortcuts—so California can build responsibly and affordably.
Learn more:
Proposition 45, its Implementation, and Its Benefits to Public Agencies (https://yesonprop45.com/2026/07/30/environment-a-factor-in-governors-race-us-house-races-2/), a letter to public agencies by Michael Conneran, Partner, Hanson Bridgett
How is Prop 45 different from other recent CEQA reforms?
Prop 45 does not exempt any projects from CEQA. Instead, it provides comprehensive reform—a uniform, statewide system that speeds up approvals while maintaining every environmental and labor protection. Past reforms have focused on providing narrow exemptions for select projects (https://www.latimes.com/homeless-housing/story/2025-07-01/what-will-the-new-change-to-ceqa-do).
Learn more:
CEQA is standing in the way of the California Dream (https://yesonprop45.com/2026/10/05/ceqa-is-standing-in-the-way-of-the-california-dream/), by Kristian Fors, Independent Institute (Orange County Register)
Ballot measure would broaden reform of California’s key environmental law (https://yesonprop45.com/2025/10/23/ballot-measure-would-broaden-reform-of-californias-key-environmental-law/) (CalMatters)
Why is Prop 45 on the ballot?
Prop 45 is on the ballot (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop45-title-summ-analysis.pdf) because, for decades, efforts to modernize California’s outdated permitting system have stalled (https://calmatters.org/environment/2018/08/brown-talks-ceqa-reform-but-hasnt-done-it/) while housing, healthcare, electricity, and infrastructure costs continued to rise. Prop 45 gives voters the opportunity to take a truly comprehensive approach—streamlining approvals for essential projects Californians need while maintaining California’s strong environmental and labor protections.
Learn more:
The debate over Prop. 45 is about California’s building future. Here is our endorsement (https://yesonprop45.com/2026/10/05/the-debate-over-prop-45-is-about-californias-building-future-here-is-our-endorsement-opinion/), by McClatchy’s California editorial board (https://yesonprop45.com/newspaper-endorsements/#mcclatchy-california) (The Sacramento Bee, Fresno Bee, Modesto Bee, Merced Sun-Star and San Luis Obispo Tribune)
Endorsement: Yes on Prop. 45 to reform CEQA, limit state dysfunction (https://yesonprop45.com/2026/09/11/endorsement-yes-on-prop-45-to-reform-ceqa-limit-state-dysfunction/), by The San Diego Union-Tribune editorial board
After 50 Years, California Voters Have a Chance to Fix CEQA (https://yesonprop45.com/2026/09/08/after-50-years-california-voters-have-a-chance-to-fix-ceqa/) (Beyond Green Jim Crow)
Does Prop 45 streamline data centers?
ICYMI: New Legislative Counsel Opinion Reinforces Legal Conclusion That Prop 45 Does Not Cover Data Centers (https://yesonprop45.com/2026/10/20/icymi-new-legislative-counsel-opinion-reinforces-legal-conclusion-that-prop-45-does-not-cover-data-centers/) (Yes on 45 press release)
Prop 45 Does Not Cover Data Centers—Here’s Why (https://yesonprop45.com/2026/10/02/prop-45-does-not-cover-data-centersheres-why/), by Kurt Oneto, the official proponent of Prop 45 (National Law Review)
California’s Proposition 45 Does Not Cover Data Centers (https://yesonprop45.com/2026/08/19/https-www-dailyjournal-com-article-393806-california-s-proposition-45-does-not-cover-data-centers/), by Rachelle Chong, former Commissioner of the Federal Communications Commission and California Public Utilities Commission (Daily Journal)
The Three Lies Prop 45 Opponents Keep Telling and Telling (https://yesonprop45.com/2026/08/20/https-advocacy-calchamber-com-2026-08-20-the-three-lies-prop-45-opponents-keep-telling-and-telling/) (CalChamber)
No on 45 Campaign Ad Spreads Lies, Lies, and More Lies (https://yesonprop45.com/2026/09/25/no-on-45-campaign-ad-spreads-lies-lies-and-more-lies/) (Yes on 45 press release)
